sourceDefinition: The first of a series of eight words comprising the letters of the Arabic alphabet [ in the order in which they were originally disposed, agreeing with that of the Hebrew and Aramaic, but with six additional letters: they are variously written and pronounced; generally as follows: A^abojada haw~azo HuT~iY kalamano saEofaSo qara$ato vaxa*o DaZago : but the Arabs of Western Africa write the latter four thus: SEfD qrst vx* Zg$ ]: (K and TA in art. bjd : [in both of which are related several fables concerning the origin of these words:]) accord. to the general opinion, the word Abjd is of foreign origin, [like each of the words following it,] and therefore its first letter [as well as each of the others] is a radical. (TA.) [Hence, AlA^abojadu signifies The alphabet. You say Huruwfu AlA^abojadi The letters of the alphabet. ― -b2- It is probable (as De Sacy has observed in his Ar. Gram., 2nd ed., i. 8,) that the Arabic alphabet originally consisted of only twenty-two letters: for some of the ancient Arabs called Saturday Abjd , Sunday hwz~ , and so on to qr$t inclusive; calling Friday Earuwbapu . ― -b3- In the lexicon entitled “El-'Eyn,” the letters of the alphabet are arranged nearly according to their places of utterance; as follows: E , H , h , x , g , q , k , j , $ , D , S , s , z , T , d , t , Z , * , v , r , l , n , f , b , m , w , A , Y : and this order has been followed in the Tahdheeb and Mohkam and some other lexicons.]

definition: A kind of trees;
sourceDefinition: A kind of trees; (S, K;) a species of the TarofaA=' [or tamarisk; so applied in the present day; termed by Forskål (Flora Aeg. Arab. p. lxiv.) tamarix orientalis ]; (S, TA;) or a kind of trees, (T, M,) or a certain tree, (Mgh,) resembling the TrfA=' , (T, M, Mgh,) except that it is of a better kind, (T,) or except that it is larger, and better in its wood, (M,) of which are made yellow and excellent [ vessels of the kind called ] A^aqodaAH , and of which was made the Prophet's pulpit; it has thick stems, of which are made doors and other things; and its leaves are of the kind called Eabal , like those of the TrfA=' : (TA:) AHn says, on the authority of Aboo-Ziyád, that it is of the kind termed EiDaAh , tail, and long in its wood, which is excellent, and is carried to the towns and villages, and the clay houses of these are built upon it; [app. meaning that its wood is used in forming the foundations of the walls;] its leaves are of the kind called hadab , [syn. with Eabal ,] long and slender, and it has no thorns; of it are made [bowls of the kinds called ] qiSaAE and jifaAn ; and it has a red fruit, like a knot of a rope: (M:) or a kind of large trees, having no fruit: (Msb:) or i. q. TrfA=' , having no fruit: (Bd in xxxiv. 15:) n. un. with p ; (S, M, Msb, K;) explained in the A as the samurap [or gum-acacia tree ]: or a tall, straight [ tree such as is termed ] EiDaAhap , of which are made the like of A^aqodaAH : (TA:) the pl. [of A^avolN ] is A^uvuwlN (M, K) and [of A^avolapN ] A^avalaAvN . (S, K, TA (in the CK AavolAtN ].) ― -b2- [See also A^avolapN , below.] -A2- fulaAnN A^avolu maAlK Such a one is a collector of wealth, or property. (Ibn-'Abbád.)

definition: n. un. of A^avolN , q. v. (S, M, &c.) Because of the tallness of the tree thus called, and its erectness, and beauty of proportion, the poets liken thereto a woman of perfect stature and erect form....
sourceDefinition: n. un. of A^avolN , q. v. (S, M, &c.) Because of the tallness of the tree thus called, and its erectness, and beauty of proportion, the poets liken thereto a woman of perfect stature and erect form. (M.) ― -b2- Metaphorically, (Msb,) (tropical:) Honour, or reputation; or grounds of pretension to respect on account of the honourable deeds or qualities of one's ancestors, &c.; syn. EiroDN ; (Msb, TA;) or HasabN (S, O, K, TA.) So in the saying, fulaAnN yanoHitu A^avolatanaA , or yanoHatu , (S accord. to different copies, and so in the O, but in the copies of the K, incorrectly, yanoHatu fiY A^avolatinaA , TA,) (tropical:) Such a one speaks evil of, (S, O,) or impugns, or speaks against, (K,) our honour, or reputation, &c. (S, O, K.) And naHata A^avolatahu (tropical:) He detracted from his reputation; spoke against him; impugned his character; censured him; blamed him. (A, Msb.) And fulaAnN tunoHatu A^avalaAtuhu (tropical:) [ Such a one's grounds of pretension to respect, &c., are impugned ]. (TA.) And huwa laA tunoHatu A^avolatuhu (tropical:) He has not any vice, or fault, nor any imperfection, or defect. (Msb.) ― -b3- The root, foundation, origin, source, stock, or the like, syn. A^SolN ; (T, S, M, Mgh, K;) of a thing, and of a man; (T;) of anything; (M;) [ a source, stock, or fund, ] of wealth, or property: (Mgh, TA:) pl. A_ivaAlN . (K.) So in the saying, lahu A^avlapu maAlK [ He has a source, or stock, or fund, of wealth, or property ]. (TA.) ― -b4- Victuals, or provision; syn. miyrapN (M, K.) ― -b5- The goods, furniture, and utensils, of a house or tent; as also ↓ A^avalapN . (M, K. *) ― -b6- Apparatus, accoutrements, implements, or the like. (Ibn-' Abbád, K.) So in the saying, A^axa*otu A^avolapa Al$~itaA='i [ I took the apparatus, &c., of, i. e. for, the winter ]. (Ibn- ' Abbád.)

definition: (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ A^udomN (the same except the K) [ Seasoning, or condiment, for bread;
sourceDefinition: (T, S, M, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ A^udomN (the same except the K) [ Seasoning, or condiment, for bread; and any savoury food; ] what is used for seasoniny ( maA yuw^otadamu bihi , T, S, M, * Mgh, Msb, K) with bread; (T, TA;) that which renders bread pleasant and good and savoury; (IAmb, Mgh;) whether fluid or not fluid; (Mgh, Msb;) SibogN and SibaAgN being peculiarly applied to that which is fluid: (Mgh:) or A^udomN is anything that is eaten with bread: (TA:) the pl. [of mult.] of A_idaAmN is A^udumN , (Mgh, Msb,) and, by contraction, A^udomN , which is also used as the sing., (Msb,) and [pl. of pauc.] A=dimapN (M, K) and A=daAmN ; (K;) or this last is pl. of A^udomN . (M, Mgh, Msb, TA.) It is said in a trad., niEoma AlA_idaAmu Alxal~u [ Excellent, or most excel-lent, is the seasoning, vinegar! ]. (T, TA.) And in another, say~idu A=daAmi Ald~unoyaA waAlA=xirapi All~aHomu [ The prince of the seasonings of the present world and of the world to come is flesh-meat ]. (TA.) ― -b2- huwa A_idaAmu A^aholihi , and A_idaAmu qawomihi : see A^adamapN . ― -b3- Anything conforming, or conformable; agreeing, or agreeable; suiting, or suitable. (M, K.) [Used also as a pl.: thus,] 'Ádiyeh Ed-Dubeyreeyeh says, kaAnuwA limano xaAlaTahumo A_idaAmaA [ They were, to those who mixed with them in social intercourse, conformable, or agreeable. ] (M.)

definition: i. q. ↓ maA^oduwmN [ Seasoned ]: (T:) or TaEaAmN ↓ maA^oduwmN [ seasoned food ]; (M, K;) food in which is A_idaAm . (TA.) Hence the prov., samonukumo huriyqa fiY A^adiymikumo [ Your clarified butter...
sourceDefinition: i. q. ↓ maA^oduwmN [ Seasoned ]: (T:) or TaEaAmN ↓ maA^oduwmN [ seasoned food ]; (M, K;) food in which is A_idaAm . (TA.) Hence the prov., samonukumo huriyqa fiY A^adiymikumo [ Your clarified butter is poured into your seasoned food ]; (T, TA;) applied to a niggardly man; (Har p. 462;) meaning, your good, or wealth, returns unto you: (TA:) or, as some say, the meaning is, into your siqaA=' [or skin ]: (T, Har * ubi suprà:) and the vulgar say, fiY daqiyqikumo [ into your flour ]. (TA.) And the saying, samonuhumo fiY A^adiymihimo [ Their clarified butter is in their seasoned food ]; meaning, their good, or wealth, returns unto them. (M.) And the saying of Khadeejeh to the Prophet, A_in~aka latakosibu wa tuToEimu AlmaA^oduwma ↓ AlmaEoduwma (M, TA) Verily thou gainest what is denied to others, or makest others to gain what they have not, of the things they want, or makest the poor to gain, (TA in art. Edm ,) and givest to eat food in which is A_idaAm . (TA in the present art.) [Hence also,] A^aToEamotuka ↓ maA^oduwmiY (M, K) meaning A^atayotuka biEu*oriY [ I gave thee my excuse; or, perhaps, my virginity; see Eu*orapN ]: (K:) [or,] as some say, the meaning is, my good manners: said by the wife of Dureyd Ibn-Es-Simmeh, on the occasion of his divorcing her. (M, TA.) ― -b2- And hence, (Ham p. 205, Mgh,) Tanned skin or hide; leather: (M, Ham, Mgh, Msb:) or skin, or hide, (M, K,) in whatever state it be: (M:) or red skin or hide: (M, K:) or skin, or hide, in the state after that in which it is termed A^afiyqN ; that is, when it is complete [ in its tanning ] and has become red: (M:) or the exterior of the skin of anything: (T:) pl. [of pauc.] A=dimapN (S, M, K) and A=daAmN and [of mult.] A^udumN , (M, K,) the last from Lh, and [says ISd] I hold that he who says rusolN says A^udomN , (M,) and ↓ A^adamN , (T, S, Msb, K,) or this is a quasi-pl. n., (Sb, M, Mgh,) [often used as a gen. n.,] of which A=daAmN may be pl. (M.) ― -b3- Aiboni A^adiymK and Aibonu A^adiymayoni and Aibonu valaAvapi A=dimapK : see AibonN in art. bnY . One says, A_in~amaA yuEaAtabu AlA^adiymu *uw Alba$arapi [lit.] Only the hide that has the exterior part, upon which the hair grows, is put again into the tan: (T:) a prov.; (TA;) meaning, only he is disciplined, or reproved, who is an object of hope, and in whom is full intelligence, and strength; (T, TA, and AHn in TA, art. b$r [where, however, in the TA, duwna is erroneously put for *w ];) and only he is disputed with in whom is place for dispute. (TA.) ― -b4- A^adiymu AlHarobi is used metaphorically for A^adiymu A^aholi AlHarobi (tropical:) [ The skin of the warriors, or of the people engaged in war or fight ]. (M.) ― -b5- fulaAnN SaHiyHu AlA^adiymi [lit. Such a one is sound of skin ] means (tropical:) such a one is sound in respect of origin, and of honour, or reputation. (Har p. 135.) You say also, fulaAnN bariYo'u AlA^adiymi mim~aA luTixa bihi [meaning (tropical:) Such a one is clear in honour, or reputation, of that with which he has been aspersed ]. (M, * TA.) And ↓ maz~aqa A^adamiY (tropical:) He rent my honour, or reputation. (Har ubi suprà.) ― -b6- A^adiymN also signifies (tropical:) The surface of the earth or ground: (S, M:) [see also A^adamapN , last sentence:] or what appears thereof, (K,) and of the sky. (M, K.) ― -b7- And (tropical:) The first part of the period called AlD~uHaY . (M, K, TA.) You say, jiy^otuka A^adiyma AlD~uHaY (tropical:) I came to thee in the first part of the DHY ; (Lh, M;) app. meaning, Einoda A@rotifaAEi AlD~uHaY [ when the morning was becoming advanced; when the sun was becoming high ]. (M.) ― -b8- And (tropical:) The whiteness of day: (IAar, M, K, TA:) and (tropical:) the darkness of night: (IAar, M, TA:) or (tropical:) the whole of the day, (M, A, K, TA,) and of the night. (A, TA.) You say, Zal~a A^adiyma Aln~ahaAri SaAy^imFA waA^adiyma All~ayoli qaAy^imFA (tropical:) He continued the whole of the day fasting, and the whole of the night standing [in prayer, &c.]. (A, TA.)

A^udomN and ↓ A^udomaAnN ; (S, M, K;) the latter like HumoraAnN as a pl. of A^aHomaru : (M:) the fem. sing. is A^adomaA='u and ↓ A^udomaAnapN ; (S M, K;) the latter anomalous; (K;) occurring in poetry, but disapproved (S, M) by As; (S;) said by Aboo-'Alee to be like xumoSaAnapN ; (M;) and the fem. pl. is A^udomN : (S, M, K:) applied to a camel, of a colour intermixed, or tinged, with blackness, or with whiteness; or of a clear white; (M, K;) or, as some say, intensely white; (TA;) or white, and black in the eyeballs; (S;) or white; (As, T;) and so applied to a gazelle: (T:) or, applied to a gazelle, of a colour intermixed, or tinged, with whiteness; (M, K;) Lth, however, says that A^adomaA='u is applied to a female gazelle, but he had not heard A=damu applied to the male gazelle; (TA;) and As says, (S,) A^udomN applied to gazelles signifies white, having upon them streaks in which is a dust-colour, (S, M,) inhabiting the mountains, and of the colour of the mountains; (S;) if of a pure white colour, they are termed A=raAmN : (T, TA:) or, accord. to ISk, white in the bellies, tawny in the backs, and having the colour of the bellies and of the backs divided by two streaks of the colour of musk; and in like manner explained by IAar: (T:) applied to a human being, A=damu signifies tawny; or dark-complexioned; syn. A^asomaru ; (S, M, K;) or, thus applied, it signifies A^Homaru All~awoni [which, in this case, means white of complexion ]; (TA;) and the pl. is A^udomiAnN . (S.) The Arabs say, qurayo$u AlA_ibili A^udomuhaA waSuhobuhaA , meaning The best of camels are those of them which are A^udom and those of them which are Suhob ; [see A^aSohabu ;] like as Kureysh are the best of men. (M.) ― -b2- Also [ Adam, ] the father of mankind; (S, M, K;) and likewise ↓ A^adamu ; but this is extr.: (K:) there are various opinions respecting its derivation; but [these it is unnecessary to mention, for] the truth is that it is a foreign word, [i. e. Hebrew,] of the measure faAEalu , like A=zaru : (MF:) and [therefore] its pl. is A^awaAdimu . (S, M, K.)

sourceDefinition: (S, M, A,) aor. , inf. n. A^asorN (S, M, K) and A_isaArN , (M, TA,) He bound, braced, or tied, him, [namely, his captive,] or it, (S, M, A, K,) namely, his qatab [or camel's saddle], (S, A,) or his horse's saddle, (A,) with an A_isaAr , i. e. a thong of untanned hide, (S, A,) by tying the two extremities of the EaroquwotaAni of the camel's saddle, or of the curved pieces of wood of the horse's saddle. (A.) ― -b2- Also, aor. as above, and so the inf. n., i. e. A^asorN (S, Msb) and A_isaArN , (Lth, S,) He made him a captive; captived him; or took him a prisoner; whether he bound him with an A_isaAr or did not; (S;) as also ↓ A=srhu , of the same form as A^akorama ; (Msb;) and ↓ AstA^srhu , accord. to a trad., in which it occurs thus used, transitively: (Mgh:) and he imprisoned him. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b3- Also, (S, Msb,) inf. n. A^asorN , (Msb,) (assumed tropical:) He (God) created him, or formed him, (S, Msb,) in a goodly manner. (Msb.) You say, A^asarahu A@ll~`hu A^aHosana AlA^asori God created him, or formed him, in the best manner. (Fr, TA.) ― -b4- A^usira , (S, A,) aor. yuw^osaru ; (S;) or A^asira , aor. yaA^osaru ; (IKtt;) or A^usira bawoluhu ; (M;) inf. n. A^asorN , (M, and so in a copy of the S,) or the latter is a simple subst.; (M, IKtt;) He (a man, S, A) suffered suppression of his urine. (S, M, IKtt, A.) [See A^usorN , below.]

sourceDefinition: i. q. A_isaArN , q. v. (S.) Hence the saying, h`*aA Al$~aYo'u laka biA^asorihi This thing is for thee, or is thine, [lit.] with its thong of untanned hide [wherewith it is bound]; meaning, altogether; like as one says, birum~atihi . (S.) And xu*ohu biA^asorihi Take thou it all, or altogether. (Msb.) And jaA='a Alqawomu biA^asorihimo The people came altogether. (Aboo-Bekr.) ― -b2- Strength of make, or form. (M, K.) [Accord. to the copies of the K in my hands, it also signifies Strength of natural disposition; but instead of waAlxuluq , in those copies, we should read waAlxaloqu , agreeably with other lexicons, as is implied in the TA: see 1.] You say, fulaAnN $adiydN A^asorK Alxaloqi (tropical:) Such a one is of strong, firm, or compact, make, or form. (TA.) ― -b3- $adadonaA A^asorahumo , in the Kur [lxxvi. 28], means (tropical:) We have strengthened their make, or form: (S, A, Msb:) or, their joints: or, their two sphincters which serve as repressers of the urine and feces ( maSar~ataYi Albawoli wa AlgaAy^iTi ), which contract when the excrement has passed forth; or the meaning is, that these two things do not become relaxed before one desires. (IAar, K.)

(TK.) -A2- A^anafati AlA_ibilu , (inf. n. as above, TA,) The camels trod herbage, or pasture, such as is termed A^unuf , (ISk, S, K,) i. e., which had not been pastured upon. (S.) [But in the TT, as from the M, I find ↓ A=Anafa , (which should rather be written A^aAnafa , or, accord. to the more usual mode, A=nafa ,) He trod such herbage, or pasture. ] -A3- A^anifa , aor. , (S, M, K,) inf. n. A^anafN , (M,) He (a camel) had a complaint of, or suffered pain in, his nose, from the burap [or nose-ring ]: (S, M, K:) from ISk. (S.) ― -b2- A^anifati AlA_ibilu , accord. to certain of the Kilábees, means The flies alighted upon the noses of the camels, and they sought places which they did not seek before. (T.) ― -b3- A^anifa minohu , aor. , inf. n. A^anafN (S, M, Msb, K) and A^anafapN , (S, M, K,) or the latter is a simple subst., (Msb,) [ He turned up his nose at it; ] he disdained it; scorned it; abstained from it, or refused to do it, by reason of disdain and pride; (S, M, Msb, K;) he disliked it, or hated it, and his soul was above it; (L;) namely, a thing: (S, M, L, Msb:) and he shunned it, avoided it, or kept himself far from it: (Msb:) and he disliked it, or hated it; namely, a saying. (AZ, T, Msb.) You say, maAraA^ayotu A^aHomaY A^anafFA mino fulaAnK [ I have not seen any one more vehemently disdainful, or scornful, than such a one ]. (S.) And Hamala mino *`lika A^anafFA He conceived, in consequence of that, disdain, or scorn, arising from indignation and anger. (TA, from a trad.) [The verb is also trans. without mn : you say,] yaA^onafu A^ano yuDAma [ He disdains, or scorns, or refuses to bear, or to submit to, being injured ]. (K.) [When immediately trans.,] A^anifa also signifies He loathed, disliked, or regarded with disgust. (IAar, T.) You say, A^anifa AlbaEiyru AlkalaA^a The camel loathed, disliked, or regarded with disgust, the herbage, or pasture. (T.) And A^anfa AlT~aEaAma wagayorahu He disliked the food &c. (M.) And A^anifato farasiY h`*ihi h`*aA Albalada This my mare disliked this region. (T, as heard from an Arab of the desert.) And taA^onafu faHolahaA She (a woman, and a mare, and a camel, being pregnant,) dislikes her male, or stallion. (T.) And A^anifato , said of a woman, signifies She, being pregnant, had no appetite for anything. (Ibn-Abbád, K.)

sourceDefinition: and ↓ Ay^tnfhu [written with the disjunctive alif Aiytanafahu ] (assumed tropical:) He took [ its A^anof , i. e.,] the first of it: (M:) he began it, or commenced it: (S, ↓ M, Msb, K: *) or i. q. Aisotaqobalahu [which has also the latter of the two significations mentioned above, (Mgh in art. qbl ,) and moreover signifies he anticipated it; and from what follows here, it seems to be probable that this last signification, as well as the other, may be meant by it in this instance]: (T, M:) namely, a thing, (M, Msb,) or an affair. (T.) You say, AstA^nfhu biwaEodK (assumed tropical:) He made him a promise in anticipation; without his asking it of him. (M.) And, of a woman, Ausotuw^onifato biAln~ikaAHi A^aw~alFA (assumed tropical:) [ She was just married, or bedded, for the first time ]. (M.) See also A^unufN , last sentence. ― -b2- [Hence, Harofu A@sotiy^onaAfK , in grammar, An inceptive particle, placed at the commencement of a new proposition grammatically independent of that which precedes it. ]

definition: a word of well-known meaning;
sourceDefinition: a word of well-known meaning; (Lth, T, K;) The nose; syn. maEoTisN ; (Msb;) the aggregate composed of the two nostrils and the septum and the [ bone called ] qaSabap , which is the hard part of the Anf ; (MF;) i. q. manoxirN [which is evidently an explanation by a synecdoche, as this word properly signifies nostril ]: (M:) it pertains to man and to others: (S:) ↓ A^unofN is a dial. var. of the same; (MF, TA;) and so is ↓ A_inofN , which is a form used by the vulgar peculiarly: (TA:) the pl. [of pauc.] is A=nufN and A=naAfN (S, M, Msb, K) and [of mult.] A^unuwfN . (T, S, M, Msb, K.) The dual is applied to The two nostrils; as in the saying of Muzáhim El-'Okeylee, yasuwfu biA^anofiyohi Aln~iqaAEa [ He scents with his two nostrils the dust ]. (TA.) You say also, huwa yatatab~aEu A^anofahu (tropical:) He scents, or sniffs, the odour, and follows it. (T, [in which, however, I find yatobaEu in the place of yttb~E ] O, L, K, TA.) And, of a she-camel, taroA^amu biA^anofihiA (assumed tropical:) [ She makes a show of affection with her nose, by smelling her young one; not having true love]. (S, M, K, voce mu*aAy^irN ; &c.: see also muEaAriDN .) And maAta Hatofa A^anofihi (S, K, &c., in art. Htf ,) and Htf A^anofiyohi , (K ibid.,) (assumed tropical:) He died [ a natural death, ] on his bed, (K,) without being slain or beaten (S, K) or drowned or burned. (K. [See art. Htf ]) And HamiYa A^anofuhu (tropical:) He became vehemently angry, or enraged; as also warima A^anofuhu . (IAth. [See also art. Hmy ]) And rajulN HamiY~u AlA^anofi (tropical:) A disdainful, or scornful, man; who disdains, or scorns, being injured. (T, K, TA. [See, again, art. Hmy .]) And samiY~u AlA^anofi (assumed tropical:) [lit. Highnosed, signifies the same;] i. q. A^anofaAnu . (T, K.) And A^anofN fiy Als~amaA='i waA@sotN fiY AlmaA='i (assumed tropical:) [ A nose in the sky and a rump in the water ]; a prov., applied to him who magnifies himself in words and is little in actions. (Har p. 641.) And HaEala A^anofahu fiY qafaAhu (tropical:) [lit. He put his nose in the back of his neck ]; meaning he turned away from the truth, or what was right, and betook himself to what was false, or vain: (K, TA:) expressing the utmost degree of turning away, or turning the head, from a thing. (TA.) And A^aDaAEa maTolaba A^anofihi , (M, K,) and muwoDiEa A^anofihi , (M,) (assumed tropical:) [ He neglected, or left unprotected, ] the womb from which he had come forth: (Th, M:) or the faroj of his mother. (Ibn-'Abbád, K.) And huwa AlfaHolu laA yuqoraEu A^anofuhu , and laA yuqodaEu , He is the speaker, or orator, who is not to be rebutted. (TA.) AlA^asdi A^anofu (assumed tropical:) [ The nose of the lion ] is the asterism called Aln~avorapu , q. v. (Kzw in his Description of the Mansions of the Moon.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) [ A prominent part of anything, as being likened to a nose;] the extremity of anything. (M.) [Thus,] A^anofu jabalK (tropical:) A prominence, or projecting part, of a mountain. (T, S, M, Msb, TA.) A^anofu Aln~aAbi , (S, M. K, TA,) in [some of] the copies of the K erroneously, AlbaAbi , (TA,) (tropical:) The extremity, (S, M, K, TA,) or edge, (M, TA,) of the canine tooth, or tush, when it comes forth. (S, M, K, TA.) A^anofu xuf~i AlbaEiyri (assumed tropical:) The extremity of the manosim [i. e. toe, or each of the two nails of the foot, ] of the camel. (T, K.) A^anofu All~iHoyapi (tropical:) The fore part, (M, TA,) or side, (K,) of the beard. (M, K, TA.) A^anofu Aln~aEoli (assumed tropical:) The toe, or foremost extremity, of the sandal [also called its A^asalap and its *unaAbap ]. (M.) A^anofaA Alqawosi (assumed tropical:) The two extremities which are in the inner sides of the two curved ends of the bow. (M.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) The first, or first part, of anything; (S, M, K;) relating also to times; (M;) as also ↓ musotaA^onafN (M, TA.) Thus, A^anofu AlmaroEaY (assumed tropical:) The first of the herbage, or pasture. (S, * M.) A^anofu AlmaTari (assumed tropical:) The first vegetation produced by the rain. (T, K.) jaA='a fiY A^anofi Alxayoli (tropical:) [ He came among the first of the horses, or horsemen ]. (TA.) saAra fiY A^anofi Aln~ahaAri (tropical:) [ He journeyed in the first part of the day ]. (TA.) h`*aA A^anofu Eamali fulaAnK (tropical:) This is the first of the things which such a one has begun to do. (T, TA.) A^anofu Al$~ad~i , (T, S, M,) and AlEadowi , (M,) (assumed tropical:) The first of the run, or running: (T:) the most vehement thereof. (T, S, M, K. *) A^anofu Albarodi (assumed tropical:) The first of the cold: (T:) the most vehement thereof; (T, S, M;) so says Yaákoob. (S.) ― -b4- (tropical:) A lord, or chief. (IAar, T, K.) You say, huwa A^anofu qawomihi (tropical:) He is the lord, or chief, of his people. (TA.) ― -b5- (tropical:) A piece broken off of a cake of bread. (K, TA.) ― -b6- (assumed tropical:) A part of ground, or land, that is hard, and lying open, exposed to the sun. (IF, K.)

definition: A camel having a complaint of, or suffering pain in, his nose, from the burap [or nose-ring ]: (ISk, S, M, K:) or wounded by the nose-rein, whether it be with a xi$aA$ or burap (A 'Obeyd, T, M) or...
sourceDefinition: A camel having a complaint of, or suffering pain in, his nose, from the burap [or nose-ring ]: (ISk, S, M, K:) or wounded by the nose-rein, whether it be with a xi$aA$ or burap (A 'Obeyd, T, M) or xizaAmap [all of which are different kinds of nose-rings]. (A' Obeyd, T.) And consequently, Submissive, and tractable: (S, TA:) or submissive and obedient, that dislikes chiding and beating, and goes as he is able to do spontaneously and easily: (Aboo-Sa'eed, TA:) and ↓ A=nifN signifies the same; (A 'Obeyd, M, K;) but the former is the more correct and the more chaste: (Sgh, K:) by rule, it should be maA^onuwfN , like maSoduwrN , (T, S, M,) and maboTuwnN . (T, S.) To such a camel, the believer is likened in a trad.; (T, S, M;) because he ceases not to complain, or suffer pain; (M;) or because he does not require to be chidden nor to be punished, but endures and performs what is incumbent on him. (Aboo-Sa'eed, TA.) ― -b2- Disdaining, or disdainful; scorning, or scornful; i. q. HamiY~u AlA^anofi : and ↓ A^anofaAnu [signifies the same;] i. q. samiY~u AlA^anofi . (T, K.) -A2- See also A=nifN .

definition: is a noun (Mughnee) syn.
sourceDefinition: is a noun (Mughnee) syn. with Hasobu : (S, Mughnee, K: *) and is also a verbal noun syn. with yakofiY . (Mughnee, K. *) You say bajaliY (S, Mughnee, K) and bajoliY , (S, K,) meaning HasobiY [ My sufficiency, or a thing sufficing me, i. e. sufficient for me, is such a thing]: (S, Mughnee, K:) [it is said in the Ham, p. 145, as on the authority of Akh, that they do not say bajolY ; but this is a mistranscription for bajaloniY , as will be seen from what follows:] and, using it as a verbal noun, (Mughnee, K,) but this is rare, (Mughnee,) you say bajaloniY , meaning yakofiyniY [ It suffices me, or will suffice me ]; (Mughnee, K;) and bajaloka , meaning yakofiyka [ It suffices thee, or will suffice thee ]: (K:) or, accord. to Akh, they say bajaloka , like as they say, qaToka ; but not bajaloniY , like qaToniY : (S:) or the n in bajaloniY is absolutely necessary accord. to him who says that bajalN is a verbal noun; and accord. to him who says that this word is syn. with Hasobu , the n is allowable. (MF.) [See, under the words qado and qaTo , what is said respecting qadoniY and qaToniY .] In the saying of Jábir Ibn-Ra-lán Es-Simbisee, lam~aA raA^ato maEo$arFA qal~ato Hamuwlatuhumo qaAlato suEaAdu A^ah`*aA maAlukumo bajalaA [ When she saw a company whose beasts of burden were few, So'ád said, Is this your property, sufficing you?] meaning, when she saw the fewness of our camels: the last word occupies the place of a denotative of state, and is made to end thus by poetic license: Abu-l-'Alà says that this word may be put in the accus. case as meaning not exceeding what I see; or it may be for bajaliY , after the manner of some of the Arabs who are related, by Akh and others, to have said gulaAmaA for gulaAmiY . (Ham pp. 299 and 300.) [See also 2: and see bajalN .] -A2- It is also a particle, (Mughnee,) meaning naEamo [ Yes; yea; or even so ]. (Mughnee, K.)

sourceDefinition: (in the Ham p. 352 burojumN ) is the sing. of baraAjimu (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and burojumaAtN ; (T, TA;) and signifies [ A knuckle, or finger-joint; ] the outer, or the inner, joint, or place of division, of the fingers: and (as some say, TA) the middle toe of any bird: (K:) or baraAjimu signifies all the finger-joints; (A'Obeyd, K;) as also rawaAjimu [a mistranscription for rawaAjib ]: (A'Obeyd, TA:) or the parts of the fingers that are protuberant when one clinches his hand: (Ham ubi suprà:) or the backs of the finger-bones: (K:) or the finger-joints (S, Mgh) that are between the A^a$aAjiE and the rawaAjib ; (S;) i. e. (S, Mgh) [the middle knuckles; (see A^a$ojaEu and raAjibapN ;)] the heads of the sulaAmayaAt , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) on the back, or outer side, of the hand, (S, Msb,) which become protuberant when one clinches his hand: (S, Mgh, Msb, K:) or, as in the Kf, the heads of the slAmyAt ; and their inner and outer sides are termed the rawaAjib : (Msb:) accord. to the T, the wrinkled parts at the joints of the fingers; the smooth portion between which is called raAjibapN : or, as in another place, in the backs of the fingers; the parts between them being called the rawaAjib : in every finger are three burojumaAt , except the thumb: or, as in another place, in every finger are two of what are thus termed: it is also explained as signifying the joints in the backs of the fingers, upon which the dirt collects. (TA.) The phrase AlA^axo*u biAlbaraAjimi , meaning The seizing with the hand, is one requiring consideration [as of doubtful character]. (Mgh.) [See also burovunN .]

sourceDefinition: , aor. yabozuw , i. q. taTaAwala [app. as meaning He stretched out his neck, looking at a thing far off ]; and taA^an~asa [here meaning the same, or he looked, raising his head; said of a hawk, or falcon]: (Az, ISd, K:) and hence IJ says that ↓ baAzN is [originally] of the measure faloEN from this verb: (TA: [and it is said in the K that baAzK seems to be hence derived:]) for [or tTAwl may here be used in another sense; for, accord. to Fei,] bazaA , aor. as above, signifies he overcame, or subdued; and hence is derived ↓ baAzK . (Msb.) You say also, bazaA Ealayohi , aor. as above, meaning tTAwl [i. e., thus followed by Elyh , He held up his head with an assumption of superiority over him; behaved haughtily towards him; exalted himself above him; or overpowered, subdued, or oppressed, him ]. (S.) And buziYa biAlqawomi The people, or company of men, were overcome, or subdued. (TA.) And bazaAhu , aor. as above, (K,) inf. n. bazowN , (TA,) He overcame, or subdued, him; and laid violent hands upon him, or assaulted him; as also ↓ AbzY bihi : (K:) or this last signifies he overcame him, and subdued him: (S:) and bazaAhu , he wronged him; or treated him wrongfully, or injuriously: and ↓ AbzAhu may signify the same; or this may mean he induced him to become A^abozaY , q. v.: (Ham p. 502:) and accord. to Aboo-Riyásh, ↓ AbzY signifies he pressed heavily upon his adversary, or imposed on him that which he was unable to do, or to bear, in order to treat him wrongfully, or injuriously. (Ham pp. 104 and 105.) [It is said that] bazawaAnN [an inf. n. of which the verb, if it have one, is bazaA ,] signifies the act of Leaping; syn. wavobN . (S: [but I think it not improbable that this may have been taken from a mistranscription of nazawaAnN , an inf. n. of nazaA .]) -A2- baziYa , (K,) aor. ; (Ham p. 502;) and bazaA , aor. ; (K;) inf. n. bazFA (S, * K, * TA) and bazowN , (TA,) He (a man, TA) had what is termed bazFA ; (K;) i. e., prominence of the breast and depression of the back: (S, K, and Ham ubi suprà:) or depression of the back and prominence of the belly: or, as some say, prominence of the breast and depression of the lower part of the belly: (Ham ubi suprà:) or depression of the breast and prominence of the lower part of the belly: (Ham p. 105:) or a bending in the back next the posteriors: (K, TA:) or a projecting of the middle of the back over the posteriors: or a backward bulging of the posteriors: (K:) or he was as though his posteriors projected over the hinder part of the thighs: or he had the breast bulging forward and the posteriors backward, so that he appeared unable to straighten his back. (T, TA.) [See also 4.] The epithet is A^abozaY : fem. bazowaA='u . (S, K.)

sourceDefinition: (S, Msb, K) and baAzN [mentioned in art. bwz ] (Msb, TA, and so in some copies of the K in this art.) and baAzN [mentioned in art. bA^z ] and ↓ baAziY~N (TA) [ A name given to several varieties of the hawk, or falcon;] a species of Saqor , (K,) that preys, or hunts or catches game; (S;) the proudest and fiercest of birds of prey, found in the country of the Turks: it is said that this name is only given to the female, and that the male is of another kind, a kite, or a white falcon ( $aAhiyn ), and hence the varieties of form &c. in different individuals of the species: that of which the prevailing colour is white is the best, and the fullest in body, and the boldest, and the easiest to train: this variety (the A^a$ohab ) is found only in the country of the Turks, and Armenia, and the country of the Khazar: (Kzw:) [see also baA$aqN :] respecting the derivation, see 1, in two places: the pl. (M, TA.) And baq~a kalaAmFA [in which case the aor., accord. to rule, unless the noun be a specificative, is yabuq~u ,] and baq~a bikalaAmK [ He was, or became, profuse in speech ]. (M.) Hence, (TA,) qado malaA^ota AlA^aroDa baqaAqFA [ Thou hast filled the earth, or land, with much discoursing ], said, in dispraise, to a voluminous writer. (M, TA.) ― -b2- baq~ato and ↓ Abq~t , said of a woman, She had many children: (JK, S, M, K:) or, as Sb says, baq~ato waladFA she brought forth many children. (M, TA.) ― -b3- baq~ati Als~amaA='u , (S, M, K,) and ↓ Abq~t , (M, TA,) The sky rained much, and consecutively, or uninterruptedly: (M, TA: *) or rained vehemently. (TA.) And baq~a lanaA AlEaTaA='a He made the gift large, or ample, to us. (M.) ― -b5- baq~a maAlahu He distributed, or dispersed, or scattered, his property; (K;) as also ↓ bq~qhu . (JK, * K.) ― -b6- baq~a Alxabara , inf. n. baq~N , He spread, and sent forth, the news, or information. definition: [ Coffee-berries, whether green or roasted, whole or reduced to powder by pounding or grinding;
sourceDefinition: [ Coffee-berries, whether green or roasted, whole or reduced to powder by pounding or grinding; ] expl. in the K as $aYo'N yut~axa*u kaAlmur~iY~i [ a certain thing that is taken like the condiment termed mur~iy~ , which is used to give relish to food or to quicken the appetite]; Ibn-Es-Sim'ánee says, huwa$aYo'N fiY AlkawaAmiyxi [app. meaning it is a thing reckoned among what are termed kwAmyx , pl. of kaAmaxN , which signifies the same as mur~iY~N , for it seems that fY is here used in the sense of mino , or it may be a mistranscription for mino ]; the physician Dáwood says, it is the produce of certain trees in El-Yemen; the berries thereof are put into the earth in A=*aAr [the Syrian month corresponding to March, O. S.], and it increases, and is gathered in A^abiyb [the Coptic month commencing on the 25th of June, O. S.; the 7th of July, N. S.]; it grows to the height of about three cubits, on a stem of the thickness of the thumb, and has a white flower, which is succeeded by a berry like the hazel-nut; sometimes it is cut like beans; and sometimes, when it is divested of its covering, it divides into two halves: it has been proved to be good for alleviating humidities, and cough, and phlegm, and defluxions, and for opening obstructions, and causing a flow of the urine: when roasted, [ and pounded or ground, ] and well cooked, [i. e. boiled in water, ] it is now commonly known by the name of qahowap . (TA.) [Golius, I think, has misunderstood the explanation of this word in the K: after having given that explanation, and rendered it by “ res quæ sumitur instar AlmrY Múrriji, ” he adds, “ Pers. AbkAmh Abcâma dictæ: hæc sorbitio est rei ex hordeo et frumento paratæ multa cura et arte, quam Malajesa et Halimæus describunt. ” He then mentions the signification of coffee-berries as a second and distinct meaning.]

definition: A sweet, or pleasant, odour;
sourceDefinition: A sweet, or pleasant, odour; (As, AA, T, S, M, K;) such as that of the apple (T, M) and the like, (M,) or the quince: (T:) Sb says that it is a name for a sweet, or pleasant, odour, like xamoTapN : (M, * TA:) and an unpleasant odour; (As, T, S;) a fetid odour; (M, K;) whence ban~apN Algazoli [ the odour of the yarn ] occurring in a saying of 'Alee, respecting a weaver; (M;) which shows that A'Obeyd erred in asserting it to have only the first of the foregoing significations; (IB, TA;) which Suh, in the R, assigns also to ↓ bunaAnapN : (TA:) the odour of sheep, or goats, (S, M,) or of camels or cattle; (Z, TA;) and of the dung of gazelles; (S, K;) and of the lodging-places of sheep or goats and of oxen or bulls or cows and of gazelles: (T, M:) and sometimes the lodgingplaces themselves, of sheep or goats: (M, TA:) pl. definition: The fingers; syn. A^aSaAbiEu : (M, Msb, K:) but whether it means peculiarly the ASAbE of the hand, or those of the foot also, [i. e. the toes, ] is disputed: (TA:) or the ends, or extremities,...
sourceDefinition: The fingers; syn. A^aSaAbiEu : (M, Msb, K:) but whether it means peculiarly the ASAbE of the hand, or those of the foot also, [i. e. the toes, ] is disputed: (TA:) or the ends, or extremities, thereof: (S, M, Msb, K:) said to be so called because by their means are ordered those circumstances whereby man continues in existence; from A^aban~a biAlomakaAni : (Msb:) mentioned in the Kur viii. 12 because therewith one fights, and defends himself: (Er-Rághib, TA:) or it there signifies all the limbs, or members, of the body: (Aboo-Is-hák, M:) or the fingers, or toes, and any other parts of all the limbs, or members: (Zj, TA:) or it means in the Kur the $awaY ; (Lth, T, TA;) so in lxxv. 4; (M;) i. e. the arms or hands and the legs or feet: (Lth, T, TA:) accord. to El-Fárisee the meaning of the words in the Kur lxxv. 4 is, we are able to make their extremities like those of the camel, so that they should not profit by them in handicraft: (M, TA:) the n. un. is with p ; (Lth, T, S, M, K;) meaning, accord. to Lth, a single A_iSobaE [i. e. finger, or toe ]; or, accord. to AHeyth, the whole ASbE ; or, as some say, the highest Euqodap [or joint ] of the ASbE : (T:) the pl. of pauc. is banaAnaAtN ; but a pl. of mult. is sometimes used as one of pauc.; and hence the saying of the rájiz, xamosa banaAnK qaAniy^i AlA^aZofaAri [ Five fingers, or ends of fingers, intensely red from the dye of hinnà in the nails ], meaning xamosFA mina AlbanaAni : and one says, banaAnN muxaD~abN [ Fingers, or ends of fingers, dyed, or much dyed, with hinnà]; for every pl. [or rather coll. gen. n.] between which and its sing., or n. un., there is no difference but p [added in the latter] may be treated as sing. and masc. (S.) Lth cites as an ex. of the n. un., layosa liHaY~K fawoqahumo banaAnaho laAhum~a A^akoramota baniY kinaAnah meaning [ O God, Thou hast honoured the sons of Kináneh: there belongs not to any tribe ] excel-lence of the measure of a finger above them. (T, TA.)

definition: Remaining, continuing, staying, dwelling, or abiding, in a place.
sourceDefinition: Remaining, continuing, staying, dwelling, or abiding, in a place. (T, TA.) Applied to a mixture of urine and dung ( Eabas ) upon the tail [of a camel &c.], it may mean Cleaving, and sticking: or it may be from ban~apN signifying “ a fetid odour ” [so as to mean having a fetid odour ]: thus, in this case, it may be either a part. n. or a possessive epithet. (M, TA.) It signifies also Having the odour of the dung of gazelles; applied to a covert, or hiding-place, of those animals, among trees. (S, K. *)

sourceDefinition: and ↓ tbw~E , said of a rope, signify the same [app. It was measured by the bAE , or fathom ]. (K, TA.) ― -b2- AnbAEt AlHay~apu The serpent extended itself, after gathering itself together and coiling itself, in order to spring. (Lh, K.) ― -b3- Also AnbAE , said of a man, He leaped, or sprang, after being still: or he made an assault; or leaped, or sprang, and made a violent seizure. (TA.) [Hence,] muxoranobiqN liyanobaAEa Silent in order to leap, or spring, (K, and S in art. xrbq ,) when he finds an opportunity; (S in that art.;) on account of a misfortune which he desires [ to effect ]; (S, K, in that art.;) or in order to make an assault: (TA:) or looking, or waiting, for an opportunity to leap, or spring, upon his enemy, or the object of his want, when able to do so; and in like manner, muxoranoTimN liyanobaAEa : (TA in art. xrbq :) a prov., (K,) applied to a man who is silent respecting a misfortune [which he desires to effect]; (TA;) or applied to a man who is long silent until he thinks his object inadvertent, and who is possessed of cunning: (As, TA in art. xrbq :) accord. to one relation, liyanobaAqa , i. e. to bring about, or effect, a baAy^iqap , meaning a calamity, or misfortune: (K:) or lynbAE may be for layonabaE , from nabaEa AlmaA='u . (Har p. 62.) [Hence also,] AnbAE Al$~ujaAEu mina AlS~af~i The courageous man went, or came, out, or forth, from the rank. (AAF.) ― -b4- AnbAE liY fiY siloEatihi He treated me in an easy manner in the sale of his commodity, or article of merchandise, and strained himself ( Aimotad~a ) to give his consent to it. (K, TA.) And hence, ↓ AinobayaAEN , as used by Sakhrel-Ghei in describing the conduct of a man towards a beautiful woman, or, accord. to one relation, ↓ AibotiyaAEN , The acting, or behaving, towards another, boldly, in a free and easy manner, or without shyness; syn. AinobisaATN ; as also bayoEN (TA.) ― -b5- AnbAE also signifies He ran in a gentle manner, with a bending and a twisting of himself; from baAEa , aor. yabuwEu . (Ahmad Ibn-'Obeyd.) ― -b6- And he went away. (Har p. 592: see 1.) ― -b7- And It (sweat) flowed: (Msb, K:) or, as El-Fárábee says, extended. (Msb.) 'Antarah says, describing the sweat of a she-camel, yanobaAEu mino *iforaY gaDuwbK jasorapK [ Flowing, or extending, from the part behind the ear of a she-camel quickly angered, spirited, or tall, or tall and bulky, or strong, and bold to endure travel ]: ynbAE being originally yanobawiEu ; or, as most of the lexicologists say, originally yanobaEu , the A being inserted after the fet-hah of the b to render its sound full. (TA.)

definition: A fathom; the space that is between [ the extremities of ] the two hands when they are extended to the right and left; (Msb;) the measure of the extension of the two arms (S, K, TA) with what is...
sourceDefinition: A fathom; the space that is between [ the extremities of ] the two hands when they are extended to the right and left; (Msb;) the measure of the extension of the two arms (S, K, TA) with what is between them of the body; (TA;) as also ↓ bawoEN and ↓ buwEN ; (K;) the last of the dial. of Hudheyl: (TA:) said by AHát to be of the masc. gender: (Msb:) pl. A^abowaAEN (Msb, K) and biyEaAnN . (Ham p. 475.) ― -b2- [And hence,] (assumed tropical:) The body, including the limbs; [because a fathom in height;] as in the phrase rajulN Tawiylu AlbaAEi (assumed tropical:) A man tall in the body; which has also another meaning, to be seen below: but you do not say, qaSiyru AlbaAEi as meaning short in the body. (TA.) ― -b3- [Also The arms; and particularly when extended to their full reach; as also the pl.: and in like manner, the fore legs of a beast: see several examples in the first paragraph of this art.] ― -b4- [And hence, (tropical:) Reach; power; or ability. ] You say, huwa qaSiyru AlbaAEi (tropical:) He is lacking in power, or ability: a phrase which has also another meaning, to be seen below. (TA.) And qaSura baAEuhu Eano *`lika (tropical:) He was unable to attain, or to do, or effect, that: in this case, ↓ bwE is not used. (TA.) ― -b5- And (tropical:) Reach, power, or ability, in the means, or causes, of attaining honour; or in generous, or honourable, qualities or actions: (TA:) (tropical:) eminence; nobility; honour; generosity: (Lth, S, K:) in which senses, ↓ bwE is not used. (Lth.) A poet says, lahu fiY Almajodi saAbiqapN wa baAEu [ He has precedence and eminence in glory, honour, dignity, or nobility ]. (Lth.) And rajulN Tawiylu AlbaAEi (tropical:) A man of large generosity. (TA.) And qaSiyru AlbaAEi (tropical:) Niggardly: a phrase which has also another meaning, mentioned above. (TA.)

definition: is the contr. of fawoq : (Msb, K:) and Alt~aHotu [signifying The location that is beneath, below, or under, ] is opposed to Alfawoqu , and is used in relation to that which is separate from another...
sourceDefinition: is the contr. of fawoq : (Msb, K:) and Alt~aHotu [signifying The location that is beneath, below, or under, ] is opposed to Alfawoqu , and is used in relation to that which is separate from another thing; AlA^asofalu being used in relation to that which is united with [or a part of] another thing. (Kull.) Sometimes, (K,) taHot is an adv. n., (Msb, K,) having a vague signification, its meaning not being clear unless it is prefixed to another word, as in the phrase h`*aA taHota h`*aA [ This is beneath, below, or under, this ]. (Msb.) And sometimes, it is a simple noun; (K;) in which case, [not having the article Al ,] it is indecl., with dammeh for its termination, (K, and I'Ak p. 204,) provided that the noun to which it should be prefixed is suppressed, and the meaning of this is intended to be understood, but not the word itself; (I'Ak ubi suprà;) as in mino taHotu [ Beneath, below, or under ]; (K;) and in the saying, A^aqabN mino taHotu EariyDN mino Ealu [ Lean beneath; broad above ]: otherwise, it is decl.; (I'Ak ibid.;) as in tajoriy mino taHotihaA AlA^anohaAru [ Rivers running beneath them ]; (Kur ii. 23, &c.;) i.e., beneath their trees, (Bd, Jel,) and their pavilions. (Jel.) [You say also, fulaAnN taHota A^amori fulaAnK (assumed tropical:) Such a one is under the command, rule, or authority, of such a one. And fulaAnN taHotahu fulaAnapu (assumed tropical:) Such a one has as his wife such a woman: see an ex. in a verse cited voce A_i*aA . The dim. is ↓ tuHayot : you say, h`daA tuHayota h`*aA , and mino tuHayoti h`*aA , This is a little beneath, below, or under, this. ] ― -b2- Alt~aHotu is also the sing. of Alt~uHuwtu , (IAth, TA,) which latter [in the CK erroneously written Alt~uHutu ] signifies The low, base, vile, or ignoble, persons. (A, IAth, K.) It is said in a trad., laA taquwmu Als~aAEapu Hat~aY taZohara Alt~uHuwtu wa taholika AlwuEuwlu , i. e. [ The hour of resurrection will not come until ] the low, or ignoble, persons [ shall prevail ], and the noble persons [ shall perish ]: (A, IAth, TA:) or, as some say, until the treasures that are beneath the earth appear. (TA.) And in another trad. it is said that among the signs of the resurrection shall be this: A^ano yaEoluw Alt~uHuwtu AlwuEuwla That the weak of mankind shall have ascendency over the strong. (TA.)

And sometimes, it is a simple noun; (K;) in which case, [not having the article Al ,] it is indecl., with dammeh for its termination, (K, and I'Ak p. 204,) provided that the noun to which it should be prefixed is suppressed, and the meaning of this is intended to be understood, but not the word itself; (I'Ak ubi suprà;) as in mino taHotu [ Beneath, below, or under ]; (K;) and in the saying, A^aqabN mino taHotu EariyDN mino Ealu [ Lean beneath; broad above ]: otherwise, it is decl.; (I'Ak ibid.;) as in tajoriy mino taHotihaA AlA^anohaAru [ Rivers running beneath them ]; (Kur ii. 23, &c.;) i.e., beneath their trees, (Bd, Jel,) and their pavilions. (Jel.) [You say also, fulaAnN taHota A^amori fulaAnK (assumed tropical:) Such a one is under the command, rule, or authority, of such a one. And fulaAnN taHotahu fulaAnapu (assumed tropical:) Such a one has as his wife such a woman: see an ex. in a verse cited voce A_i*aA . The dim. is ↓ tuHayot : you say, h`daA tuHayota h`*aA , and mino tuHayoti h`*aA , This is a little beneath, below, or under, this. ] ― -b2- Alt~aHotu is also the sing. of Alt~uHuwtu , (IAth, TA,) which latter [in the CK erroneously written Alt~uHutu ] signifies The low, base, vile, or ignoble, persons. (S.) -A2- Also, (S, M, K,) and ↓ tarabapN , and ↓ tarobaA='u , (M, K,) A certain plant, (S, M, K,) growing in the plains, or in soft land, having serrated leaves: or, as some say, a certain thorny tree, of which the fruit is like a suspended unripe date, growing in the plains, or in soft land, and in rugged ground, and in Tihámeh: accord. to AHn, the taribap is a green herb, or leguminous plant, that has a purging effect upon camels: (M:) [accord. to Meyd, as stated by Golius, what is called in Persian xnfj ; i. e. the plant thlaspi; and to this it is applied in the present day.]

definition: A submissive, or tractable, camel;
sourceDefinition: A submissive, or tractable, camel; applied to the male (T, S, M, K) and to the female: (T, S, K:) from turaAbN , (S, M,) because of the abasement thereof; or, as Sb holds it to be, for darabuwtN , by the change of d into t : accord. to Lh, a [camel such as is termed] bakor that is trained, or rendered submissive or tractable; and in like manner a she-camel, one that will follow a person if he takes hold of her lip or her eyelash: and As, who derives it from tNraAbN , says that this epithet is applied to land, or ground, and any other thing, that is *aluwl [i.e. easy to walk or ride upon, &c.]. (M.)

sourceDefinition: and ↓ turobN (Lth, T, S, M, A, Msb, K) and ↓ tarobN (CK [but this I do not find elsewhere]) and ↓ turobapF (S, A, * K) and ↓ tarobaA='u (Lth, T, S, A, * K) and ↓ turabaA='u (S, M, K) and ↓ taworaAbN and ↓ taworabN and ↓ tayoraAbN and ↓ tayorabN [and ↓ tayrabN as will be seen below] and ↓ tariybN (S, M, K) and ↓ tiroyabN , (M, K) accord. to MF ↓ taroyabN , which is perhaps a dial. var., and accord. to some ↓ tiroyibN , and ↓ taroyaAbN , (TA,) signify the same, (Lth, T, S, M, A, K,) and are words of which the meaning is well known: (A, K:) [i. e. Dust: and earth: generally the former; i. e. fine, dry, particles of earth; as when we say, Alr~iyHu tasuwqu Alt~uraAba The wind drives along the dust: but we also use the expression turaAbN nadK , meaning moist earth, the explanation, in Lexicons, of the word varFY :] ?varFY is turaAbN ; and when it ceases to be moist, it is still trAb , but is not then called vrY : (Msb voce vrY :) accord. to Fr, turaAbN is a gen. n., from which is formed neither dual nor pl.: and its rel. n. is ↓ turaAbiY~N : (TA:) [but when it means a kind of dust or earth, as ↓ turobapN also does sometimes, it has a pl.: in this case,] accord. to Lh, (M,) its pl. is A^atoribapN [a pl. of pauc.] and tirobaAnN [a pl. of mult.]; (S, M, K) and some add turobaAnN : (TA:) [and when ↓ turobapN has this, or a similar, meaning, it has for its pl. turabN ; as in the phrase A^aToyabu Alt~urabi the best of the kinds of earth, occurring in this art. in the A:] but no pl. of any of the other syn. words mentioned above has been heard: (M, K:) AAF says that trAb is the pl. of trb ; [app. meaning that turaAbN is a quasi-pl. n. (which is often called in lexicons a pl.) of turobN ;] but MF observes that this requires consideration: (TA:) Lth says that ↓ turobN and turaAbN are syn.; but when the fem. forms of these words are used, they say, ↓ A^aroDN Tay~bapu Alt~urobap meaning Land that is good in respect of the natural constitution of its dust or earth; and ↓ turaAbapN when meaning A layer, or lamina, of dust or earth, such as is not perceived by the sight, but only by the imagination: (T:) or this last word and ↓ turobapN signify a portion of dust or earth: and AlA^aroDi ↓ turobapu signifies the exterior, or external part, of the earth: (M:) and ↓ Alt~arobaA='u , the earth (S, K) itself. (S.) The Arabs said, Alt~uraAbu laka [ Dust, or earth, be thy lot ]; using the nom. case, although meaning an imprecation, because the word is a simple subst., not an inf. n.: but Lh mentions the phrase Alt~uraAba liloA^aboEadi [ Dust, or earth, be the lot of the remote from good ]; saying that the accus. case is used, as though the phrase were an imprecation [of the ordinary kind, in which an inf. n. is used in the accus. case as the absolute complement of its own verb understood]. (M.) And lahu Alt~uraAbu is a phrase used as meaning (assumed tropical:) [ He has, or shall have, or may he have, ] disappointment, (Msb in art. Ehr ,) or, nothing. (A 'Obeyd, Mgh in art. fr$ .) lahu wajanodalFA ↓ turobFA is also a form of imprecation, in which substs. in the proper sense of the term are used in the manner of inf. ns., put in the accus. case by reason of a verb unexpressed; as though it were for taribato yadaAhu wajunodilato [ May his arms, or his hands, cleave to the dust, or earth, and the stones, by reason of poverty]: and some of the Arabs put the nouns in the nom. case, still using the phrase in the same sense, as though they were in the accus. (M.) One says also, ↓ bifiyhi Alt~aworabu and ↓ Alt~ayorabu and ↓ Alt~iyirabu and ↓ Alt~arobaA='u and ↓ Alt~aworaAbu [ In his mouth is dust, or earth: or may dust, or earth, be in his mouth; i. e. may he die, or be in his grave]. (T.) It is said in a trad. that God created the ↓ turobap [meaning the dust, or soil, or, accord. to the TA the earth ( A^aroD ),] on the seventh day of the week; and created upon it the mountains on the first day; and the trees, on the second day. (T.) And one says, ↓ laA^aDoriban~ahu Hat~aY yaEaD~a biAlt~arobaA='i , (Lth, T, A,) meaning [ I will assuredly beat him so that he shall bite ] the dust, or earth. (Lth, T.) And ↓ bayonahumaA maA bayona AljarobaA='i waAlt~arobaA='i , meaning [ Between them two is the space that is between ] the heaven and the earth. (A.)

definition: , (S, M, TA,) which signifies The part of the breast which is the place of the collar, or necklace: (T, M, K:) so by the common consent of the lexicologists: (T:) or the bones of the breast: (M, A,...
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, TA,) which signifies The part of the breast which is the place of the collar, or necklace: (T, M, K:) so by the common consent of the lexicologists: (T:) or the bones of the breast: (M, A, K:) or the bones of the breast that are between the collar-bone and the pap: (S:) or the part of the breast, or chest, that is next to the two collar-bones: or the part that is between the two breasts and the collar-bones: or four ribs of the right side of the chest and four of the left thereof: (M, K:) or the two arms and two legs and two eyes: (T, M, K:) it is also said that the tariybataAni are the two ribs that are next to the two collar-bones: IAth says that the tariybap is the uppermost part of the human breast, beneath the chin; and its pl. is as above: accord. to IF, in the Mj, the ↓ tryb is the breast, or chest: MF says that trAy^b relates to males and females in common; but most of the authors on strange words affirm decidedly that it is peculiar to women: (TA:) the tariybap of the camel is the part in which it is stabbed, or stuck; syn. manoHar . (M.)

definition: Possessing much wealth;
sourceDefinition: Possessing much wealth; (T, K;) rich; without want; or having wealth like the dust, or earth: (Lh and M: [in the TA, Atrb is mentioned as having this meaning; perhaps by a mistranscription: if not, it must be ↓ A^atorabu :]) and having little wealth: thus it bears two contr. significations: (K:) but the former is the more known. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: Moisture; humidity; (S, M, K;) of the earth: (S, Msb:) and moist earth; (S, M, Msb, K;) turaAb that is not moist is not called varFY ; (Msb;) or such as, when moistened, does not become cohesive mud or clay; (M, K;) as also ↓ varoyaA='u [an epithet used as a subst.]: (AO, T, * K, TA: [in the CK, erroneously, varayA' :]) and the earth; ; (M, K) maA taHota Alv~aray , in the Kur [xx. 5], being explained as meaning what is beneath the earth: (M:) Alv~araY and * A^avoraY both signify the earth; and the latter, being thus used as a proper name, is imperfectly decl.: (Ham p. 351:) dual varayaAni (S, M, K) and varawaAni : (Lh, M, K: [but the sing. of the latter should be written varFA :]) pl. A^avoraA=o . (M, K.) AilotaqaY Alv~arayaAni [ The two moistures met, or have met, ] is said when the rain has sunk into the ground so that it has met the moisture of the earth. (S, M, K.) Accord. to IAar, it was also said by a man, (M,) or by an Arab of the desert, (K,) who, (M, K,) being naked, (K,) clad himself with a fur-garment, (M, K,) without a shirt; (M;) meaning the hair of the pubes and the soft hair of the fur-garment. (M, K.) And the Arabs say, $ahorN varaY wa$ahorN taraY wa$ahorN maroEaY wa$ahorN A@sotawaY , meaning A month [ of moisture ] in which the rain begins, and sinks into the ground, and moistens and softens the earth; for $ahorN *uw varFY : and a month in which thou seest the heads of the herbage grown forth; for $ahorN taraY fiyhi ruw^uwsa Aln~abaAti : and a month in which the herbage is tall enough to be pastured upon by the cattle: (As, S, * M:) and a month in which it is full-grown and erect. (As, M.) One says also, badaA varaY AlmaA='i mina Alfarasi , meaning The sweat of the horse appeared. (S, * M.) And A_in~iY laA^aray varaY AlgaDabi fiY wajohi fulaAnK , meaning (assumed tropical:) Verily I see the effect of anger in the face of such a one. (T.) And huwaA@bonu varaAhaA (assumed tropical:) He is the knowing with respect to it. (T in art. bnY .) ― -b2- [Hence, as being likened to moist earth,] i. q. xayorN (assumed tropical:) [ Good; anything good; &c.]. (M, K. [For xayor , Golius appears to have found, in a copy of the K, Hayoz ; and this, which he has rendered “Terræ tractus,” he has given as a signification, not of varFY , but of varaA='N , which, like varFY , he also explains as meaning “ terra. ” ]) So in the saying, fulaAnN qariybu Alv~araY [app. meaning (assumed tropical:) Such a one is a person from whom good is easy of attainment: or it may mean, a person from whom good seems to be easy of attainment: in either case likened to land of which the moist earth is near the surface: that the phrase may have the latter meaning appears from what here follows]. (M.) You say, A_in~a fulaAnFA laqariybu Alv~ariY baEiydu Aln~abaTi , meaning (assumed tropical:) Verily such a one is a person who promises but who does not fulfil. (IAar, T.) ― -b3- [Hence also, (assumed tropical:) Fresh and vigorous friendship. ] You say, lamo yabobasi Alv~araY bayoniY wabayonahu (assumed tropical:) [ The fresh and vigorous friendship between me and him has not withered ]: whence the phrase, maA bayoniY wabayona fulaAnK * muvorK (assumed tropical:) [ That friendship which is between me and such a one is fresh and vigorous ]; i. e., it has not ceased, or become severed. (S, * M.) Jereer says, falaA tuwbisuwA bayoniY wabayonakumu Alv~araY ↓ faA_in~a Al~a*ay bayoniY wabayonakumu muvoriY [ And wither not the fresh and vigorous friendship between me and you; for that which is between me and you is fresh and vigorous ]. (S, M.)

(Aboo-Málik, T.)

sourceDefinition: [ An ore of antimony: or antimony itself; stibium; or stimmi: ] collyrium-stone ( Hajaru AlkuHoli ), (K, TA,) which is black inclining to red, the mines whereof are in Ispahán, whence the best is obtained, and in the West, whence the hardest is obtained: (TA:) a certain stone used as a collyrium: (S:) a certain stone from which collyrium ( kuHol ) is prepared: or collyrium ( kuHol ) itself: (M:) or a substance resembling it: (Seer, M:) or a species thereof: (Lth, T:) or black kuHol , the mine whereof is in the East: said by some of the lawyers to be that of Ispahán: and said to be an arabicized word. (Msb.) The women of the Arabs used also to sprinkle [or rub] it upon the lips and gums, in order that the teeth might glisten the more. (EM p. 62.) [And for the same purpose, many of them tattoo their lips, so as to make them of a uniform dull bluish hue.] ― -b2- One says of a man who remains awake at night, journeying or working, fulaAnN yajoEalu All~ayola A_ivomidFA [ Such a one makes the night a collyrium ]; the blackness of the night being as though it were a collyrium to his eyes because he labours all the night in seeking the means of attaining to eminence. (AA, T, L.)

definition: The reaching of the [ whiteness termed ] taHojiyl , in a horse, to the knee and the hock: (S:) or the rising of the whiteness to [ the extent of ] what is termed Aljababu .
sourceDefinition: The reaching of the [ whiteness termed ] taHojiyl , in a horse, to the knee and the hock: (S:) or the rising of the whiteness to [ the extent of ] what is termed Aljababu . (K.) You say of a horse, fiyhi tajobiybN [ In him is a rising of the tHjyl to the knee and the hock ]: and in this case, the horse is said to be mujab~abN : and the subst. is ↓ jababN [meaning a whiteness of the legs rising to the knee and the hock ]. (S.) [See mujab~abN .] -A2- The act of shrinking [from a thing]; or the being averse [from it]; or the act of withdrawing; (S, K, TA;) outwardly or inwardly. (TA.) You say of a man, jab~aba fa*ahaba [ He shrank, or was averse, or withdrew, and went away ]. (S.) And jay~aba Aln~aAsu Eano TaAEapi A@ll~`hi The people forsook, or relinquished, the obeying of God. (TA from a trad.) ― -b2- The act of fleeing. (K.) You say of a man, jbab He fled. (TA.) El-Hotei-ah says, wanaHonu A_i*aA jab~abotumu Eano nisaAy^ikumo kamaA jab~abato mino Einodi A^awolaAdihaA AlHumuro [ And we, when ye flee from your women, like as the wild asses have fled from the presence of their young ones ]. (TA.) And ↓ jab~a , said of a man, [if not a mistranscription for jab~aba ,] signifies He went quickly, fleeing from a thing. (TA.) -A3- The act of satisfying with water (K, TA) the earth, ( Aljabuwb , TA,) or cattle. (K, TA.)

definition: The act of vying, or contending for superiority, in goodliness, or beauty, &c.
sourceDefinition: The act of vying, or contending for superiority, in goodliness, or beauty, &c., (K,) as, for instance, in grounds of pretension to respect or honour, and in lineage: (TA:) and mujaAb~apN the vying, or contending for superiority, in goodliness, or beauty, (K,) &c., (TA,) and in food: (K:) but [SM says,] I know not whence this addition, respecting food, is derived. (TA. [See, however, what follows, from the A.]) You say, ↓ jaAb~aniY fajababotuhu He vied with me, or contended with me for superiority, and I overcame him. (TA.) And jaAb~ati AlmaroA^apu SaAHibatahaA HusonFA ↓ fajab~atohaA The woman vied, or contended for superiority, with her fellow, and surpassed her in beauty. (TA.) And ↓ jaAb~ahu fiY AlqiraY fajab~ahu He vied with him, or contended with him for superiority, in the entertainment of guests, and he overcame him therein. (A.)

definition: A well: (A, K:) or a well not cased with stone or the like: (S, A, Msb, K:) or a well containing much water: or a deep well: (A, K:) or of some other description: (A:) or a well in a good situation...
sourceDefinition: A well: (A, K:) or a well not cased with stone or the like: (S, A, Msb, K:) or a well containing much water: or a deep well: (A, K:) or of some other description: (A:) or a well in a good situation with respect to pasture: or one that people have found; not one that they have dug: (K:) or a well that is not deep: (Lth, TA:) or a well that is wide, or ample: (ElKilábeeyeh, TA:) or a well that is cut through rock, or smooth rock, or stones, or smooth stones, or hard and smooth and large stones: (Aboo- Habeeb, TA:) of the masc. gender; (Msb, TA;) [not fem. like biy^orN ;] or masc. and fem.: (Fr, Msb:) pl. [of pauc.] A^ajobaAbN (Msb, K.) and [of mult.] jibaAbN and jibabapN . (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- A well that is dug wherein a grape — vine is planted; like as one is dug for the shoot of a palm — tree: pl. jibaAbN . (ISh, TA.) ― -b3- The inside of a well, from its bottom to its top, whether cased with stone or the like or not. (Sh, TA.) ― -b4- The juron of a well [app. meaning A hollowed stone, or stone basin, for water, placed at the mouth of a well: or, perhaps, a hollowed stone placed over the mouth; for many a well has such a stone, forming a kind of parapet]. (Zeyd Ibn-Kuthweh, TA.) -A2- [ A kind of leathern bag; ] a mazaAdap of which one part is sewed to another, (K, TA,) wherein they used to prepare the beverage termed nabiy* , until, by use, it acquired strength for that purpose; mentioned in a trad., forbidding the use of it; and also called ↓ majobuwbapN . (TA.) -A3- The spathe, or envelope, of the spadix, or flowers, of the palmtree; also called juf~N : the former word was unknown to A'Obeyd: both occur, accord. to different readings, in a trad., where it is said that a charm contrived to bewitch Mohammad was put into the jub~ , or juf~ , of a TaloEap : accord. to Sh, (TA,) it means the inside of a TaloEap [which latter here app. signifies, as it does in some other instances, the spathe, not the spadix, of a palmtree]; (K, TA;) in like manner as the inside of a well, from its bottom to its top, is called jub~ : the pl. is jibaAbN . (TA.) Hence the well-known prov., jibaAbN falaA taEan~a A^aborFA [They are merely envelopes of the flowers of palm-trees; therefore weary not thyself to effect fecundation ]; applied to a man in whom is little or no good; meaning he is like the spathes of the palm-tree in which are no flowers; therefore weary not thyself by attempting to make him good; laA taEan~a being for laA tataEan~a . (MF.)

rawSourceText: A well: (A, K:) or a well not cased with stone or the like: (S, A, Msb, K:) or a well containing much water: or a deep well: (A, K:) or of some other description: (A:) or a well in a good situation with respect to pasture: or one that people have found; not one that they have dug: (K:) or a well that is not deep: (Lth, TA:) or a well that is wide, or ample: (ElKilábeeyeh, TA:) or a well that is cut through rock, or smooth rock, or stones, or smooth stones, or hard and smooth and large stones: (Aboo- Habeeb, TA:) of the masc. gender; (Msb, TA;) [not fem. like biy^orN ;] or masc. and fem.: (Fr, Msb:) pl. [of pauc.] A^ajobaAbN (Msb, K.) and [of mult.] jibaAbN and jibabapN . (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- A well that is dug wherein a grape — vine is planted; like as one is dug for the shoot of a palm — tree: pl. jibaAbN . (ISh, TA.) ― -b3- The inside of a well, from its bottom to its top, whether cased with stone or the like or not. (Sh, TA.) ― -b4- The juron of a well [app. meaning A hollowed stone, or stone basin, for water, placed at the mouth of a well: or, perhaps, a hollowed stone placed over the mouth; for many a well has such a stone, forming a kind of parapet]. (Zeyd Ibn-Kuthweh, TA.) -A2- [ A kind of leathern bag; ] a mazaAdap of which one part is sewed to another, (K, TA,) wherein they used to prepare the beverage termed nabiy* , until, by use, it acquired strength for that purpose; mentioned in a trad., forbidding the use of it; and also called ↓ majobuwbapN . (TA.) -A3- The spathe, or envelope, of the spadix, or flowers, of the palmtree; also called juf~N : the former word was unknown to A'Obeyd: both occur, accord. to different readings, in a trad., where it is said that a charm contrived to bewitch Mohammad was put into the jub~ , or juf~ , of a TaloEap : accord. to Sh, (TA,) it means the inside of a TaloEap [which latter here app. signifies, as it does in some other instances, the spathe, not the spadix, of a palmtree]; (K, TA;) in like manner as the inside of a well, from its bottom to its top, is called jub~ : the pl. is jibaAbN . (TA.) Hence the well-known prov., jibaAbN falaA taEan~a A^aborFA [They are merely envelopes of the flowers of palm-trees; therefore weary not thyself to effect fecundation ]; applied to a man in whom is little or no good; meaning he is like the spathes of the palm-tree in which are no flowers; therefore weary not thyself by attempting to make him good; laA taEan~a being for laA tataEan~a . (MF.)

definition: A well-known garment [or coat ], (Msb, K, TA,) of the kind of those called muqaT~aEaAt : (TA:) accord.
sourceDefinition: A well-known garment [or coat ], (Msb, K, TA,) of the kind of those called muqaT~aEaAt : (TA:) accord. to ' Iyád, a garment cut out and sewed: accord. to Ibn-Hajar and others, a double garment quilted with cotton; or, sometimes, if of wool, a single garment, not quilted with anything: (MF:) [most probably not so much resembling the modern garment more generally known by the same name (for a description and representation of which see my “ Modern Egyptians, ” ch. i.,) as a kind of jub~ap still worn in Northern Africa, described in this Lexicon voce midoraEapN : accord. to Golius, “ tunica ex panno gossipino, cui pallium seu toga imponitur, cum subductitio panno et intercedente gossipio punctim consuta: Italis consona voce giuppa: si ita cum gossipio consuta non sit, dur~aAEapN tunica illa gossipina dicitur: ”] pl. jubabN (Msb, K) and jibaAbN . (S, K.) ― -b2- I. q. diroEN [ A coat of mail; or any coat of defence ]: (K:) pl. jubabN . (TA.) Er-Rá'ee says, lanaA jubabN waA^aromaAHN TiwaAlN bihin~a numaArisu AlHaroba Al$~aTuwnaA [ We have coats of mail, or of defence, and long spears: with them we ply distant war ]. (TA.) -A2- The part of a spear-head into which the shaft enters: (S, K:) and the vaEolab is the part of the spear-shaft that enters into the head. (TA.) ― -b2- [In the TA, jub~apu Alr~umoHi is also explained as meaning mA dxl mn AlsnAn fyh The part of the spearhead that enters into the shaft: but it seems that mn has been inserted here by a mistake of the copyist; and that the true meaning intended is the part of the spear-shaft into which the head enters; though in general the shaft enters into the head.] ― -b3- The part in which is the mu$aA$ap [q. v.] of a horn. (Zeyd Ibn-Kuthweh, TA.) ― -b4- The HijaAj [or bone that surrounds the cavity (see art. Hj )] of the eye. (K.) ― -b5- The contents ( Ha$ow ) of the solid hoof: or the horny box ( qaron ) of the solid hoof: or the joint between the sAq [which seems to mean here, as it does in many other instances, the hind shank, ] and the thigh: (K:) or the shank-joint of a horse or the like ( mawoSilu AlwaZiyfi [commonly applied, as in the S and K voce rusog , to the upper extremity of the pastern, i. e. the fetlock-joint, which seems to be the meaning intended in this instance,]) in the *iraAE [which here app. means the fore leg, not the arm]: or, accord. to As, the part where the wZyf [or shank ] is set into the hoof: (S:) or the part of the rsg [or pastern ], of a horse, where the wZyf [or shank ] joins upon the Hawo$ab [which seems here to mean the upper pasternbone ]: or, as AO says, the part where a horse's wZyf joins to the upper part of the Hw$b : or, as he says in another place, the place where each tibia and hind shank, of a horse, meet; [the hockjoint; ] expl. by mltqY sAqyh wwZyfY rjlyh : and the place of junction of any two bones, except in the back-bone. (TA.) ― -b6- Accord. to Lth, Whiteness of the bTAnyp [a word which I have not found anywhere but in this instance] of a horse or similar beast, extending to the hairs that surround the hoof. (TA.)

definition: Butter, or what is produced by churning, of camels' milk;
sourceDefinition: Butter, or what is produced by churning, of camels' milk; like as zubod is what is produced by churning of cows' or sheep's or goats' milk: (Msb in art. zbd :) what rises upon the surface, (T, S,) or what has collected together [or coagulated ], (K,) of the milk of camels, resembling zubod , (T, S, K,) which camels' milk has not: (S, K:) when a camel shakes about a skin of camels' milk, suspended to him, what is termed jbAb collects at the mouth of the skin. (T.)

definition: The earth, (Lh, K,) in general;
sourceDefinition: The earth, (Lh, K,) in general; (Lh;) sometimes written jabuwbu , as a proper name, without the article, and imperfectly decl., like $aEuwbu : (TA:) so called because it is cut, i. e. dug; or because it cuts, i. e. dissunders, the bodies of those buried in it: (Suh, TA:) and hence ↓ jab~aAnN and ↓ jab~aAnapN , signifying a burial-ground; from Aljab~u and Aljabuwbu ; accord. to Kh; but others derive these two words from jbn : (TA:) or rugged land: (As, S, K:) or hard or rugged land, composed of rock, not of soil: (IAar, TA:) or earth, or dust: (Lh, K:) or the surface of the earth; (ISh, S, K;) whether plain or rugged or mountainous: (ISh:) a word without a pl.: (S:) also coarse, or big, lumps or clods of clay or mud; or of dry, or tough, or cohesive, clay or mud; plucked from the surface of the ground: (TA:) or crumbled clods of clay or mud; or of dry, or tough, or cohesive, clay or mud: (IAar, TA:) and with p , a lump, or clod, of clay or mud; or of dry, or tough, or cohesive, clay or mud. (K.)

sourceDefinition: , (S,) or ↓ jabojabapN , (A,) or both, (K,) and jabaAjibu [which is the pl.], (L, TA,) The stomach of a ruminant animal * (S, A, K, TA) in which xaloE [q. v.] is put, (S, TA,) i. e., (TA,) in which is put flesh-meat cut in pieces; (K, TA;) or in which is put flesh-meat to be used as provision in travelling; (TA;) or in which melted grease (S, K) is collected (S) or put: (K:) or the skin of the side of a camel, cut out in a round form, in which is prepared flesh-meat, (K, TA,) such as is called wa$iyqap , (TA,) which is flesh-meat that is boiled once, and then cut into strips, and dried, or salted and sun-dried; the most lasting of all provision [of the kind]: (S, TA:) or the first and second both signify tripe; in Persian, $knbh or A_i$okanobah . You say, jr~dhu mino viyaAbihi , (A,) or mn vawobihi , (Th, L, K,) as also ↓ jaradahu , (K,) and jr~dhu vawobahu , (Th, L,) He stripped, divested, or denuded, him of his garments, or of his garment: (Th, A, L, K:) [this is the only signification of the verb given in the A as proper; its other significations given in that lexicon being there said to be tropical:] or jar~adotuhu mino viyaAbihi signifies I pulled off from him his garments: and Al$~aYo'a ↓ jaradotu , aor. , inf. n. jarodN , (assumed tropical:) I removed from the thing that which was upon it. (Msb.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) He peeled, or pared, a thing; divested it of its peel, bark, coat, covering, or the like; as also ↓ jarada , (L, K,) aor. and inf. n. as above: (L:) and ↓ the latter, (assumed tropical:) he peeled off anything, Eano $aYo'K from a thing. (S, L.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) He stripped skin of its hair; as also ↓ jarada . (L, K.) ― -b4- (tropical:) It (drought) rendered the earth, or land, bare of herbage: so in the L and other lexicons: in the K, ↓ jarada : but the former is the right. (TA.) ― -b5- (assumed tropical:) I. q. $*~b [generally signifying He pruned a tree or plant]. sourceDefinition: [a coll. gen. n., (tropical:) Locusts; the locust; a kind of insect ] well known: (S, Msb, K:) so called from stripping the ground, (A, Msb,) i. e., eating what is upon it: (Msb:) n. un. with jrAd : (S, Msb:) applied alike to the male and the female: (S, Msb, K:) jrAdp is not the masc. of baqarN , but is a [coll.] gen. n.; these two words being like baqarN and baqarapN , and tamorN and tamorapN , and HamaAmN and HamaAmapN , &c.: it is therefore necessary that the masc. should be [in my copies of the S, “should not be,” but this is corrected in the margin of one of those copies,] of the same form as the fem., lest it should be confounded with the pl. [or rather the collective form]: (S:) but some say that jrAd is the masc.; and jrAdp , the fem.; and the saying raA^ayatu jaraAdFA EalaY jaraAdapK [as meaning I saw a male locust upon a female locust ], like raA^ayotu naEaAmFA EalaY naEaAmapK , is cited: (TA:) it is first called sirowapN ; then, dabFY ; then, gawogaA='u ; then, xayofaAnN ; then, kuitofaAnN ; and then, jrAd : (A 'Obeyd, TA:) As says that when the males become yellow and the females become black, they cease to have any name but jrAd . (AHn, TA.) [Hence,] Aibonu AljaraAdi , (T in art. bnY ) or Abn AljaraAdapi (TA in that art.,) (assumed tropical:) The egg of the locust. (T and TA ubi suprà.) ― -b2- maA A^adoriY A^aY~u jaraAdK EaArahu , (S, K,) or A^aY~u AljaraAdi , (A, L,) (tropical:) I know not what man, (S, K,) or what thing, (A,) took him, or it, away. (S, A, K.)

sourceDefinition: A sect of the Zeydeeyeh, ( of the Shee'ah, TA,) so called in relation to Abu-lJárood Ziyád the son of Aboo-Ziyád: (S, K:) Abu-l-Járood being he who was named by the Imám El-Bákir “Surhoob,” explained by him as a devil inhabiting the sea: they held that Mo- hammad appointed 'Alee and his descendants to the office of Imám, describing them, though not naming them; and that the Companions were guilty of infidelity in not following the example of 'Alee, after the Prophet: also that the appointment to the office of Imám, after El-Hasan and El-Hoseyn, was to be determined by a council of their descendants; and that he among them who proved himself learned and courageous [above others] was Imám. (MF.)

definition: (tropical:) A man having no hair upon him;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) A man having no hair upon him; (S, A, L, K;) i. e., upon his body; or except in certain parts, as the line along the middle of the bosom and downwards to the belly, and the arms from the elbows downwards, and the legs from the knees downwards; contr. of A^a$oEaru , which signifies “having hair upon the whole of the body:” (IAth, L:) [fem. jarodaA='u : and] pl. jurodN . (A, TA.) The people of Paradise are said (in a trad., TA) to be jurodN murodN (tropical:) [ Having no hair upon their bodies, and beardless ]. (A, TA.) ― -b2- Also applied to a horse, (S, A, K,) and any similar beast, (TA,) meaning (tropical:) Having short hair: (TA:) or having short and fine hair. (S, K.) This is approved, (S,) and is one of the signs of an excellent and a generous origin. (TA.) Pl. as above. (A.) In like manner, A^ajoradu AlqawaAy^imi means (tropical:) Having short, or short and fine, hair upon the legs. (TA.) ― -b3- Also (tropical:) A check upon which no hair has grown. (TA.) And (assumed tropical:) A sandal upon which is no hair. (L from a trad.) ― -b4- Applied also to a place; and the fem., jarodaA='u , to land: see jaridN , in three places. ― -b5- Also (tropical:) Milk free from froth. (A.) And the fem., (assumed tropical:) Wine that is clear, (AHn, K,) free from dregs. (AHn, TA.) And (assumed tropical:) A sky free from clouds. (L.) ― -b6- (assumed tropical:) Smooth. (Ham p. 413.) ― -b7- (assumed tropical:) A heart free from concealed hatred, and from deceit, dishonesty, or dissimulation. (L.) ― -b8- (tropical:) Complete; (A, K;) free from deficiency; (A, TA;) as also ↓ jariydN ; (S, A, K;) applied to a year ( EaAmN ), (S, A,) and to a month, (Th, TA,) and to a day: (K:) fem. as above, applied to a year ( sanapN ). (A.) Accord. to Ks, (S,) you say, maA raA^ayotuhu mu*o A^ajoradaAni and ↓ m* jariydaAni , meaning (tropical:) [ I have not seen him, or it, for, or during, ] two days, (S, A, K,) or two months, (S, K,) [or two years, ] complete. (A, TA.) ― -b9- (tropical:) A horse wont to outstrip others; (K;) that outstrips others, and becomes separate from them by his swiftness. (IJ, TA.) ― -b10- And the fem., (tropical:) A voracious she-camel. (A.) -A2- It is also used as a subst.: see jaradN : ― -b2- and see AljurodaAnu . ― -b3- Also (assumed tropical:) The sea. (AAF, M in art. jrb .) ― -b4- And the fem., (assumed tropical:) A smooth rock. (S, TA.)
