definition: , (S, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) aor. and , inf. n. jafolN (Msb) and jufuwlN , (Msb, K,) He (a camel) took fright, or shied, and fled, or ran away at random; or became refractory, and went away at random; or ran away, or broke loose, and went hither and thither by reason of his sprightliness: and ↓ Ajfl he (a bird) took fright, and flew away; or became scared away: (Msb:) or the former, he (an ostrich, K) hastened, or sped, (S, K,) in his pace, (TA,) and went away in the land, or country; as also ↓ Ajfl ; (IDrd, K;) both, said of an ostrich, mean he spread his wings, running; (Ham p. 555;) or spread his wings, and ran quickly, or went away at random and swiftly: (TA:) or jafalati Aln~aEaAmapu means the ostrich fled: (Msb:) and Eanohu ↓ Ajfl , said of anything, he fled from it: (TA, Ham p. 555:) and jafaluwA , aor. , inf. n. jafolN ; (Msb;) and ↓ AjflwA (S, Msb) and ↓ AnjflwA and ↓ tjf~lwA ; (Msb;) they (a company of men) fled quickly; (S, Msb;) or the second (K) and third (S, K) signify they became displaced, (S, K, TA,) and quickly defeated, (TA,) and went away; (S, K, TA;) or these two and the fourth, (TA,) or all the four, (Har p. 373,) they hastened in defeat and flight: (TA, and Har ubi suprà:) and jafalati Alr~iyHu , (K,) and ↓ Ajflt , (S, K,) the wind was swift (S, K, TA) in blowing. (TA.) ― -b2- jafala , inf. n. jufuwlN , (tropical:) It (hair) became shaggy, or dishevelled, and frouzy, or altered in smell, in consequence of its being seldom dressed; or dusty and matted, by reason of its being seldom anointed; (K, TA;) and became raised and spread. (TA.) -A2- jafala is also trans., signifying He made a bird to take fright, and fly away; or he scared it away: its quasi-pass. is ↓ Ajfl [explained above]; the reverse of the rule commonly obtaining: (Msb:) or the former verb, as in the O; not the latter, as in the K; he made a male ostrich to hasten, or speed, in his pace, and to go away in the land, or country; or made him to spread his wings, and run quickly, or go away at random and swiftly: (TA:) and ↓ jf~l he, or it, made an animal, or animals, to take fright, and flee, or run away at random; or scared away it, or them: (TA:) [and, app., he frightened; tajofiylN being also said in the TA to be syn. with taforiyEN , which, I think, is evidently a mistranscription for tafoziyEN .] You say, Alqan~aASu AlwaHo$a ↓ jf~l [ The sportsman scared away the wild animals ]. (TA.) And Eano maraAkizihimo ↓ A^atawohumo fajaf~aluwhumo [ They came to them, and scared them, or frightened them, or made them to flee, away from their stations ]. (TA.) And jafalati Alr~iyHu AlZ~aliyma The wind put in motion the male ostrich, and drove him away, or along: (K:) and [in like manner] Als~afiynapa [(assumed tropical:) the ship ]. (TA.) And jafalati Alr~iyHu Als~aHaAba (tropical:) The wind smote the clouds, and put them into a state of commotion, (K, TA,) and made them to speed along. (TA.) And Alr~iyHu tajofilu AljahaAma (assumed tropical:) The wind carries away the rainless clouds. (Mgh. [See also 4.]) Whence, app., (Mgh,) jafala AlbaHoru samakFA (assumed tropical:) The sea cast fish upon the shore; (Lth, Mgh, K;) a verb like Daraba ; occurring in a trad., in which it is erroneously said to be A^ajofala . (Mgh.) ― -b2- Also, (K,) aor. , inf. n. jafolN , (TA,) He prostrated a man; threw him down upon the ground. (K.) definition: , (A, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (A, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. jahorN and jihaArN , (Er-Rághib, TA,) It (a thing, A, Msb) was, or became, plain, apparent, conspicuous, open, or public; syn. Zahara , (A, Msb,) and badaA , (TA,) and Ealana : (K:) or the radical signification is, it (a thing) was, or became, exceedingly plain to be perceived, either by the sense of sight or by that of hearing. (Er-Rághib, TA.) [Accord. to some, when relating to what is visible, it is tropical; and when relating to what is audible, proper: but if so, it seems to be so much used in the former sense as to be, in that sense, conventionally regarded as proper. See also jahorapN .] -A2- jahura , aor. , [inf. n., app., jahaArapN and juhuwrapN ,] He (a man, TA) was, or became, great, or bulky, (K, TA,) [and therefore a conspicuous object, ] before the eyes of the beholder. (TA.) [And He was, or became, pleasing, or goodly, in aspect: see jahaArapN , below.] ― -b2- Also, (A, Msb, K,) inf. n. jahaArapN , (A, Msb,) It (the voice) rose [ so as to be plainly heard ]; was, or became, high, or loud. (A, Msb, * K.) ― -b3- Also, (S,) inf. n. jahaArapN , (TA,) He, (a man) was, or became, high, or loud, of voice. (S, TA.) -A3- jibir aor. , (Msb,) inf. n. jaharN , (S, Msb,) He (a man) was unable to see in the sun. (S, Msb, TA.) And in like manner said of the eye. (K.) -A4- jaharahu , (Msb, TA,) inf. n. jahorN ; (TA;) and jahara bihi ; (A, Msb;) and ↓ Ajhrhu , (A, Msb, TA,) [and bihi ↓ Ajhr ;] and ↓ jahowarahu ; (TA;) He made it plain, apparent, conspicuous, open, or public. (A, Msb, TA.) ― -b2- jahara AlkalaAma , and jaharabihi ; (K;) and ↓ Ajhrhu , inf. n. A_ijohaArN ; (S;) and bihi ↓ Ajhr ; (K;) and ↓ jahowara ; (TA;) and jahara biAlqawoli , and biduEaAy^ihi , and biSalaAtihi , (TA,) and biqiraA='atihi , (Sgh, Msb, TA,) aor. , inf. n. jahorN and jihaArN ; (TA;) and bqr'A=th ↓ Ajhr ; (Sgh, Msb, TA;) He uttered the speech, and the saying, and his supplication, and his prayer, and his recitation, with a plain, or an open, voice; openly; publicly: (S, Msb, K, TA:) or jahara bikalaAmihi , (A,) and biAlqawoli , and ↓ jahowara ; (S;) and biqiraA='atihi ; (A;) he uttered his speech, and the saying, and his recitation, with a raised, or loud, voice; aloud: (S, A:) and jahara AlS~awota he raised the voice [ so as to make it plainly heard ]. (K.) ― -b3- jahara biAlmaEaASiY , and ↓ Ajhr , and ↓ jAhr , he made known the acts of disobedience that he had committed, by talking of them: he who does so is termed biAlmuEaASiY ↓ mujaAhirN , and simply mujaAhirN . (TA.) And maA fiY Sadorihi ↓ Ajhr He revealed what was in his bosom. (A.) And AlHadiyva baEoda maA hayonamahu ↓ jahowara He revealed the story after he had concealed it. (A.) And ↓ Ajhr AlA^amora He made the case, or affair, notorious. (TA.) ― -b4- Also jaharahu He discovered it (K, TA) ocularly. (TA.) ― -b5- He saw him (a man) without any veil (K, TA) intervening; (TA;) as also ↓ Ajthrhu : (K:) or he looked towards him, or regarded him. (K.) You say, maA fiY AlHaY~i A^aHadN tajoharahu EayoniY There is not in the tribe any one whom my eye regards as worthy of notice or respect by reason of his greatness therein; syn. taA^oxu*uhu . (TA.) And Alqawomu fulaAnFA ↓ Ajthr The people looked towards such a one without any veil intervening between them and him. (TA.) ― -b6- He treated him, or regarded him, with reverence, veneration, respect, or honour: (K:) or (TA) he regarded him as great in his eyes: (K, TA:) he saw him to be great in aspect, or appearance; (S;) as also ↓ Ajthrhu (S, K) and ↓ Astjrhu : (A:) he was pleased with his beauty, and his form, or appearance, or state of apparel or the like; as also ↓ Ajthrhu : (Lh, * K:) or he pleased him by his beauty and form or appearance &c.: (A:) or it pleased him by its beauty; as also ↓ Ajthrhu . (TA.) ― -b7- He saw it (an army, S, A, K, and a people, TA) to be numerous in his eyes; as also ↓ Ajthrhu . (S A, K.) -A5- jahara Albiy^ora , (S, K,) aor. , inf. n. jahorN , (TA,) He cleared out the well, (S, K,) and took forth from it the black fetid mud that it contained; as also ↓ AjtrhA : (S:) or both signify he entirely, or nearly, exhausted the well of its water: (K:) or the former, he reached the water of the well, (K, TA,) in digging: or so jahara alone: (TA:) and accord. to Akh, jaharotu Alr~akiy~apa signifies I cleared out the mud that the water covered in the well, so that the water appeared and became clear. (S.) 'Áïsheh said, describing her father, dufuna Alr~awaA='i ↓ Ajthr , lit., He cleared out the filled-up wells of abundant water so as to make the water well forth; alluding to his rectifying affairs that had become disordered. (TA from a trad.) -A6- jaharonaAhumo We came to them in the morning, at the time called AlS~abaAH , (S, A, K, TA,) when they were inadvertent. (S, K, TA.) ― -b2- jahara AlA^aroDa He traversed the land (S, K) without knowledge. (S.) -A7- jahara Als~iqaA='a He shook the milk-skin to make butter, (Fr, S, K,) and took forth its butter. (Fr, TA.) -A8- jaharati Al$~amosu AlmusaAfira The sun dazzled the eye, and confused the sight, of the traveller; syn. A^asodarato Eayonahu . (K.)

sourceDefinition: : see 1. ― -b2- [Its inf. n.] mujaAharapN signifies The fighting [ with any one ] face to face: and the showing open enmity, or hostility, with any one: and the reading, or reciting, a thing aloud: and the speaking loudly. (KL.) You say, jAhr biAlEadaAwapi , (Msb,) inf. n. mujaAharapN (S, Msb) and jihaArN , (Msb,) He showed open enmity or hostility, with another. (S, * Msb.) And jaAharotuhumo biAlA^amori I acted openly with them in the affair, or case; syn. EaAlanotuhumo bihi . (JK.) [And jAhrhu He treated him openly with enmity &c.] ― -b3- jaAharahumo biAlA^amori , (TA,) inf. n. mujaAharapN and jihaArN , (K,) [is explained as signifying] He vied with them, or strove to overcome or surpass them, in the affair, or case. (K, * TA.) [But gAlbhm , in the TA, and AlmugaAlabapu , in the K, are here evidently mistranscriptions for EaAlanahumo and AlmuEaAlanapu .]

definition: A thing that is plain, apparent, conspicuous, open, or public.
sourceDefinition: A thing that is plain, apparent, conspicuous, open, or public. (K.) You say, raA=hu jahorapF (S, A, &c.) He saw him, or it, [ plainly, ] without the intervention of any veil: (TA:) and ↓ rA=h jihaArFA [signifies the same: or] he saw him, or it, with exceeding plainness: (Er-Rághib, TA:) or the former signifies he saw him, or it, with his eyes, ocularly, or before his eyes, (S, A, Bd in ii. 52, Msb,) without anything intervening: (S:) so in the Kur. [ii. 52], Hat~aY naraY A@ll~`ha jahorapF : (S, Bd:) and [some say that] jahorapF is here originally an inf. n. of jaharotu in jaharotu biAlqiraA='api , [like ↓ jahorFA ,] and metaphorically used in the sense of muEaAyanapF : it is in the accus. case as an inf. n.: or it is thus used as a denotative of state relating to the agent or the object: and some read ↓ jaharapF , as an inf. n. like galabap , or as pl. of jaAhirN , and as such it is a denotative of state: (Bd:) or jahorapF is here from jaharotu Alr~akiy~apa : (Akh, S:) accord. to Ibn-' Arafeh, it here signifies unconcealed from us: (TA:) and in the Kur. iv. 152, ocularly; not concealed from us by anything. (K, * TA.) ― -b2- You say also, kal~amahu jahorapF [and ↓ jahorFA He spoke to him plainly, with an open voice, aloud, or publicly ]. definition: a word of well-known meaning, (Msb,) [a coll.
sourceDefinition: a word of well-known meaning, (Msb,) [a coll. gen. n., Jewels; precious stones; gems; pearls: any kind of jewel, precious stone, or gem: and also applied (as in the T, M, Mgh, Msb, and K, voce tiborN , q. v.,) to native ore: ] any stone from which is extracted, or elicited, anything by which one may profit: (K:) n. un. with p : (S:) [pl. jawaAhiru :] it is of the measure fawoEalu , (Msb,) and is from Aljahoru signifying a thing's “ becoming exceedingly plain to be perceived by the sense of sight: ” (Er-Rághib, TA:) or it is of Persian origin, (TA,) arabicized, (S, TA,) [from Gawoharo ,] accord. to most persons. (TA.) ― -b2- jawoharu sayofK The diversified wavy marks, streaks, or grain, of a sword; syn. firinodN . (T and K voce firinodN .] ― -b3- jawoharu $aYo'K [ The essence of a thing; or that whereby a thing is what it is; the substance of a thing: the constituent of a thing; the material part thereof;] that upon which the natural con- stitution of a thing is as it were based; or of which its natural constitution is made to be; [or, as IbrD thinks to be meant in the K, the collective parts and materials of a thing, of which its natural constitution is moulded; ] expl. by maAwuDiEato Ealayohi jibil~atuhu , (K,) or, as in some Lexicons, [as the JK and the Msb,] maA xuliqato Ealayohi jibil~atuhu [which is virtually the same]: (TA:) Aljawoharu and Al*~aAtu and AlmaAhiy~apu and AlHaqiyqapu are all syn. terms; and the first has other significations; but in the classical language it signifies AlA^aSolu , i. e., A^aSolu Almurak~abaAti [ the original of compound things ]; and not what subsists by itself. (Kull.) ― -b4- [Hence, Aljawoharu Alfarodu (assumed tropical:) The indivisible atom. ] ― -b5- In the conventional language of scholastic theology, jawoharN signifies (tropical:) Substance, as opposed to accident; in which sense, some assert the word to be so much used as to be, in this sense, conventionally regarded as proper. (TA.) -A2- See also jahowarN .

definition: Free, ingenuous, or free-born;
sourceDefinition: Free, ingenuous, or free-born; contr. of EabodN : (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K:) fem. Hur~apN : (S, Mgh, Msb, K:) pl. masc. A^aHoraArN (Msb, K) and HiraArN ; (IJ, K;) not HaraArN , as some say; nor is HiraArN an inf. n. as well as a pl., as others say: (MF:) pl. fem. HaraAy^iru , (Msb, K,) contr. to analogy, and, as Suh says, the only instance of the kind except $ajarN maraAy^iru as pl. of $ajarapN mur~apN ; for the [regular] pl. of fuEolapN is foEalN ; but Hur~apN has this form of pl. because it is syn. with kariymapN and EaqiylapN [as will be seen in what follows]; and mur~apN , because it means xabiyvapu AlT~aEomi . (Msb.) Omar said to the women who used to go forth to the mosque, laA^arud~an~akon~a HaraAy^ira [lit. I will assuredly make you to become free women ]; meaning I will assuredly make you to keep to the houses : for the curtain is lowered before free women; not before slavewomen. (TA.) sourceDefinition: A stony tract, of which the stones are black (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and worn and crumbling, (S, K,) as though burned with fire: (S:) or a hard and rugged tract of ground, strewn with black and worn and crumbling stones, as though they were rained down: (TA:) or a level tract abounding with stones, over which it is difficult to walk, and hard: (IAar:) or one [ whereof the stones are ] black above and white beneath: accord. to AA, of a round form: such as is oblong, not wide, is termed kuraAE : (TA:) pl. ↓ Har~N , (K,) or rather this is a coll. gen. n., (MF,) and HiraArN (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and Har~aAtN and Har~uwna , (S, K,) with w and n like A^araDuwna , (Yoo, S,) to which it is made like because it is fem., as A^aroDN is, (Yoo,) and ↓ A^aHar~uwna , (S, K,) as though the sing. were A^aHar~apN , (Yoo, Sb, S,) though this sing. is not used; (Yoo;) or as though its sing. were A^aHar~u , accord. to Th, who app. means that this place is hotter than others. (TA.)

HaDonN and HiDaAnapN , He put the child in his HiDon [i. e. under his arm, or in his bosom ]: or he nourished him, reared him, fostered him, brought him up, (K, TA,) and took care of him; (TA;) as also ↓ AHtDnhu . (K, TA.) And HaDanato waladahaA , (S, Mgh,) aor. , (Mgh, TA,) inf. n. HiDaAnapN , (Mgh,) said of a woman, (S, Mgh, TA,) She put her child in her HiDon , and [ thus ] carried him [ under her arm, ] on one of her two sides: (TA:) it has a similar meaning to the phrase next following: (S:) or it means she had charge of her child, and carried him, and reared him, or fostered him. (Mgh.) ― -b2- HaDana bayoDahu , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) and EalaY bayoDihi , (TA,) aor. , (S, Msb,) inf. n. HaDonN (Mgh, Msb) and HiDaAnapN (Msb, K) and HiDaAnN and HuDuwnN , (K,) said of a bird, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) He pressed, or compressed, his eggs (S, Msb) to himself, (S,) beneath his wing, (S, Msb,) or beneath his two wings; (so in some copies of the S;) he sat upon his eggs, protecting them with his two sides ( biHiDonayohi ); (Mgh;) he brooded upon his eggs to hatch them: (K:) as also ↓ AHtDn . (KL.) ― -b3- HaDana bayoDapF taHota dajaAjapK lahu Hat~aY A^aforaxato , meaning He put an egg beneath a hen belonging to him, and made her to sit [or brood ] upon it [ until it became hatched ], if remembered to have been heard [from any of the Arabs of pure speech], is a tropical usage of the verb, like as when one says ” The Emeer built the city: “ otherwise, it is correctly [↓ HaD~ana ,] with teshdeed. (Mgh.) ― -b4- HaDanahu Eano ka*aA , inf. n. HaDonN and HiDaAnapN , (tropical:) He made him to turn away, withdraw, or retire, from such a thing, and had it to himself exclusively; (S, K, TA;) as though he put him aside from it, or by its side: he excluded him from participation in it; in which sense minohu ↓ A^aHoDanahu is disapproved: (TA:) he impeded him, or debarred him, from it. (ISd, TA.) It is related in a trad. of Ibn-Mes'ood that, when he made his will, he said, wa laA tuHoDanu zayonabu Eano *`lika , meaning (assumed tropical:) And Zeyneb (his wife) shall not be precluded from looking into that and executing it; namely, his will: or shall not be precluded from it, nor shall any matter [ relating to it ] be decided without her. HaDonN , (K,) (assumed tropical:) He turned his beneficence, (K, TA,) and his discourse, (TA,) from his neighbours, (K, TA,) and his acquaintances, to others: on the authority of Lh. (TA.) -A2- HaDanato , aor. , inf. n. HiDaAnN , (K,) or this is a simple subst., (A 'Obeyd, TA,) She (a ewe [or goat], and a camel, and a woman,) had one of her teats, or breasts, larger than the other. (K.) [See HaDuwnN .]

(S and K in art. rvA^ , &c.) Halabota biAls~aAEidi AlA^a$ad~i [ Thou hast milked with the strongest fore arm ] is a prov., meaning thou hast asked aid of him who will perform thine affair, or thy want: (TA:) or, accord. to A'Obeyd, HalabotuhaA Alx I have milked her &c., meaning I have taken it by force when I could not by gentle means. (TA in art. $d .) And Hulibato SaraAmi , (TA,) or SuraAmu , (S, and some copies of the K, in art. definition: and ↓ HaluwbapN (of which the latter is the more common, TA) A she-camel that is milked;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ HaluwbapN (of which the latter is the more common, TA) A she-camel that is milked; (K;) both signify alike: (TA:) or the former is an epithet, signifying as above; and the latter is a subst., signifying the animal that is milked; (S, * A, Mgh, Msb, TA;) though some say the reverse: or sometimes the former is used for the latter, meaning a milch camel, &c.: accord. to Meyd, the latter signifies a she-camel that is milked for the guest, and for the people of the tent or house: (TA:) the former is used by some as a sing., and by others in a pl. sense: (IB, TA:) and [in like manner] the latter is applied to a single she-camel or ewe or she-goat, and to more: (K:) the pl. (of the latter, TA) is HalaAy^ibu (S, K) and HulubN ; (K;) and HulobN , supposed to be a contraction of HulubN , also occurs as a pl. epithet applied to ewes and to she-goats. (Lh, TA.) You say HaluwbapN tuvomilu walaA tuSar~iHu A milch camel that gives much froth in her milk, and does not give pure, or clear, milk: a prov., applied to him who promises much, but performs little. (Meyd, TA.) And d~r~ato Haluwbapu Almusolimiyna (assumed tropical:) [ The milch camel of the Muslims has yielded a copious supply of milk ] is said when the dues of the government-treasury are in a good state. (IAar, Suh, TA.) ↓ HalobaAnapN , also, signifies A she-camel having milk; (IAar, S, K;) that is milked; a milch camel; (A, K;) like HaluwbN ; (TA;) and so ↓ HalobaApN (IAar, K) and ↓ HalabuwtN (ISd, K) and ↓ HalobaY and ↓ HalabuwtaY , (K,) like as they said rakobaAnapN and rakobaApN and rakabuwtN (TA) and rakobaY and rakabuwtaY : (K:) or fit to be milked: (S and TA voce rakuwbN :) and HaluwbN and the rest of the foregoing epithets, except HalabuwtN , [which I nevertheless believe to be perfectly syn. with them, like as xalabuwtN is syn. with xal~aAbN accord. to the S,] are also mentioned as having an intensive signification. (TA.) You say ↓ naAqapN HalobaAnapN rakobaAnapN (A, K) and rakobaApN ↓ HalobaApN (TA) [and rakabuwtN ↓ HalabuwtN ] and rakobaY ↓ HalobaY and ↓ HalabuwtaY rakabuwtaY (K) A she-camel that is milked and ridden: (A, K:) or that yields abundance of milk and that is submissive to be ridden. (TA.) AZ mentions ↓ naAqapN HalobaAtN , the latter word in the pl. form; as also naAqapN rakobaAtN . (TA. [But in each case I think that the t is a mistake for p .]) -A2- See also HaAlibN . ― -b2- [Hence,] haAjirapN HaluwbN (assumed tropical:) [ A summer-midday ] that draws forth the sweat. (K.)

definition: A certain plant, (S, K,) that grows in the hot season, in the plains and on the sides of valleys, cleaving to the ground so as almost to be buried in it, not eaten by the camels, but only by the...
sourceDefinition: A certain plant, (S, K,) that grows in the hot season, in the plains and on the sides of valleys, cleaving to the ground so as almost to be buried in it, not eaten by the camels, but only by the sheep or goats, (TA,) and by the gazelles: (S, TA:) it increases the milk, and fattens; and gazelles are snared [ while pasturing ] upon it ( tHtbl ElyhA ): (TA:) hence the expressions tayosu AlHul~abi and tayosN *uw Hul~abK [ a buck-gazelle that feeds upon the Hl~b ]: (S:) it is a curling herb, of a dusty colour inclining to green, that spreads upon the ground; when a piece of it is cut off, a milky fluid flows from it: (As, S:) AHn says, it is a plant that spreads upon the ground, evergreen, having small leaves, with which they tan: Aboo-Ziyád says, it is included among what are termed Alxilofap , and is a tree that expands over the ground, cleaving thereto, intensely green, growing most when the heat becomes great: and he adds, on the authority of Arabs of the desert, that it lies upon the ground, having small and bitter leaves, and a root penetrating deep into the earth, and small twigs: it is of the kind of plants termed ray~iHapN . (TA.)

definition: A milker; (S, K;) as also ↓ HaluwbN ; (K;) but the latter has an intensive signification: (TA:) pl. HalabapN . (S, A.) You say, humo Halabapu AlA_ibili [ They are the milkers of the camels ]. (A.)...
sourceDefinition: A milker; (S, K;) as also ↓ HaluwbN ; (K;) but the latter has an intensive signification: (TA:) pl. HalabapN . (S, A.) You say, humo Halabapu AlA_ibili [ They are the milkers of the camels ]. (A.) And $~t~aY taw^uwbu AlHalabaho [ Separately the milkers return ]: (S, A:) for when they assemble to milk their camels, each occupies himself with milking his own, and then they return, one after another; (S, TA;) or they water them together, and return separately to their abodes, where each one milks: (TA:) a prov., (S, A, TA,) relating to the manners of men in assembling and separating: (TA:) you should not say AlHalamaho . (S.) IKtt gives it differently, thus: Hat~aY taw^uwba AlHalabaho [ Until the milkers return ]: but the former reading is that commonly known. (IB, TA.) layosa lahaA raAEK wal`kin~a HalabapN [ They (i. e. camels) have not a pastor, but milkers ] is another prov., applied to a man who asks thine aid, and whom thou aidest, but on whose part there is no aid. (TA. [That is, You ask aid of one to whom you render no aid. See also Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 427.]) ― -b2- [Hence,] AlHaAlibaAni (tropical:) [ The two spermatic ducts; ] two veins, or ducts, which supply the penis with [ the spermatic ] fluid; whence the phrase, dar~a HaAlibaAhu , meaning (tropical:) his penis became erect: (A, TA:) (assumed tropical:) two veins, or ducts, in the kidneys: (Zj in his “ Khalk el-Insán: ”) or (assumed tropical:) two veins, or ducts, (S, TA,) of a green colour, (TA,) on either side of the navel: (S, TA:) accord. to some, (assumed tropical:) two veins, or ducts, within the two horns. (TA. [But I think that, in this instance, Alqrnyn is a mistranscription for AlEroniyn , meaning the nose: see what follows.]) HawaAlibu [is the pl., and] signifies (tropical:) The sources [ whence flows the milk ] of the udder: (A, TA:) and (tropical:) the sources whence flow the tears of the eye: (A, K:) and (tropical:) the sources of a spring, (A,) or of a well: (K:) and HawaAlibu AlA^asoharayoni (assumed tropical:) the veins, or dusts, that excern the mucus from the nose, and the spermatic fluid from the penis. (AA, T. [But see art. shr .])

You say, humo Halabapu AlA_ibili [ They are the milkers of the camels ]. (A.) And $~t~aY taw^uwbu AlHalabaho [ Separately the milkers return ]: (S, A:) for when they assemble to milk their camels, each occupies himself with milking his own, and then they return, one after another; (S, TA;) or they water them together, and return separately to their abodes, where each one milks: (TA:) a prov., (S, A, TA,) relating to the manners of men in assembling and separating: (TA:) you should not say AlHalamaho . (S.) IKtt gives it differently, thus: Hat~aY taw^uwba AlHalabaho [ Until the milkers return ]: but the former reading is that commonly known. (IB, TA.) layosa lahaA raAEK wal`kin~a HalabapN [ They (i. e. camels) have not a pastor, but milkers ] is another prov., applied to a man who asks thine aid, and whom thou aidest, but on whose part there is no aid. (TA. [That is, You ask aid of one to whom you render no aid. See also Freytag's Arab. Prov. ii. 427.]) ― -b2- [Hence,] AlHaAlibaAni (tropical:) [ The two spermatic ducts; ] two veins, or ducts, which supply the penis with [ the spermatic ] fluid; whence the phrase, dar~a HaAlibaAhu , meaning (tropical:) his penis became erect: (A, TA:) (assumed tropical:) two veins, or ducts, in the kidneys: (Zj in his “ Khalk el-Insán: ”) or (assumed tropical:) two veins, or ducts, (S, TA,) of a green colour, (TA,) on either side of the navel: (S, TA:) accord. to some, (assumed tropical:) two veins, or ducts, within the two horns. (TA. (AA, T. [But see art. shr .])

sourceDefinition: A place of milking. (Msb.) -A2- [Also The prunus mahaleb of Linn.; a small kernel of the stone of a wild cherry, much esteemed by the Egyptians, ( and by the Arabs in general, E. W. L.,) and employed by them in many diseases, as a bechic and carminative; brought from Europe: (Rouyer, in the “ Descr. de l'Egypte, ” xi. 452 of the 8vo. ed.:)] a kind of odoriferous tree: (A:) a certain tree having a grain ( Hab~ [which may mean a kernel ]) that is put into perfumes and aromatics; (Msb, * TA;) the perfume in which it is incorporated being termed ↓ maHolabiy~apN : so say IDrst and others: AHn says that he had not heard of its growing anywhere in the country of the Arabs: accord. to Aboo-Bekr Ibn-Talhah, a tree having a grain ( Hab~ ) like that of the rayoHaAn [which is likewise used in medicine, called bizoru Alr~ayoHaAni , i. e. the seed of the ocimum basilicum, or common sweet basil]: accord. to Aboo-'Obeyd El-Bekree, the [ tree called ] A^araAk : (TA:) [J says,] Hab~u AlmaHolabi is an aromatic medicine, the place whereof is AlmaHolabiy~apu , (S,) which is a town ( baladN ) near El-Mósil: (K, TA:) IKh calls it a kind of perfume: some say it is the grain of the xirowaE [or castor-oil-plant ]: others, that the mHlb is the fruit, or produce, of the kind of tree termed $ajaru Alyusori , which the Arabs call AlA^usor : IDrd says that it is the grain with which one perfumes; calling the grain by the name of mHlb : (TA:) the best is the white, pearly, and clear. (Ibn-Seenà, book ii. p. 210.) Accord. to IDrst, this word is originally an inf. n., and Hb~ AlmHlb and $jrp AlmHlb mean Hb~ AlHlb and $jrp AlHlb . (TA. [IbrD informs me that it is a custom of some of the Arabs, previously to their milking, to chew some mHlb , and to anoint with it the teat of the animal.]) -A3- Honey. (K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yaHiyku , inf. n. HayokN and HayakN and HiyaAkapN , accord. to Lth, signifies He wove a piece of cloth: [and it is said in the K, in art. Hwk , that the root of the verb in this sense is with w and with Y :] but Az says that this is a mistake; and that the verb is only HAk having for its aor. yaHuwku , inf. n. HawokN . (TA. [See, however, what follows.]) -A2- HAk , (S, K,) or HAk fiY mi$oyatihi , (TA,) aor. yaHiyku , inf. n. HayakaAnN (S, K) and HayokN (K) and HayakaY (Mbr, TA) [and HiyaAkapN , which see in what follows], He (a man, TA) walked with an elegant and a proud and selfconceited gait, with an affected inclining of the body from side to side, or with a twisting of the back: or he moved about his shoulder-joints and his body in walking, (K, TA,) having much flesh; which manner of walking in women is commended, but in men it is discommended; for the woman walks thus by reason of the largeness of her thighs; but the man, when his thighs, or legs, are wide apart: or, as some say, it signifies he trod the ground vehemently: (TA:) or he moved about his shoulder-joints, and parted his legs widely, in walking, [ as short persons do: for] HayakaAnN signifies the manner of walking of him who is short: (S:) or a walking in which a man moves about his posteriors: all which meanings are borrowed from the action of the HaAy^ik [or weaver, who straddles when at work]: HiyaAkapN , likewise, signifies a walking with an elegant and a proud and self-conceited gait, with an affected inclining of the body from side to side, or with a twisting of the back, and in a lagging manner. (TA.) And you say also, ↓ jA='a yataHay~aku , and ↓ yataHaAyaku , meaning He came walking with his legs parted as though there were something between them. (Mgh, L, TA.)

definition: , (S, Msb, K, &c,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K, &c,) inf. n. [ A_ixoraAjN and] bihi , (S, K,) He made, or caused, him, or it, to go, come, pass, or get, out, or forth; to issue, emanate, proceed, or depart: [ he put, cast, or thrust, him, or it, out, or forth; expelled, ejected, or dislodged, him, or it: he took, led, drew, or pulled, him, or it, out, or forth: he gave it forth: he, or it, produced it: ] as also bihi ↓ xaraja : [but it should be observed that this latter properly and generally denotes accompaniment, like *ahaba bihi ; and may be literally rendered he went, came, passed, or got, out, or forth, with him, or it: ] and ↓ Axtrj , also, is syn. with A^axoraja ; as in the saying, in a trad., faA@xotaraja tamaraAtK mino qirobapK [ And he took forth, or took forth for himself (accord. to a property of many erbs of this form), some dates from a water-skin ]: (TA:) [so, too, is ↓ Astxrj ; as meaning he took, led, drew, or pulled, out, or forth: but this generally implies some degree of effort, or labour; as does also ↓ Axtrj ; and likewise, desire: i. e. it means he sought, or endeavoured, to make a thing come forth: the former is also syn. with A^abodaEahu (q. v.) and A^aHodavahu : and both of them signify, and so does Axrj in many instances, he drew out, or forth; extracted; educed; produced; elicited; fetched out by labour or art; got out; or extorted: this is what is meant by its being said that] ↓ AlAisotixoraAju is syn. with AlAisotinobaATu , (S, K,) and so is ↓ AlAixotiraAju . (K.) A^axorijoniY maxoraja SidoqK , in the Kur xvii. 82, means Cause Thou me to go forth from Mekkeh in a good, or an agreeable, manner, so that I may not turn my heart [or affections] towards it: (Jel: [see also various similar explanations in Bd:]) or mxrj is here a n. of place, or, accord. to the more approved opinion, of time. (TA.) ― -b2- Axrj maA fiY Sadorihi (assumed tropical:) [ He vented that which was in his bosom, or mind ]. (TA in art. srH .) ― -b3- [ Axrj said of a definition or a rule or the like, or of a portion thereof, means (assumed tropical:) It excluded something.] ― -b4- Axrjhu mina AlA^amori (assumed tropical:) [ He excluded him from participation in the affair ]. (TA in art. HDn , &c.) -A2- Axrj [intrans.] He paid his xaraAj ; (K;) i. e. his land-tax, and poll-tax. (TA.) -A3- He hunted ostriches such as are termed xurojN , (K, TA, [in the CK Alxaraja is erroneously put for Alxuroja ,]) pl. of A^axoraju . (TA.) ― -b2- He married to a woman of brown complexion, white intermixed with black, whose parents were, one, white, and the other, black. (T, K.) ― -b3- (tropical:) He passed a year of fruitfulness and sterility, (K, TA,) or half fruitful and half sterile. (TA.) ― -b4- Axrjti Alr~aAEiyapu (tropical:) The pasturing animals ate part of the pasture and left part. (K, TA. [See also 2.])

sourceDefinition: i. q. tanaAhudN ; (S;) similar to muxaArajapN with the fingers, as explained above. (TA.) You say, txArjwA , meaning tnAhdwA [i. e. (TA.)

A_itaAwapN ; (S, K;) A tax, or tribute, which is taken from the property of people; an impost, or a certain amount of the property of people, which is given forth yearly; a tax upon lands &c.: (TA:) or the revenue, or gain, derived from land, (A, Mgh, Msb,) or from a slave, (Mgh,) or also from a slave: (A:) and then applied to the land-tax, which is taken by the Sultán: (A, Mgh:) and the poll-tax paid by the free non-Muslim subjects of a Muslim government: (A, Mgh, Msb:) or xaraAjN signifies especially a land-tax: and ↓ xarojN , a poll-tax: (IAar:) or the former also signifies the poll-tax paid by the free non-Muslim subjects of a Muslim government: it is a term which was applied to a yearly land-tax which 'Omar imposed upon the people of the Sawád [ of El-'Irák ]: then, to the landtax which the people of a land taken by convention agreed to pay; and their lands were termed xaraAjiy~apN : accord. to Bd, it is a name for the proceeds of land: and has then been used to signify the profits arising from possessions; such as the revenue derived from the increase of lands, and from slaves and animals: accord. to Er-Ráfi'ee, its primary signification is an impost which the master requires to be paid him by his slave: accord. to Zj, ↓ xarojN is an [obsolete] inf. n.: and xaraAjN , a name for that which comes forth: and he also explains the latter word by faYo'N : and ↓ xarojN , by DariybapN and jizoyapN : (TA:) the pl. (of xaraAjN , L, TA) is A^axoraAjN and A^axaAriyju [a pl. pl.] and A^axorijapN . (S, K.) AlxaraAju biAlD~amaAni , a saying ascribed to Mohammad, (K, TA,) occurring in a trad. of 'Áïsheh, of disputed authority, but affirmed by several authors to be genuine, means, accord. to most of the lawyers, (TA,) The revenue derived from the slave is the property of the purchaser because of the responsibility which he has borne for him: (A, * Mgh, * K, TA:) for one purchases a slave, and imposes upon him the task of producing a revenue for a time, and then may discover in him a fault which the seller had concealed; wherefore he has a right to return him and to receive back the price; but the revenue which he had required the slave to produce is his lawful property, because he had been responsible for him; and if he had perished, part of his property had perished: (K, * TA:) in a similar manner IAth explains it, as relating to a male or female slave or to other property. (TA.) ― -b2- ↓ xarojN and xaraAjN as used in the Kur xxiii. 74 mean A recompense, or reward. (Fr.) Some, for ↓ xarojFA , in this instance, read xaraAjFA . (TA.) ― -b3- And xaraAjN is also used as meaning (tropical:) The taste of fruit; this being likened to the xrAj of lands &c. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b4- See also xariyjN , in five places.

definition: (S, K) and ↓ xaraAjN and ↓ taxoriyjN (TA) A certain game, (S, K, TA,) played by the Arab youths, (TA,) in which they say ↓ xaraAji xaraAji : (S, K, TA:) accord.
sourceDefinition: (S, K) and ↓ xaraAjN and ↓ taxoriyjN (TA) A certain game, (S, K, TA,) played by the Arab youths, (TA,) in which they say ↓ xaraAji xaraAji : (S, K, TA:) accord. to ISk, you say, laEiba ↓ AlS~iboyaAnu xaraAji [ The boys played at xrAj ], with kesr to the j : Fr says, xrAj is the name of a well-known game of the Arabs, in which one of the players holds a thing in his hand and says to the others, Elicit ye ( A^axorijuwA ) what is in my hand: in the T, ↓ xrAj and xryj are explained by the word muxaArajapN [meaning micare digitis; and hence it appears that the game thus termed, accord. to the T, is the morra, a game common in ancient and modern Italy, and in very remote times in Egypt, in which one of the players puts forth some, or all, of his fingers, and another is required to name instantly the number put forth, or to do the same ]; and it is there added, that it is A game of the Arab youths: Aboo-Dhueyb El-Hudhalee says, A^aziqato lahu *aAta AlEi$aA='i kaA^an~ahu maxaAriyqu yudoEaY taHotahun~a xariyju I was sleepless in consequence of it, (referring to lightning,) at nightfall, as though it were kerchiefs twisted for the purpose of beating with them, under which was uttered the cry xryj ; likening the thunder to the cry of the players: but Aboo-'Alee says that xryj [thus used] is incorrect; that he should have said ↓ xaraAji , but that the rhyme required him to say xryj . (TA.)

definition: One who makes himself a lord, or chief, (S, K, TA,) and goes forth [ from his party, or fellows ], and becomes elevated, or exalted, (TA,) without his having noble ancestry: (S, K, TA:) and it is...
sourceDefinition: One who makes himself a lord, or chief, (S, K, TA,) and goes forth [ from his party, or fellows ], and becomes elevated, or exalted, (TA,) without his having noble ancestry: (S, K, TA:) and it is also said to signify anything that surpasses, or excels its kind and fellows: (TA:) accord. to Abu-l-'Alà, in ancient times, before El-Islám, it was applied to a courageous, or generous, man, the son of a coward or niggard, and the like: ― -b2- and in like manner, to a A fleet, or swift, horse; or one excellent in running; or that outstrips others; not the offspring of a sire and dam possessing the like qualities: [and in the TA, the coll. gen. n. xaArijiy~apN is explained as applied to such horses:] ― -b3- then, in the times of El-Islám, it was applied to A rebel: and a heretic. (Ham p. 188.) [The pl.] AlxawaAriju is the appellation of A party [ of heretics, or schismatics, ] of those following erroneous opinions, having a singular, or particular, persuasion: (K:) they are [ said by some to be ] the Haruwriy~ap [q. v.]; and the xaArijiy~a are [ said to be ] a sect of them; and they consist of seven sects: (TA:) they were so called because they went forth from, (as in one copy of the K,) or against, (as in other copies,) the rest of the people; (K, TA;) or from the religion, or from the truth, or from 'Alee after [the battle of] Siffeen. (TA.) ― -b4- [Also (assumed tropical:) Relating to what is external, or extrinsic, to the mind; objective; real. Hence, AlA^umuwru AlxaArijiy~apu (assumed tropical:) The things that are external, or extrinsic, to the mind; the things that are considered objectively; real things; opposed to AlA^umuwru Al*~ihoniy~apu . (See also xaArijN .)]

sourceDefinition: A ram, (S, K,) and (so in the S, but in the K “ or ”) a male ostrich, (AA, S, A, K,) of two colours, white and black: (S, A, * K:) or a male ostrich of a colour in which black predominates over white, like the colour of ashes: and in this sense also applied to a mountain: (Lth, TA:) and a goat half white and half black: and a horse of which the belly, and the sides as far as the back, but not the back itself, are white, and the rest of any colour: (TA:) fem. xarojaA='u : (A, TA:) which is applied to a female ostrich: (A:) and to a ewe or she-goat having white hind legs and flanks: (AZ, S:) or a ewe that is black, with one hind leg, or both hind legs, and the flanks, white; the rest being black: (TA:) or a ewe white in the hinder part, half of her being white, and the other half of any colour: (T, TA:) and a small isolated mountain ( qaArapN ) of two colours, (A, TA,) white and black: (A:) pl. xurojN . (K.) Also (tropical:) A garment white and red; rendered so by being besmeared with blood. (TA.) (S, TA.) ― -b2- AlA^axoraju The [ bird called ] muk~aA=' ; (K;) because of its colour. (L in art. SH .) ― -b4- EaAmN A^axoraju (TA) and ↓ muxar~ajN (A, TA) and ↓ fiyhi taxoriyjN (S, A, K) and *uw taxoriyjK (K) (tropical:) A year of fruitfulness, or of abundant herbage, and of sterility: (S, A, K, TA:) or half fruitful, or abundant in herbage, and half sterile. (TA.)

(TA.) ― -b2- See also 4, in two places. -A2- xaTaA^ati Alqidoru bizabadihaA , aor. , (tropical:) The cooking-pot threw up its froth, or foam, or scum, (K, TA,) in boiling. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. taxoTiy^apN and taxoTiYo'N , (S, K,) He said to him, A^axoTaA^ota [meaning Thou hast done wrong, or committed a mistake or an error ]: (S, Msb, K:) or he pronounced him, or asserted him, to be doing wrong, or committing a mistake or an error. (Msb.) You say, A_ino A^axoTaA^otu faxaT~iy^oniY [ If I do wrong, &c., tell me that I have done so ]. (S.) ― -b2- Also He made it to miss: so in the saying, xaT~aA^a A@ll~`hu nawo'ahaA God made, or may God make, its [i. e. a land's] star, or asterism, to miss; so that the rain which the star or asterism should have brought did not, or shall not, fall upon it. (TA.) This was [also] said by I'Ab [in a tropical sense] with reference to a woman, as an imprecation, in disapproval of her conduct. (Mgh.) As some relate this saying, the verb is xaT~aY , (Mgh, TA,) and the meaning, God made, or may God make, its [ rain-giving ] star or asterism, to pass it over, and not send rain upon it: and in this case it may be, (TA,) or it is, (Mgh,) from xaTiyTapN , signifying “ a land not rained upon (Mgh, TA) between two lands that have been rained upon; ” (Mgh;) the verb being originally xaT~aTa , and the final T being changed into Y . (Mgh, TA. [See art xT .]) nawo' is [here] the sing. of A^anowaA='N meaning the “ Mansions of the Moon, ” also called the “ stars, or asterisms, of rain. ” (Mgh.) [See more in the first paragraph of art. xT : and see also 4 in the present art.] Accord. to Fr, xaT~aY Als~ahoma and xaT~aA^ahu are syn. [as meaning He made the arrow to pass over, or to miss, the mark]. (TA.) One says also, xuT~iy^u Eanoka Als~uwo'u [ May evil be made to miss thee; ] i. e. may evil be repelled from thee. (ISk.) And xaT~aA^a Eanoka Als~uwo'u [app. for ↓ taxaT~aA^a ] Evil missed thee, or may evil miss thee. (AZ.)

(S, K, TA.) [See also 2, last sentence.] You say, AxTA^ Alr~aAmiY AlgaraDa The archer, or thrower, missed the mark; or failed of hitting it. (TA.) (S.)

definition: , (S, Mgh, Msb,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Mgh, Msb,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. xaloEN , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) He pulled it off; syn. nazaEahu ; (Mgh, Msb;) or stripped it off; or took it off; (TA;) or put it, or threw it, or cast it, off from him; (IAth;) namely, his garment, (S, IAth, Mgh, Msb,) Eano badanihi from his body; (Mgh;) and his sandal, (S, Mgh, Msb,) Eano rijolihi from his foot; (Mgh;) &c.; (Msb, TA;) [as also ↓ AxtlEhu , as appears from its being said that] AixotilaAEN is syn. with xaloEN : (TA:) accord. to some, xaloEN is syn. with nazoEN ; but accord. to Lth, (TA,) the former is like the latter, except that the former is a somewhat leisurely action. (K, TA.) (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence, used as a subst., A cast-off, or] an old, and wornout, garment. (K, TA.) You say, huwayakosuwhu mino xaliyEihi [ He clothes him with some of his cast-off, or old, and worn-out, apparel ]. (TA.) ― -b3- See also xaloEN . ― -b4- (assumed tropical:) A person whose property is won from him in a game of hazard; as also ↓ maxoluwEN . (L.) ― -b5- xaliyEu AlEi*aAri (assumed tropical:) (assumed tropical:) A man who does and says what he pleases; not caring, nor fearing God nor the blame of men; like the beast that has no halter on its head. (Har p. 676.) Also applied to a woman in a state of estrangement [from her husband; lit., Having her headstall, or halter, pulled off, or thrown off; she being likened to a mare; meaning, (assumed tropical:) (assumed tropical:) without restraint ]; having none to command or forbid her: [see 1:] incorrectly written xaliyEapu AlEi*aAri ; for xlyE is here of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN : or you say xaliyfapN without mentioning the E*Ar , from xalaEapN , like ZariyfapN and laTiyfapN [from ZaraAfapN and laTaAfapN ]. (Mgh.) [See also xaAliEN .] ― -b6- xaliyEN is also applied to a Khaleefeh, and a prince or the like, meaning (tropical:) Divested of his authority; removed from his office; deposed; (L;) as also ↓ maxoluwEN : and it is a strange thing, noticed by Dmr and others, that every sixth is mxlwE . (TA.) ― -b7- Also (tropical:) A young man, (S,) or a son, (K,) and a confederate, (IAth, L,) cast off, repudiated, or renounced, (S, IAth, L, K,) by his family, (S,) or father, (K,) or confederates, (IAth, K,) so that if he commit a crime, or an offence rendering liable to punishment, they, i. e. his family, or he, i. e. his father, or they, i. e. his confederates, shall not be prosecuted, or punished, for it; (S, IAth, L, K;) as also ↓ maxoluwEN : (K:) pl. of the former, xulaEaA='u : (K:) and (tropical:) a young man (K, TA) thus cast off by his family, (TA,) who commits, or has committed, many crimes, or offences rendering him liable to punishment; as also ↓ xawolaEN : (K, TA:) (assumed tropical:) one alienated or estranged [ from his family ]: (TA:) (tropical:) one who has broken off from his family, and disagreed with them, and wearied them by his wickedness and baseness and guile; (Mgh, K, * TA; *) as though he had thrown off his headstall or halter, [i. e., restraint,] and who does what he will; or because his family have cast him off, and declared themselves clear of him; (Mgh;) or because he has cast off his kinsfolk, and they have declared themselves clear of him; or because he is divested of religion and shame; (TA;) fem. with p : (K: [indicating that it is a part. n. of xaluEa ; not of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN , as is implied by some portions of the explanations here given:]) (assumed tropical:) bad, evil, wicked, or mischievous: (TA:) (tropical:) [ vitious, or immoral: (see xalaAEapN , whence it is derived:)] (assumed tropical:) notorious for drinking and play: (TA:) [in the present day commonly used in this sense; and as signifying (assumed tropical:) waggish; or a way: ] (assumed tropical:) a player, with another, at a game of hazard, or for stakes laid by both of them to be taken by the winner; (IDrd, K;) as also ↓ muxaAliEN ; (TA.) ― -b10- (assumed tropical:) A wolf; (S, K;) as also ↓ xawolaEN (K) and ↓ xayolaEN . AixowiySaASN ; She (a ewe) had one of her eyes black, and the other white. (AZ, TA.)

definition: A man (S, Mgh) having the eye sunk, or depressed;
sourceDefinition: A man (S, Mgh) having the eye sunk, or depressed; (S, Mgh, K;) having the quality of the eye termed xawaSN : [see 1:] fem. xawoSaA='u : (TA:) which is [also] applied to the eye, meaning sunk, or depressed: (Mgh:) or small, and sunk, or depressed: (A:) and to a ewe, meaning having one of her eyes black, and the other white: (AZ, K:) or having one eye black, and the other, with the rest of the body, white: (TA:) pl. xuwSN , which, prefixed to AlEuyuwn , is applied to camels. (A.) ― -b2- [Hence,] biy^orN xawoSaA='u (tropical:) A deep well; a well of which the bottom is deep; (A, K, TA;) of which the beasts see not the water: (TA:) because one contracts his eyelids ( yataxaAwaSu ) in looking into it: (A, TA:) or xwSA' applied to a well ( rakiy~ap ), signifies of which the water has sunk into the earth. (TA.) And the same epithet applied to a [mountain of the kind called] haDobap , (A,) or qaArap , (K,) (tropical:) High; lofty: (A, K:) because one contracts his eyelids in looking at it. (A, TA.) And riyHN xawoSaA='u (tropical:) A hot wind: (K:) or a vehemently-hot wind: (A:) that makes the eye to blink, or contract the eyelids, ( takosiruhaA ,) by reason of heat: (K, * TA:) in which one does not see without blinking, or contracting the eyelids. (A.) And ZahiyrapN xawoSaA='u (tropical:) A summer mid-day vehemently hot: (A:) or most vehemently hot; (K, TA;) in which one cannot look without blinking, or contracting the eyelids. (TA.)

definition: , inf. n. tadobiyHN , (S, Msb, K, &c.,). said of a man, (S, Msb, &c.,) He stretched out his back, and lowered his head, (As, S, Msb, * K,) so that his head was lower than his posteriors; (As, S, Msb;...
sourceDefinition: , inf. n. tadobiyHN , (S, Msb, K, &c.,). said of a man, (S, Msb, &c.,) He stretched out his back, and lowered his head, (As, S, Msb, * K,) so that his head was lower than his posteriors; (As, S, Msb; *) as also ↓ AndbH ; (K;) and so db~x , [q. v.,] with x : (Msb:) the doing thus in inclining the body in prayer, like as the ass does [when he is mounted], is forbidden in a trad.: (S, Msb:) i. e. he lowered his head in inclining his body in prayer so that it was lower than his back: (A'Obeyd, Msb:) or he lowered his head, and raised his posteriors, in prayer: (TA:) or [simply] he lowered his head; (IAar, T, TA;) as also db~x [q. v.]: (T, TA:) or he did so in walking: (TA:) or he bent his back; (Lh, T, Msb, TA;) as also db~x ; with which As says that dn~x , with n and x , is syn.: (Msb:) and db~H Zahorahu signifies he (a man) bent his back, raising the middle of it as though it were a camel's hump: erroneously related by Lth with * . (T, TA.) ― -b2- Also He (a boy, in play,) lowered his back in order that another might come running from a distance and mount upon him. (Aboo- 'Adnán, TA.) And one says, dab~iHo liY Hat~aY A^arokabaka , meaning Stoop for me in order that I may mount upon thee. (TA.) ― -b3- Also, said of an ass having a sore back, He relaxed his legs, and lowered his back and rump, by reason of pain, on being mounted. (L.) ― -b4- And He was, or became, low, base, abject, or ignominious. (IAar, K.) [And so dan~aHa and dan~aHa .] ― -b5- db~Ht AlkamoA^apu [ The truffles pushed up the ground above them, or] the ground swelled up from the truffles, without their appearing (K) as yet. (TA.) ― -b6- db~H fiY bayotihi He kept in his house, or tent; not going forth. (K.)

definition: , aor. and , inf. n. dubuwrN , He followed behind his back; he followed his back; (M, TA;) he followed him, with respect to place, and also with respect to time, and also (assumed tropical:) with...
sourceDefinition: , aor. and , inf. n. dubuwrN , He followed behind his back; he followed his back; (M, TA;) he followed him, with respect to place, and also with respect to time, and also (assumed tropical:) with respect to rank or station. (TA.) You say, jaA='a yadoburuhumo He came following them. (M, TA.) And dabaraniY fulaAnN Such a one came after me, behind me, (T, A,) or following me nearly. (A.) And dabarahu , inf. n. daborN , He succeeded him, and remained after him. (TA.) And qabaHa A@ll~`hu maA qabala minohu wa maA dabara [ May God curse the beginning of it and the end ]. (S, A.) ― -b2- See also 4, in four places. ― -b3- dabara said of an arrow, (S, Msb,) or dabara Alhadafa , (M, A,) aor. , (S, M, Msb,) inf. n. dubuwrN (S, M, Msb, K) and daborN , (M, K,) It passed forth from the butt: (S, Msb:) or passed beyond the butt, (M, A, K,) and fell behind it. (M, A.) ― -b4- dabara bihi He, or it, went away with it; took it away; carried it off; or caused it to go away, pass away, or cease. (S, K.) ― -b5- dabara Alqawomu , aor. , (M, TA,) inf. n. dabaArN , (As, S, M, K,) like damaArN , (As, S,) [and dabaArapN , like damaArapN (q. v.), and app. ↓ dabaraY , (see AlxayobaraY ,) or dabraY may be a simple subst.,] The people, or company of men, perished; (As, * S, * M, K * TA;) went away, turning the back, and did not return. (TA. [And Adbr (q. v.) has a similar, or the same, meaning.]) Hence, Ealayohi Ald~abaAru Perdition befall him; may he go away, turning the back, and not return. (M, TA.) ― -b6- And dabara (tropical:) He became an old man. (S, A, K.) Hence, as some say, the expression in the Kur [lxxiv. 36], waA@ll~ayolu A_i*aA dabara (tropical:) [ And the night when it groweth old ]. (TA. [See also 4.]) ― -b7- dabarati Alr~iyHu , (S, M, A, K,) aor. , inf. n. dubuwrN , (M,) The wind blew in the direction of that wind which is termed dabuwr [i. e. west, &c., which is regarded as the hinder quarter]: (M, A:) or changed, and came in that direction. (S, K.) [Hence,] dabarato lahu Alr~iyHu baEoda maA A^aqobalato [lit. The wind became west to him after it had been east: meaning (tropical:) his fortune became evil after it had been good]: and dabara baEoda A_iqobaAlK [(tropical:) which means the same: see dabuwrN ; and see also 4 in this art., and in art. qbl ]. (A.) ― -b8- And dubira , (S, K,) a verb of which the agent is not named, (S,) He, (K,) a man, (TA,) or it, a people, (S, M,) was smitten, or affected, by the wind called Ald~abuwr . (S, M, K.) -A2- dabara AlHadiyva Eanohu : see 2. -A3- qabalotu AlHabola wadabarotuhu : see dabiyrN . -A4- dabara , aor. , inf. n. daborN , signifies, accord. to Kr, He wrote a writing or letter or book: but none other says so; and the known word is *abara . (M.) [The inf. n. is explained in the K as syn. with AikotitaAbN .] -A5- dabira , (S, M, Mgh, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. dabarN , (M, Mgh,) He (a horse or the like, M, K, and a camel, S, M, Mgh) had galls, or sores, on his back, (M, Mgh, K, * TA,) produced by the saddle and the like; (Mgh;) as also ↓ Adbr . (K. [But the corresponding passage in the M shows that this is probably a mistake for A^adobaru a syn. of dabirN .])

definition: , (T, M, A,) or fiY AlA^amori (S,) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (T, M, A,) or fiY AlA^amori (S,) inf. n. tadobiyrN , (T, S, K,) He considered, or forecast, the issues, or results, of the affair, or event, or case; (TA;) and so ↓ tdb~rhu : (Mgh:) or its end, issue, or result; (T, M, K;) as also ↓ tdb~rhu : (T, M, Msb, K:) or he looked to what would, or might, be its result: and fiyhi ↓ tdb~r he thought, or meditated, upon it; (S;) [as also ↓ tdb~rhu :] Aktham Ibn-Seyfee said to his sons, A^aEojaAza ↓ yaAbaniY~a laA tatadab~aruwA A^umuwrK qado wal~ato SuduwruhaA [ O my sons, think not upon the ends of things whereof the beginnings have passed ]: (T: [see EajuzN :]) and in the Kur [iv. 84] it is said, AlquroA=na ↓ A^afalaA yatadab~aruwna Will they, then, not consider the meanings of the Kur-án, and endeavour to obtain a clear knowledge of what is in it? (Bd:) and again, in the Kur [xxiii. 70], Alqawola ↓ A^afalamo yad~ab~aruwA Have they, then, not thought upon, (TA,) and endeavoured to understand, ( yatafah~amuwA , K,) what has been said to them in the Kur-án? for ↓ tadab~urN signifies the thinking, or meditating, upon [a thing], and endeavouring to understand [it]; syn. tafak~urN and tafah~umN : (TA:) and ↓ tdb~rhu he looked into it, considered it, examined it, or studied it, repeatedly, in order to know it, or until he knew it. (Msb in art. Aml .) db~r A^amorFA , inf. n. as above, signifies [also] He did, performed, or executed, a thing, or an affair, with thought, or consideration. (Msb.) [And He devised, planned, or plotted, a thing, EalaY gayorihi against another. And hence, He managed, conducted, ordered, or regulated, an affair; because the doing so requires consideration of the issues, or results, of the affair. You say, db~r A^umuwra AlbilaAdi , and, elliptically, db~r AlbilaAda , He managed, conducted, ordered, or regulated, the affairs of the provinces, or country: and in like manner, the affairs of a house. tadobiyrN is also attributed to irrational animals; as, for ex., to horses; meaning their conducting the affair of victory: and to inanimate things; as, for ex., to stars; meaning their regulating the alternations of seasons &c.: see Bd in lxxix. 5. And db~r alone signifies He acted with consideration of the issues, or results, of affairs, or events, or cases; acted with, or exercised, forecast, or forethought; or acted with policy. ] ― -b2- db~r Eabodahu , (M, Msb,) inf. n. as above, (T, S, Mgh, Msb, K,) He made his slave to be free after his own death, (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K,) saying to him, Thou art free after my death: (T, TA:) he made the emancipation of his slave to depend upon his own death. (TA.) ― -b3- db~r AlHadiyva , (inf. n. as above, K,) He related the tradition, narrative, or story, having received it, or heard it, from another person: (As, T, S, K: *) and huwa yudab~iru Hadiyva fulaAnK He relates the tradition, &c., of, or received from, or heard from, such a one: (As, S:) and db~r AlHadiyva Eanohu ; (M;) or Eanohu ↓ dabarahu , (S, K,) aor. ; (TA;) He related the tradition, &c., having received it, or heard it, from him, (S, M, K,) after his death: (S, K:) Sh says that db~r AlHadiyva is unknown; but so the phrase is related on the authority of A'Obeyd: Ahmad Ibn-Yahyà [i. e. Th] disallows yudab~iruhu as meaning he relates it; and says that it is ya*oburuhu , with * , meaning “he knows it, or learns it, well, soundly, or thoroughly;” syn. yutoqinuhu . (T.)

definition: , (S, A, *) inf.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, *) inf. n. mudaAbarapN and dibaArN , (K,) [ He turned his back upon him: see 6. ― -b2- And hence,] (assumed tropical:) He severed himself from him, and avoided him, or shunned him; (TA;) became at variance with him; (A;) regarded him, or treated him, with enmity, or hostility. (S, A, K.) And dAbr raHimahu (assumed tropical:) He cut, or severed, the ties, or bonds, of his relationship; disunited himself from his relations. (A.) ― -b3- daAbarotuhaA I made a slit such as is termed A_idobaArap in her (a ewe's or goat's or camel's) ear. (As, S, K.) -A2- See also 4.

definition: , (M, K, and Bd in ix.
sourceDefinition: , (M, K, and Bd in ix. 25,) inf. n. A_idobaArN (S, M) and ↓ duborN , accord. to Kr, but correctly the latter is a simple subst. [or quasi-inf. n.]; (M;) and ↓ dabara , (IAar, S, K,) inf. n. daborN (TA) and dubuwrN ; (TK;) He went, turning his back; turned back; went back; took a backward course; retreated; retired; retrograded; declined; syn. wal~aYi (S, M, K) and taA^ax~ara (IAar) and *ahaba A_ilaY xalofK ; (Bd ubi suprà, and S and K in art. qbl ;) contr. of A^aqobala . (S, Bd.) And Adbr bihi [ He went back, or backward, with it, or him; removed, or turned, it, or him, backward ]. (S, K.) You say, yudobiru biAld~alowi A_ilaY AlHawoDi [ He goes back with the bucket to the watering-trough ]: opposed to the phrase yuqobilu bihaA A_ilaY biy^ori . (A.) See also dabiyrN , first sentence. And Adbr Eanohu [ He went back, &c., from it, or him ]. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] (assumed tropical:) He feigned himself negligent of, or inattentive to, the want of his friend; (K;) as though he turned back from him. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] Adbr signifies (assumed tropical:) It went backward, to a bad state; said of the affair, or case, of a people. (M, TA.) You say also, A^amorN fulaAnK A_ilaY A_iqobaAlK and [in the contr. sense] AlY A_idobaArN (assumed tropical:) [ The affair, or case, of such a one is inclining to advance, and to go backward, to a bad state ]. (A.) [ A_idobaArN often signifies The retiring, or declining, of good fortune; opposed to A_iqobaAlN : see also 1, in the latter part of the paragraph.] And Adbr Alqawomu (assumed tropical:) The case of the people took a backward course, and there remained none of them. (TA.) And Adbr Aln~ahaAri and ↓ dabara (inf. n. of the latter dubuwrN , A) signify the same; (Fr, T, S, M;) i. e. The day went, or departed; (M, A;) and so AlS~ayofu [ the summer, or the spring ]: and in like manner one says [in the contr. sense] A^aqobala and qabala : so says Fr, and he adds, but you say of a man, Aqbl Alr~aAkibu and Adbr only, with A , though [Az says] it seems to me that the two forms are applicable in the same manner to men as they are to times. (T.) Some read, in the Kur [lxxiv. 36], ↓ waA@ll~ayoli A_i*aA dabara , (T, S,) which, accord. to some, means And the night when it cometh after the day; (T;) or when it followeth the day: (S: [for another rendering, see 1:]) others, (T, S,) the greater number, (T,) read A*A A^adobara , (T, S,) meaning when it retreateth to depart. (T.) [Hence,] Adbrt AlS~alaApu (assumed tropical:) The prayer ended. (Bd in l. 39.) And waA_idobaAra Als~ujuwdi : and waA_idobaAra Aln~ujuwmi : see duburN . And Adbr (assumed tropical:) He died; (K;) as also ↓ dAbr . (Lh, M, K. [See also dabara Alqawomu , in the first paragraph.]) ― -b4- maA A^aqobala mina Aljabali wamaA A^adobara and maA qabala ↓ minohu wamaA dabara signify the same [i. e. What is in front, of the mountain; and what is behind ]. (JK.) -A2- Adbr also signifies He made a man to be behind him. (M.) -A3- And It, (the saddle, S, K, or a burden, M, TA,) and he, (a man, S, Mgh,) caused a camel, (S, M, Mgh,) or a horse or the like, (K,) to have galls, or sores, on the back; galled the back. (M, Mgh, K. *) ― -b2- And His camel became galled in the back. (S, K.) ― -b3- See also 1, last signification. -A4- It is also said [app., of a man, as meaning He slit the ear of a she-camel in a particular manner, i. e.,] when (T) the fatolap [or twisted slip formed by slitting (see A_idobaArapN )] of the ear of a she-camel, (T, K,) it being slit, (T, [but for A*A nHrt in the TT and TA, from which this is taken, I read A_i*aA buHirato , an emendation evidently required,]) turns towards the back of the neck: (IAar, T, TT, K, * TA:) and A^aqobala is said in like manner when this ftlp is turned towards the face. (IAar, T, TT, TA. [See also 3.]) -A5- It signifies also Earafa dabiyrahu mino qabiylihi , (IAar,) or Earafa qabiylahu mino dabiyrihi ; (K;) said of a man. (IAar. [See dabiyrN .]) -A6- Also He, (K,) a man, (TA,) or it, a company of men, (S, M,) entered upon [ a time in which blew ] the wind called Ald~abuwr . (S, M, K.) -A7- And He journeyed on the day called dubaAr , i. e. Wednesday. (K, TA.) -A8- And He became possessed of much property or wealth, or of many camels or the like. (Msb, * K.)

definition: They turned their backs, one upon another.
sourceDefinition: They turned their backs, one upon another. (A'Obeyd, T.) ― -b2- And hence, (A'Obeyd, T,) (assumed tropical:) They severed themselves, one from another, (A'Obeyd, T, S, M, K,) and avoided, or shunned, one another; (A'Obeyd, T;) became at variance, one with another; (A;) regarded, or treated, one another with enmity, or hostility: (M, A:) or it is only said of the sons of one father, or ancestor. (M.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) They spoke [ evil ], one of another, behind the other's back. (TA.) ― -b4- (assumed tropical:) They abstained from, or neglected, aiding, or assisting, one another. (TA in art. x*l .)

(M.)
(assumed tropical:) They spoke [ evil ], one of another, behind the other's back. (TA.)
(assumed tropical:) They abstained from, or neglected, aiding, or assisting, one another. (TA in art. x*l .)

sourceDefinition: contr. of Astqblhu . (S, * Msb, K. *) [As such it signifies He turned his back towards him, or it. ] You say, Astdbr Alqibolapa He turned his back towards the kibleh. (TA.) ― -b3- [As such also, He saw it behind him: he looked back to it: he saw it, or knew it, afterwards: ] he saw, (M, K,) or knew, (TA,) at the end of it, namely, an affair, or a case, what he did not see, (M, K,) or know, (TA,) at the beginning of it: (M, K:) [or rather] he knew it at the end of an affair, or a case; namely, a thing that he did not know at the beginning of it. (T, A.) You say, Aisotadobara mino A^amorihi maAlamo yasotaqobilo He knew at the end of his affair, or case, what he did not know at the beginning of it. (A.) And A_in~a fulaAnFA lawi A@sotaqobala mino A^amorihi maA A@sotadobarahu lahudiYa liwijohapi A^amorihi Verily such a one, had he known at the beginning of his affair, or case, what he knew at the end thereof, had been directed to the right way of executing his affair. (T.) [See also 5.] ― -b4- Astdbrhu EalaY gayorihi He appropriated it to himself exclusively, in preference to others: (AO, K:) because he who does so turns his back upon others, and retires from them. (TA.) El-Aashà says, describing wine, EalaY Al$~arobi A^awo munokirK maA Eulimo tamaz~arotuhaAgayora musotadobirK i. e. [ I sipped it ] not appropriating [it] to myself exclusively [ in preference to the other drinkers, nor denying what was known ]. (AO, TA.)

definition: The location, or quarter, that is behind a thing.
sourceDefinition: The location, or quarter, that is behind a thing. (K. [In the CK, for xalof is put xalaf .]) Hence the saying, (TA,) jaEalotu kalaAmahu dabora A^u*uniY (assumed tropical:) I turned away from his speech, and feigned myself deaf to it: (T, S:) I did not listen to his speech, nor care for it, or regard it. (M, K, * TA.) You say also, A^u*unihi ↓ jaEalahu daAbira (tropical:) He turned away from him, avoided him, or shunned him. (T, * A.) ― -b2- See also dabariY~N . ― -b3- Also, [like A_idobaArN , inf. n. of 4,] (assumed tropical:) Death. (K.) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) Constant sleep: (M, K:) it is like tasobiyxN . (M.) -A2- I. q. ↓ dibaArN ; these two words being pls. [or rather coll. gen. ns.] whereof the sings. [or ns. un.] are ↓ daborapN and ↓ dibaArapN ; which signify A ma$aArap [explained in the TA as meaning a channel of water; but it seems to be here used as meaning a portion of ground separated from the adjacent parts, for sowing or planting, being surrounded by dams, or by ridges of earth, which retain the water for irrigation, as explained in art. $wr , and as is indicated by its Persian equivalent here following,] in, (S,) or of, (K,) land that is sown or for sowing; (S, K;) called in Persian kurod : (S:) and dibaArN signifies small channels for irrigation between tracts of seedproduce; (K;) and its sing. is daborapN : (TA:) [Mtr says,] daborapN is syn. with ma$aArapN ; in Persian karodah [app. a mistranscription for kurod as above]; and the pl. is daborN and dibaArN : (Mgh:) [ISd says,] daborapN signifies a small channel for irrigation between tracts of land sown or for sowing: or, as some say, i. q. ma$aArapN : and the pl. is dibaArN : it is also said that dibaArN signifies i. q. kurodapN ; and its n. un. is dibaArapN : and dibaAraAtN signifies rivulets that flow through land of seed-produce; and its sing. is daborapN : but I know not how this is, unless daborapN have dibaArN for its pl., and this have p added to it, as in fiHaAlapN , and so dbArAt be a pl. pl., i. e. perfect pl. of dibaArapN : AHn says that daborapN signifies a patch of ground that is sown; [as is also said in the K;] and the pl. is dibaArN . (M.) ― -b2- Also A piece of rugged ground in a baHorN [i. e. sea or large river ], like an island, which the water overflows [ at times ] and from which [ at times ] it recedes. (M, K.) ― -b3- And A mountain; (T, K;) in the Abyssinian language: (TA: [Az says, “I know not whether it be Arabic or not:”]) whence the saying of the King of Abyssinia, (T, * K, * TA,) maA A^uHib~u A^an~a liY daborFA *ahabFA waA^an~iYA=*ayotu rajulFA mina Almusolimiyna [ I would not that I had a mountain of gold and that I had harmed a man of the Muslims ]: (T, K:) but [SM says that] this is a confounding of two readings; which are, daborFA mino *ahabK and A^ano yakuwna daborN liY *ahabFA : (TA:) another reading is *aborFA mino *ahabK . (TA in art. *br .) ― -b4- See also diborN . ― -b5- Also, (S, M, K, &c.,) and ↓ diborN , (AHn, M, K,) A swarm of bees: and hornets, or large wasps; syn. zanaAbiyru : (S, M, K:) and the like thereof, having stings in their hinder parts: (B:) it has no sing., or n. un.: (As, M:) or the n. un. is ↓ daborapN or ↓ diborapN ; of which the dim. ↓ dubayorapN occurs in a trad.: (TA:) pl. [of pauc.] A^adoburN (K) and [of mult.] dubuwrN : (As, S, K:) and ↓ dabuwrN , with fet-h to the first letter, signifies bees; and has no proper sing. (M.) 'Ásim Ibn-Thábit El-Ansáree was called HamiY~u Ald~abori [ The protected of hornets, or bees ], because his corpse was protected from his enemies by large hornets, (S,) or by a swarm of bees. (M, Mgh * in art. HmY .) ― -b6- daborN also signifies The young ones of locusts; (AHn, K;) and so ↓ diborN . (AHn, M, K.)

definition: [app. signifies A tract of the western sky at sunset: for] the Arabs said, A_i*aA raA^ayota Alv~uray~aA bidabaro fa$ahorN nitaAjo wa$ahorN maTaro waA_i*aA raA^ayota Al$~iEoraY biqabalo famajodu fatFY...
sourceDefinition: [app. signifies A tract of the western sky at sunset: for] the Arabs said, A_i*aA raA^ayota Alv~uray~aA bidabaro fa$ahorN nitaAjo wa$ahorN maTaro waA_i*aA raA^ayota Al$~iEoraY biqabalo famajodu fatFY waHimolu jamalo , meaning When thou seest the Pleiades near to setting with sunset, then [ is a month which ] is a time of breeding of camels, and [ a month which is ] a time of rain: and when thou seest Sirius [ near to rising ] with sunset, [ then is the glory of the generous man, and the time for the burden of the full-grown hecamel; for] then is the most intense degree of cold, when none but the generous and noble and ingenuous man will patiently persevere in the exercise of hospitality and beneficence, and when the heavy burden is not laid save upon the strong full-grown he-camel, because then the camels become lean and the pasturage is scanty. (M.) -A2- Also, and so is A^adobaArN , a pl. [or rather the former is a coll. gen. n.] of ↓ dabarapN , (S, M, K,) which signifies A gall, or sore, on the back (M, * Mgh, K, * TA) of a horse or the like (M, K, TA) and of a camel, (M, Mgh,) produced by the saddle and the like; (Mgh;) and also on the kirokirap [or callous projection on the breast ] of a camel. (S and K in art. sr .) They used to say, in the Time of Ignorance, A_i*aA baraA^a Ald~abaru waEafaA AlA^avaru , explained as meaning [ When ] the galls on the back of the beast or upon the foot of the camel [ shall heal, and the footstep, or mark, become obliterated ]. (TA from a trad.) -A3- Also inf. n. of dabira . (M, Mgh.)

definition: (M, K) and ↓ A^adobaru (M) A horse or the like, (M, K,) and a camel, (M,) having galls, or sores, (M, K,) on his back (TA) [ produced by the saddle and the like;
sourceDefinition: (M, K) and ↓ A^adobaru (M) A horse or the like, (M, K,) and a camel, (M,) having galls, or sores, (M, K,) on his back (TA) [ produced by the saddle and the like; having his back galled: see dabarN ]: fem. [of the former] dabirapN and [of the latter] ↓ daboraA='u : and pl. [of either] daboraY . (M, TA.) [Hence the prov.,] haAna EalaY AlA^amolasi maA laAqaY Ald~abiru [ What he that had galls on his back experienced was a light matter to him that had a sound back ]: applied to one who has an ill concern for his companion. (M in art. dmr .) You say also A^aHomaqN daAmirN ↓ xaAsirN daAbirN : (T in art. bt : [see art. xsr :]) and daAbirN is said to be an imitative sequent to xaAsirN . (TA.)

sourceDefinition: and ↓ duborN , (the latter a contraction of the former, Msb, [and not so commonly used, like as A_ibolN is not so commonly used as A_ibilN ,]) The back; syn. ZahorN : (S, A, B, K;) the first signification given in the [S and] A and B: pl. A^adobaArN . (TA.) You say, wal~aY duburahu [lit., He turned his back; and tropically,] (tropical:) he was put to flight. (A.) And wal~aAhu duburahu [lit., He turned his back to him; and tropically,] the same as the phrase immediately preceding. (Mgh, Msb.) It is said in the Kur [liv. 45], wayuwal~uwna Ald~ubura [ And they shall turn the back, in flight]: where Aldbr is used in a collective sense, agreeably with another passage in the Kur [xiv. 44], laA yarotad~u A_ilayohimo Tarofuhumo . (S, B.) You also say, ↓ wal~awoA daborapF (tropical:) They turned back in flight, or being routed. (A, TA.) ― -b2- The back, or hinder part, contr. of qubulN , (S, A, Msb, K,) of anything: (Msb:) as, for instance, of a shirt. (Kur xii. 25, 27, and 28.) You say, waqaEa Als~ahomu bidubori Alhadafi The arrow fell behind the butt. (TA in art. qbl .) ― -b3- The backside; posteriors; buttocks; rump; or podex: and the anus: syn. AisotN . (K.) [It has the former of these two significations in many instances; and the latter of them in many other instances: in the S and K in art. jEr , it is given as a syn. of majoEarN , which has the latter signification in the present day. This latter signification may also be intended in the S, M, A, Msb, and K, by the explanation “ contr. of qubulN , ” as well as the “ back, or hinder part, ” of anything: for qubulN very often signifies the “ anterior pudendum ” of a man or woman, and is so explained. The anus is also called Haloqapu Ald~uburi and HitaAru Ald~uburi and $araju Ald~uburi .] Its pl. A^adobaArN is also applied to the part which comprises the Aisot [or anus ] and the HayaA=' [or vulva, i. e., external portion of the female organs of generation, ] of a solid-hoofed animal, and of a cloven-hoofed animal, and of that which has claws, or talons: or, as some say, of a camel, or an animal having feet like those of the camel: and the sing., to the HayaA=' [or vulva ] alone, of any such animal. (M, TT.) ― -b4- (assumed tropical:) The latter, or last, part, (T, S, M, Msb, K,) of a thing, an affair, or an event, (T, S, Msb,) or of anything: (M, K:) pl. A^adobaArN (M) [and dibaArN : see dabariY~N ]. [See also daAbirN .] One says, jiy^otuka duburi Al$~ahori , and fiY duburihi , and EalaY duburihi , and A^adobaAra Al$~ahori , and fiY A^adobaArihi , (tropical:) I came to thee in the latter, or last, part or parts, of the month. (M, K.) And A^adoEuw laka fiY A^adobaAri AlS~alawaAti (assumed tropical:) [ I will petition for thee in the latter, or last, parts, or the conclusions, of the prayers ]. (A.) See also dabariY~N . In the Kur [I. xxxix.], waA^adobaAra Als~ujuwdi signifies (assumed tropical:) And in the latter parts, or the ends, of the prayers: and Als~ujuwdi ↓ waA_idobaAra [virtually] signifies the same [i. e. and in the ending of prostration ], and is another reading of the text: Ks and Th adopt the former reading, because every single prostration has its latter part: or, accord. to the T, the meaning is, and in the two rek'ahs ( Alr~akoEataAni ) after sunset; as is related on the authority of 'Alee the son of Aboo-Tálib. (TA.) The similar expression in the Kur [lii. last verse] waA^adobaAra Aln~ujuwmi is explained by the lexicologists as signifying (assumed tropical:) And during the consecution of the stars, and their taking towards the west, to set: but [ISd says,] I know not how this is, since A^axo*N , by which they explain it, is an inf. n., and A^adobaAr is a pl. of a subst.: Aln~ujuwmi ↓ waA_idobaAra , which is another reading of the text, signifies and during the setting of the stars: and Ks and Th adopt this latter reading: (M:) or, accord. to the T, both mean and in the two rek'ahs before daybreak. (TA.) ― -b5- Also The hinder part, (M,) and angle, ( zaAwiyap ,) of a house or chamber or tent. (M, K.) ― -b6- Eitoqa AlEabodi Eano duburK (S, K) means The emancipation of the slave after the death of his owner. (S, Mgh, * Msb. * [See 2.]) ― -b7- [See also dabiyrN , of which, and of dibaArN , duburN is said in the TA in art. qbl to be a pl.].

sourceDefinition: : see duburN . ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) A turn of evil fortune; an unfavourable turn of fortune: or a turn to be vanquished; contr. of dawolapN : (As, M, K:) dawolapN relates to good; and daborapN , to evil: one says, jaEala A@ll~`hu Ealayohi Ald~aborapa (assumed tropical:) [ May God make the turn of evil fortune to be against him ]: (As, T, M:) this [says ISd] is the best explanation that I have seen of daborapN : (M:) or (so accord. to the M, but in the K “ and ”) it signifies (assumed tropical:) the issue, or result, of a thing or an affair or a case; (M, K;) as in the saying of Aboo-Jahl to Ibn-Mes'ood, when he [the former] lay prostrate, wounded, limani Ald~aborapu (assumed tropical:) In whose favour is the issue, or result? and was answered, “ In favour of God and his apostle, O enemy of God: ” (T, TA:) also (tropical:) defeat in fight; (S, A, Mgh, K;) a subst. from AlA_idobaAru , as also ↓ dabarapN , (S,) and ↓ daAbirapN : (IAar, A, K:) you say, kaAnati Ald~aborapu lahu , meaning (tropical:) His adversary was defeated; and Ealayohi meaning (tropical:) He was himself defeated: (A:) and limani Ald~aborapu , meaning (assumed tropical:) Who is the defeater? and EalaYmani Ald~aborapu (assumed tropical:) Who is the defeated? the pl. of daborapN in the last sense is dibaArN : (TA:) which also signifies conflicts and defeats; (K;) as in the saying, A^awoqaEa A@ll~`hu bihimu Ald~ibaAra God caused, or may God cause, to befall them conflicts and defeats. (TA.) -A2- See also daborN , in two places.

definition: [ Backward: and hence, (tropical:) late ].
sourceDefinition: [ Backward: and hence, (tropical:) late ]. You say, AlEilomu qabaliY~Nwalayosa biAld~abariY~i (assumed tropical:) [True learning is prompt, and is not backward ]: i. e., the man of sound learning answers thee quickly; but the backward says, I must consider it. (Th, T.) And tabiEotu SaAHibiY dabariy~FA (assumed tropical:) I followed my companion, fearing that he would escape me, after having been with him, and having fallen back from him. (M.) And $ar~u Alr~aA^oYi Ald~abariY~u (T, S, A, K *) (tropical:) The worst opinion, or counsel, is that which occurs [ to one ] late, when the want [ of it ] is past; (T, S, K, * TA;) i. e., when the affair is past: or raA^oYN dabariY~N signifies an opinion, or a counsel, not deeply looked into; and in like manner, jawaAbN , an answer, or a reply. (M.) And fulaAnN laA yuSal~iY AlS~alaApa A_il~aA dabariy~FA (AZ, S, M, A, K) and ↓ daboriy~FA , (AHeyth, K,) and the relaters of traditions say ↓ duburiy~FA , (S,) which is said in the K to be a corruption, but it may have been heard from a good authority, and with respect to the rules of the language is chaste, for, accord. to IAth, dabariY~N is a rel. n. irregularly formed from duburN , (TA,) (tropical:) Such a one performs not prayer save in the last part of its time. (AZ, S, K *) It is said in a trad., laA yaA^otiY AlS~alaApi A_il~aA dabariy~FA ; and in another, ↓ Al~A duborFA or ↓ daborFA , accord. to different relations; (tropical:) He will not come to prayer save at the last, or late: and in another, ↓ A^ataY AlS~alaApa dibaArFA (tropical:) He came to prayer at the latest of the times thereof; (IAar, TA;) or after the time had gone: (S:) ↓ dibaArN being a pl. of ↓ duburN and ↓ duborN meaning the last of the times of prayer &c. (IAar, TA.) One says also, ↓ jaA='a fulaAnN daboriy~FA (tropical:) Such a one came last, or latest. (A, * TA.) dbry~FA is in the accus. case as an adv. n. of time [like duborFA and daborFA and dibaArFA ], or as a denotative of state with respect to the agent of the verb. (TA.) In the passage in the K [where it is said that dabariY~N signifies Prayer in the last of its time, &c.], there is a looseness. (TA.)
