definition: , used as a subst.
sourceDefinition: , used as a subst. and as an epithet, [of the fem. gender,] so that one says either riyHu Ald~abuwri or riyHN dabuwrN and simply dabuwrN , but more commonly used as an epithet, (M,) [The west wind: or a westerly wind: the west being regarded as the hinder quarter:] the wind that is opposite to that called AlS~abaA (S, L, Msb, K) and Alqabuwlu , (L,) blowing from the direction of the place of sunset: (L, Msb:) or the wind that comes from [ the direction of ] the back, or hinder part, of the Kaabeh, going towards the place of sunrise: (M:) but IAth rejects this explanation: (TA:) or the wind that comes from the quarter behind a person when he is standing at the kibleh: [but this is a most strange explanation:] or, accord. to IAar, the wind that blows from the tract extending from the place where En-Nesr et-Táïr [or Aquila ] sets [i. e. about W. 10° N. in Central Arabia] to the place where Suheyl [or Canopus ] rises [about S. 29° E. in Central Arabia]: (M:) or that comes from the direction of the south ( Aljanuwb ), going towards the place of sunrise: (Msb:) it is the worst of winds: it is said that it does not fecundate trees, nor raise clouds: (Meyd, TA:) and in a trad. it is said that the tribe of 'Ád was destroyed by it: (T, TA:) it blows only in the hot season, and is very thirsty: (TA voce nakobaA='u :) pl. duburN and dabaAy^iru . (M.) [Hence the saying,] EaSafato dabuwruhu wasaqaTato Eabuwruhu [lit. His west wind, or westerly wind, blew violently, and his Sirius set: meaning (tropical:) his evil fortune prevailed, and his good fortune departed: for the dbwr is the worst of winds, as observed above, and Sirius sets aurorally in the beginning of winter, when provisions become scarce]. (A.) -A2- See also daborN , last sentence but two.

definition: A twist which a woman turns backward ( bihi ↓ maA A^adobarato ), in twisting it: (S, K:) or what one turns backward from his chest [ in rolling it against the front of his body ]: (Yaakoob, S, A, K:)...
sourceDefinition: A twist which a woman turns backward ( bihi ↓ maA A^adobarato ), in twisting it: (S, K:) or what one turns backward from his chest [ in rolling it against the front of his body ]: (Yaakoob, S, A, K:) and qabiylN signifies “ what one turns forward ( maA A^aqobala bihi ) towards his chest: ” (Yaakoob, S, A:) or the former, what the twister turns backward towards his knee [ in rolling it against his thigh; against which, or against the front of the body, the spindle is commonly rolled, except when it is twirled only with the hand while hanging loosely]: and the latter, “ what he turns forward towards his flank or waist: ” (As, T:) [whence the saying,] qabalotu A^uxoraY ↓ AlHabolu mar~apF wa dabarotuhu [ I turned the rope, or cord, forward, or toward me, in twisting it, one time, and turned it backward, or from me, another time ]: (TA in art. qbl :) or dabiyrN signifies the twisting of flax and wool: and qabiylN , the “ twisting of cotton. ” (Lth, T.) One says, Earafa qabiylahu mino dabiyrihi , meaning (tropical:) He knew, or distinguished, his obedience from his disobedience; (K,) TA;) or dabiyrahu mino qabiylihi his disobedience from his obedience. (Aboo-' Amr Esh-Sheybánee, IAar, T.) And fulaAnN maA yaEorifu qabiylFA mino dabiyrK (S, A) or qabiylahu mn dabiyrihi (TA) (tropical:) [ Such a one knows not &c.]: or maA yaEorifu qabiylFA mino dabiyrK and ↓ qibaAlFA mino dibaArK he knows not the ewe, or she-goat, that is termed muqaAbalap from that which is termed mudaAbarap : or him who advances towards him from him who goes back from him: or the parentage of his mother from that of his father: (K in art. qbl :) or that of his father from that of his mother: so says IDrd in explaining the former phrase: or a qubul from a dubur : or a thing when advancing from a thing when going back: and the pls. of each are qubulN and duburN . (TA in that art.) Accord. to El-Mufaddal, dabiyrN signifies An arrow's losing in a game of chance [such as Almayosir ]; and qabiylN , its “ winning therein. ” (T, TA.) [See qabiylN , in art. qbl .] ― -b2- Also The upper [because it is the hinder ] part of the ear of a camel: the lower part is called the qabiyl . (TA in art. qbl .)

definition: act. part. n. of dabara , Following (S, K, TA) behind the back; following the back; following, with respect to place, and also with respect to time, and also (assumed tropical:) with respect to rank...
sourceDefinition: act. part. n. of dabara , Following (S, K, TA) behind the back; following the back; following, with respect to place, and also with respect to time, and also (assumed tropical:) with respect to rank or station. (TA.) [Hence,] daAbiru qawomK The last that remains of a people or party; he who comes at the end of a people or party; as also ↓ daAbiratuhumo ; which likewise signifies those who remain after them: and ↓ daAbirapN [so in the TA, but accord. to the T daAbirN , which I think the right reading,] signifies one who comes after; or follows, another. (TA.) And Ald~alowu bayona qaAbilK wadaAbirK The bucket is between one who advances with it to the well and one who goes back, or returns, with it to the wateringtrough. (A.) And jaEalahu daAbira A^u*unihi : see daborN . And A^amosi Ald~aAbiru and ↓ Almudobiru Yesterday that is past: (S, M, K:) the epithet being here a corroborative. (S, * M.) You say, SaAruwA kaA^amosi Ald~aAbiri [ They became like yesterday that is past ]. (A.) And hayohaAta *ahaba kamaA *ahaba A^amosi Ald~aAbiru [ Far distant is he, or it! He, or it, hath gone like as hath gone yesterday that is past ]. (S.) ― -b2- Also An arrow that passes forth from the butt, (S, Msb, K,) [or passes beyond it, (see 1,)] and falls behind it: (TA:) you say sahomN daAbirN , and sihaAmN daAbirapN and dawaAbiru . (Msb.) ― -b3- An arrow that does not win [in the game called Almayosir ]; (K, TA;) contr. of qaAbilN . (S, TA.) ― -b4- The last arrow remaining in the quiver. (A.) ― -b5- The last of anything; (Ibn-Buzurj, T, M, K;) and so ↓ daAbirapN : (M:) [see also duburN :] and (accord. to As and others, TA) the root, stock, race, or the like; syn. A^aSolN . (K.) One says, qaTaEa A@ll~`hu daAbirahumo May God cut off the last that remain of them. (S.) And qaTaEa A@ll~`hu daAbirahu May God cut off the last of him, or it: (A:) or may God extirpate him. (As, T.) And in the Kur [vi. 45] it is said, faquTiEa daAbiru Alqawomi And the last of the people were extirpated. (M, TA.) And in a trad., yuqoTaEu bihi daAbiruhumo All of them shall be cut off thereby, not one remaining. (TA.) ― -b6- See also dabirN , last sentence. ― -b7- As an epithet applied to a camel: see gud~apN .

definition: A slit in the ear [of a ewe or she-goat or she-camel], which being made, that thing [ thus made, meaning the pendulous strip, ] is twisted, and turned backward: if turned forward, it is termed...
sourceDefinition: A slit in the ear [of a ewe or she-goat or she-camel], which being made, that thing [ thus made, meaning the pendulous strip, ] is twisted, and turned backward: if turned forward, it is termed A_iqobaAlapN : and the hanging piece of skin of the ear is termed A_idobaArapN [in the former case] and A_iqobaAlapN [in the latter case]; as though it were a zanamap [q. v.]; (As, S, M, * K;) and, respectively, ↓ A_idobaArN and A_iqobaAlN , and ↓ diborapo and qibolapN . (TA in art. qbl .) The ewe or she-goat [to which this has been done] is termed ↓ mudaAbarapN [in the former case] and muqaAbalapN [in the latter]: and you say of yourself [when you have performed the operation, in these two cases respectively], daAbarotuhaA and qaAbalotuhaA : and the she-camel is termed *aAtu A_idobaArap and *aAtu A_iqobaAlapN ; (As, S, K;) and so is the ewe or she-goat; (As, T;) and the she-camel, ↓ *aAtu A_idobaArK and *aAtN A_iqobaAlK . definition: , (S, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. daqaEN , (Msb,) He (a man, S) clave to the dust, or earth, (S, Msb, K,) by reason of abasement, or abjectness; (S, Msb;) or, as some say, by reason of poverty: or he clave to the dust, or earth, and became poor; as also ↓ AdqE : or he clave to the dust, or earth, or some other thing, by reason of anything whatever: (TA:) and he became lowly, humble, or submissive, and clave to the dust, or earth. (S, TA.) It is said in a trad. [cited voce xajila ], A_i*aA juEotun~a daqiEotun~a When ye [women] are hungry, ye become lowly, humble, or submissive, and cleave to the dust, or earth; (S, TA;) or ye bear poverty ill. (TA in art. xjl .) ― -b2- He was, or became, grieved, unhappy, or disquieted in mind; as also daqaEa , inf. n. daqoEN and duquwEN ; and lowly, humble, submissive, or abased. (TA.) ― -b3- He was, or became, lowly, humble, or submissive, in seeking, or requesting, an object of want, and desired it vehemently. (TA.) ― -b4- He was, or became, content with mean sustenance. (K; but only the inf. n., namely daqaEa , of the verb in this sense, is there mentioned.) ― -b5- [And, as shown above,] He bore poverty ill. (S, K; but only the inf. n., as above, is mentioned in them.) [Thus the verb bears two contr. meanings.] El-Kumeyt says, walamo yadoqaEuwA Einoda maA naAbahumo liSarofi zamaAnK walamo yaxojaluwA i. e. They did not bear poverty ill [ on the occasion of what befell them by reason of a changing of fortune ], nor did they bear richness ill: or, as some say, they did not cleave to the ground in consequence of poverty and hunger, &c., nor did they become lazy, or indolent, and remiss, in seeking subsistence. (TA.) ― -b6- He (a young camel) turned away with disgust from the milk; was averse from it; loathed, or nauseated, it; syn. ba$ima Eani All~abani . (K.) ― -b7- daqaEa , inf. n. daqoEN , [mentioned above,] also signifies He pursued small means of gain; as also ↓ AdqE . (TA.)

definition: A disease, disorder, distemper, sickness, illness, or malady;
sourceDefinition: A disease, disorder, distemper, sickness, illness, or malady; syn. maraDN , (Lth, T, S, M, Msb, K,) or Eil~apN ; (Mgh;) external or internal: (Lth, T:) [it is both physical and moral: ] signifying also a vice, defect, fault, or blemish; external or internal: so that one says, daA='uAl$~uH~a A^a$ad~u AlA^adowaA='i [ The vice of avarice is the most grievous of vices ]: (Lth, T, TA:) for the pl. is A^adowaA='N , (S, M, Msb, K,) the only instance of a sing. memdood having a pl. memdood: (IKh, TA:) hence also, ↓ A^aY~N daA='K A^adowaA^u mina Albuxoli (Mgh,) or A^adowaY , but IAth says that the correct word is A^adowaA^u , (TA,) i. e. [ What vice is ] more grievous, (Mgh,) or worse, (TA,) [ than niggardliness? ] occurring in a trad.: and the saying of a woman, kul~u daA='K lahu daA='N , meaning Every vice that is in men is in him: (Lth, T, TA:) and may~itu Ald~aA='i One whose evilness is dead, (K and TA in art. blh ,) so that he is not cognizant of it; (TA in that art.;) said of a person when he does not bear malice towards him who does evil to him. (Lth, T, and TA in the present art.) daA='u Alfiyli : see art. fyl . daA='u Alv~aEolabi : see art. vElb . daA='u Al*~iy^obi [ The disease of the wolf ] means (assumed tropical:) hunger. (Th, M, K. [See also art. *A^b .]) daA='N AlA^asadi [ The disease of the lion ] means AlHmY [app. AlHum~aY , i. e. (assumed tropical:) fever ]. (AM, TA.) daA='u AlZ~aboYi , (S, TA,) or daA='u ZaboYK , (M, TA,) [ The disease of the gazelle, or of a gazelle, ] accord. to AA, (M, TA,) means (assumed tropical:) health, or soundness, and briskness, or sprightliness; (TA;) or no disease; like as [it is said that] there is no disease in the gazelle: (S, M:) or, accord. to ElUmawee, binaA daA='u ZaboYK means that when he desires to leap, he pauses a little and then leaps: but A'Obeyd prefers the former explanation. (M.) daA='u Almuluwki [ The disease of kings ] means (assumed tropical:) the enjoyment of plenty and pleasure and softness or delicacy. (TA.) daA='u AlkiraAmi [ The disease of the generous ], (assumed tropical:) debt and poverty. (TA.) daA='u AlD~araAy^iri [ The disease of fellow-wives ], (assumed tropical:) constant evil. (TA.) daA='u AlbaToni . [ The disease of the belly ], (assumed tropical:) trial, or dissension, or the like, ( Alfitonapu ,) in which one cannot find the right way to act. (TA.) -A2- daA='N as an epithet, (Lth, Sh, T, M, and so in some copies of the K,) or ↓ daA='K (S, and so in other copies of the K,) applied to a man, Diseased, disordered, distempered, sick, or ill; or having a disease, disorder, &c.: (Lth, Sh, T, S, M, K:) the former is [originally an inf. n., and therefore is] also applied to a woman; (A, TA;) or it is [originally dawiy^N ,] of the measure faEilN , and the fem. is daA='apN , (Lth, T, M, TA,) which is also mentioned in the A as applied to a woman, as well as daA='N ; (TA;) and the dual is daAA=ni ; and the pl. A^adowaA='N : (Lth, Sb, Sh, T, TA:) and ↓ mdiYo'N signifies the same; (S, K;) fem. with h : and so ↓ dyiy^ ; [as though originally dawiYo'N or dayowiy^N , of the measure faEiylN or fayoEilN , like jay~idN and say~idN ;] fem. with p : (K:) or, accord. to the O, day^iY~N , of the measure faEiylN , applied to a man; and day^iy~apN , of the measure faEiylapN , applied to a woman: or, accord. to the T, dayoA^FY , of the measure fayoEalN , applied to a man; and dayoA^ayapN , of the measure fayoEalapN , applied to a woman. (TA.) The saying, in a trad., waA_il~aA fayamiynuhu A^an~ahu maA baAEaka daA='K means [ And otherwise, his oath shall be, that he did not sell to thee ] a girl having a disease, or vice, or the like: and similar to this is the saying, rud~a Ald~aA='u bidaAy^ihi That which had a vice, or the like, was returned because of the vice, &c., thereof. (Mgh.)

definition: The ninth letter of the alphabet;
sourceDefinition: The ninth letter of the alphabet; called *aAlN : it is one of the letters termed majohuwrap [or vocal, i. e. pronounced with the voice, and not with the breath only]: and of the letters termed livawiy~ap [or gingival], which are v and * and Z ; wherefore it is substituted for v in talaEo*ama for talaEovama ; and it is said to be substituted for the unpointed d in fa$ar~i*o bihimo , [as some read] in the Kur [viii. 59, for fa$ar~ido bhm ]. (TA.) -A2- [As a numeral, it denotes Seven hundred. ]

definition: He (a man, M) was frightened by the wolf;
sourceDefinition: He (a man, M) was frightened by the wolf; (M, K;) as also *ay^iba , aor. ; and *aw^uba , aor. : (K:) or he (a man) was assailed, fallen upon, come upon, or overtaken, by the wolf. (Ibn-Buzurj, T.) And [hence, in the opinion of ISd, as he says in the M,] (tropical:) He was frightened by anything; (M, K;) and so ↓ A*A^b , (AA, T, S, M, K,) inf. n. A_i*oA=bN ; (TA;) said of a man. (S.) [Hence also,] *aA^abahu , (M, K,) aor. , (K,) [inf. n. *aA^obN ,] (tropical:) He frightened him [ like as does a wolf ]: (M, A, K, TA:) and *aA^abatohu Aljin~u (A, TA) and ↓ t*A^~bthu , as also t*E~bthu , (T, TA,) (tropical:) The jinn, or genii, frightened him. (T, A, TA.) [And hence, app.,] *aA^abotuhu Alr~iyHu (tropical:) The wind came to him from every side, like the wolf; when guarded against from one direction, coming from another direction: (A:) and Ailr~iyHu ↓ t*A='bti , (T, S, M, K,) and ↓ t*A^~bt , (S, M, K,) (tropical:) The wind varied, (T, S, M,) or came now from one direction and now from another direction, (S, M, K,) so says As, (S,) feebly: (M, K:) accord. to As, from Al*~iy^obu , (S,) [i. e.] it is likened to the wolf, (M,) because his motions are of the like description: (S:) or, accord. to some, Al*~iy^obu is derived from ↓ t*A='bt AlryH meaning the wind blew from every direction; because the wolf comes from every direction. (MF, TA.) ― -b2- Also, (i. e. *uy^iba ) He (a man) had his sheep, or goats, fallen upon by the wolf. (S, K.) ― -b3- And *aw^uba , (T, S, M, A, K,) aor. , (T, S, K,) inf. n. *aA=bapN ; (S, M, K;) and *ay^iba ; (M, A, K;) and ↓ t*A^~b ; (M, K;) (tropical:) He (a man, T, S, M) was, or became, bad, wicked, deceitful, or crafty, (T, S, M, A, K,) like the wolf, (S, M, A, K,) or as though he became a wolf. (T.) ― -b4- And *aA^aba , aor. , (tropical:) He acted like the wolf; when guarded against from one direction, coming from another direction. (TA.) [And probably (assumed tropical:) He howled like the wolf; for,] accord. to Kr, (M,) *aA^obN signifies the uttering a loud, or vehement, cry or sound. (M, K.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) He hastened, or was quick, in pace, or journeying; (K;) as also ↓ A*A^b . (TA.) -A2- *aA^abahu , [aor. ,] inf. n. *aA^obN , also signifies He despised him; and so *aA^amahu : (T:) or he drove him away, and despised him: (ISk, T, S, M, K:) or he drove him away, (Lh, M, TA,) and beat him; (Lh, TA;) and so *aA^amahu : (M, TA:) [or he blamed, or dispraised, him; like *aA^amahu ; for,] accord. to Kr, (M,) *aA^obN signifies the act of blaming, or dispraising. (M, K.) ― -b2- And He drove him, or urged him on: (K:) or *aA^aba AlA_ibila , inf. n. *aA^obN , he drove, or urged on, the camels. (S, M.) -A3- He collected it; (T, K;) namely, a thing. (T.) ― -b2- He made it even; syn. saw~aAhu . (CK: omitted in other copies of the K and in the TA.) One says of the woman who makes even ( tusaw~iY ) her vehicle, [meaning the part of her camel-vehicle upon which she sits,] maA A^aHosana maA *aA^abatohu [ How well has she made it even! ] (T.) ― -b3- He made it; namely, a [camel's saddle such as is called] qatab (K) and [such as is called] a raHol (TA.) -A4- He made, [or disposed, ] for him, (namely, a boy,) a *uw^aAbap [q. v.]; as also ↓ A*A^bhu and ↓ *A^~bhu . (K.) -A5- *uy^iba said of a horse, He was, or became, affected with the disease termed *iy^obap . (T, Mgh.)

sourceDefinition: , also pronounced *iybN , without ' , (S, Msb, K,) originally with ' , (T, S,) The wolf, wild dog, or dog of the desert; kalobu Albar~i : (M, A, K:) applied to the male and the female; (Msb;) and sometimes, also, (Msb,) the female is called *iy^obapN : (S, M, Msb, K:) pl. (of pauc., S, Msb) A^a*ow^ubN , and (of mult., S, Msb) *iy^aAbN , (S, M, Msb, K,) which may also be pronounced *iyaAbN , with Y , because of the kesreh, (Msb,) and *uw^baAnN (S, M, Msb, K) and *iy^obaAnN . (TA.) ― -b2- You say, Al*~iy^obu yukan~aY A^abaA jaEodapa [ The wolf is surnamed Aboo-Jaadeh ]: i. e. its surname is good, but its actions are foul. (TA. [See art. jEd ; and see also Freytag's Arab. Prov., i. 449.]) ― -b3- And Al*~iy^obu yaA^o*uw AlgazaAla [ The wolf lies in wait for the young gazelle ]: a prov. alluding to perfidy. (TA.) ― -b4- And huwa *iy^obN fiY val~apK (tropical:) [ He is a wolf among a flock of sheep ]. (A.) ― -b5- And *iy^obapu miEozFY waZaliymN fiY Alxubori [ A she-wolf among the goats, and a heostrich when tried ]: i. e., in his evil nature he is like a [she-] wolf that attacks a herd of goats; and when tried, like a he-ostrich, which, if one say to it “ Fly, ” says “ I am a camel, ” and when one says to it “ Carry a burden, ” says “ I am a bird: ” a prov. applied to a crafty and deceitful person. (TA.) ― -b6- And A^akalahumo AlD~abuEu wa Al*~iy^obu [ The hyena and the wolf devoured them ]; meaning (tropical:) dearth, or drought: and A^aSaAbatohumo sanapN DabuEN wa*iy^obN , meaning (tropical:) A year that was one of dearth, or drought, befell them. (A.) ― -b7- *iy^obuhu laA ya$obaEu [ His wolf will not be satiated ], a phrase used by a poet, means (assumed tropical:) his tongue [ will not be satisfied ]; i. e. he devours the reputation of another like as the wolf devours flesh. (M.) ― -b8- *iy^obu yuwsufa [ The wolf of Joseph ] is a prov. applied to him who is charged with the crime of another. (TA.) ― -b9- *uw^obaAnu AlEarabi , (S, M, A, K,) also pronounced *uwbaAn , without ' , (TA,) [ The wolves of the Arabs, ] means (tropical:) the thieves, (M, K,) or sharpers, (A,) and paupers, (A, K,) of the Arabs; (M, A, K;) or the paupers of the Arabs, who practise thieving: (T, S:) because they act like wolves. (TA.) ― -b10- *iy^aAbu AlgaDaA The wolves of the ghadà, that frequent the trees so called, (TA,) is an appellation of the sons of Kaab Ibn-Málik Ibn-Handhalah; (M, K;) because of their bad character; (M;) for the wolf that frequents those trees is the worst of wolves. (TA.) ― -b11- daA='u Al*~iy^obi [ The wolf's disease ] means (assumed tropical:) hunger; for they assert that the wolf has no other disease than hunger; (K, TA;) and they say A^ajowaEu mino *iy^obK [ More hungry than a wolf ]; because he is always hungry: or (assumed tropical:) death; because [it is said that] the wolf has no other sickness than that of death; and hence they say A^aSaH~u mina Al*~iy^obi [ More sound than the wolf ]. (TA.) [Hence the prov., ramaAhu A@ll~`hu bidaA='i Al*~iy^obi : see 1 in art. rmY .] ― -b12- Al*~iy^obaAni , in the dual form, [ The two wolves, ] is the name of (assumed tropical:) two white stars [app. ζ and η of Draco ] between those called AlEawaAy^i*u and those called AlfaroqadaAni : and A^aZofaAru Al*~iy^obi [ The claws of the wolf ] is the name of (assumed tropical:) certain small stars before those called Al*~iy^obaAni . (K.) ― -b13- Einabu Al*~iy^obi : see vaEolabN . ― -b14- See also the next paragraph.

sourceDefinition: (also pronounced *uwaAbapN , T and K in art. *wb ,) A portion [or lock ] of hair, (S, A,) hanging down loosely from the middle of the head to the back: (A:) or the hair of the fore part of the head; the hair over the forehead; syn. naASiyapN ; (M, K;) so called because, hanging down, it moves to and fro, or from side to side: (M:) or the place whence that hair grows: (M, K:) or the hair that surrounds the duw~aArap [or round part ] of the head: (AZ, T:) or plaited hair of the head: and the part of the head which is the place thereof: (Lth, T:) or a plait of hair hanging down: if twisted, it is called EaqiySapN : (Msb:) and [a horse's forelock; or] hair (M, K) of the head, (M,) in the upper part of the naASiyap , of the horse: (M, K:) pl. (in all its senses, M, TA) *awaAy^ibu , (T, S, M, Msb, K,) originally, (S, K,) or regularly, (T,) *aA=y^ibu , changed to render it more easy of pronunciation, (T, S, K,) and *uw^aAbaAtN also. (Msb.) Hence, futila *awaAy^ibuhu [ His pendent locks of hair were twisted; ] meaning (tropical:) he was made to abandon, or relinquish, his opinion or idea or judgment. (A.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) Anything that hangs down loosely. (TA.) (tropical:) The end of a turban, (A, Msb,) that hangs down between the shoulders. (A.) (assumed tropical:) The end of a whip. (Msb.) (tropical:) Of a sandal. The thing, or portion, that hangs down from, or of, [ the upper part of ] the qibaAl [or thong that passes, from the sole, between two of the toes; it is generally a prolongation of the qibaAl ]: (T:) or the part that touches the ground, of the thing that is made to fall down upon the foot, (M, A, K,) attached to the $iraAk [or thong extending from the qibaAl above mentioned towards the ankle ]; (A;) so called because of its waggling. (M.) (tropical:) Of a sword, The thong [or cord ] which is attached to the hilt, (T, A,) and which [ is sometimes also made fast to the guard, and at other times ] hangs loose and dangles. (A.) definition: He, or it, became mounted, or fixed, upon the head of the thing.
sourceDefinition: He, or it, became mounted, or fixed, upon the head of the thing. (M, TA. *) In the saying, yarotaAsu Als~inaAna fayuqotalu [ He becomes fixed upon the point of the spear-head, and is slain ], in a verse cited by Th, yarotaAsu is for yarotay^isu . (M.) -A2- See also 5. -A3- ArtA^s zayodFA He took Zeyd by the neck, and lowered it to, or towards, the ground. (K, from the “ Nawádir el-Aaráb. ”) ― -b2- Hence, (assumed tropical:) He occupied Zeyd so as to divert his attention: (K, from the same:) and AikotaAsahu and Airotakasahu and AiEotakasahu also signify the same [app. in the former sense, or perhaps in both senses.] (TA, from the same.)

definition: , (S, M, A, Msb, K,) generally with ' , except in the dial.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, Msb, K,) generally with ' , except in the dial. of Benoo-Temeem, who constantly suppress the ' , (Msb,) [The head of a man and of any animal;] a certain part of an animal, (Msb,) well known: (Msb, K:) masc., (Msb, TA,) by common consent: (TA:) and (K) the highest or uppermost part, or top, or summit, (M, A, K,) of a thing, (M,) or of anything; (A, K;) as, for instance, of a mountain, &c.; (the Lexicons, passim;) and the upper, or uppermost, part of a valley: (TA: see raAy^isN :) pl. (of pauc., S, TA) A^arow^usN , (S, M, Msb, K,) and, by transposition, A=rusN , (M, TA, * [originally A^aA^orusN , in the L, erroneously, A^=ArAs ,]) and (of mult., S, TA) ruw^uwsu , (S, M, Msb, K, [by some carelessly written ruw^usN , and by some, allowably, ruw^u=sN ,]) which is not transposed, and ruwosN , which is elliptical. (M, TA.) A poet uses the pl. for the dual, saying, ruw^uwsu kabiyrayohin~a yanotaTiHaAni [ The heads of the two great ones, or old ones, of them, smite each other with their horns ]. (M.) ― -b2- A^um~u Alr~aA^osi : see A^um~N . ― -b3- yawomu Alr~uw^uwsi [ The day of the heads ] is applied by the people of Mekkeh to the day called yawomu Alqar~i , because then they eat the heads of the animals sacrificed. (A, TA.) ― -b4- A^aSaAba raA^osahu (tropical:) He kissed his head: a metonymical phrase. (TA.) ― -b5- rumiYa fulaAnN minohu fiY Alr~aA^osi [lit., Such a one was shot by him in the head; meaning,] (assumed tropical:) he turned away from him, and did not look towards him nor pay any regard or attention to him, and deemed him troublesome. (S, TA.) You say also, rumiytu minoka fiY Alr~aA^osi , meaning, (assumed tropical:) Thou hast an evil opinion of me (S, K) so that thou canst not look towards me. (S.) ― -b6- rakiba raA^osahu : see art. rkb . ― -b7- waladato waladahaA EalaY raA^osK waAHidK (assumed tropical:) She brought forth her children one after, or near after, another. (IAar, M.) In like manner you say, wulida lahu valaAvapu A^awolaAdK raA^osFA EalaY A_ivori raA^osK , (M,) or raA^osFA EalaY raA^osK , (TA,) (assumed tropical:) He had three children born to him one after, or near after, another. (M, TA.) And AijoEalo h`*aA Al$~aYo'a raA^osFA waAHidFA (assumed tropical:) Make thou this thing to be [ uniform, or] of one way, or mode, or manner. (ISK, TA in art. bA^j .) ― -b8- EinodiY raA^osu mina Alganami (tropical:) [ I have one head of sheep or goats ]: and Eid~apN mino A^arow^usK (tropical:) [ a number of head thereof]. (A, TA.) It is said in a trad. of' Omar, waA@joEaluwA Alr~aA^osa raA^osayoni (tropical:) And make ye the one head two head, by buying two animals with the price of one, that, when one dies, the second may remain. (Mgh in art. frq .) And you say, fulaAnN yarotabiTu ka*aA raA^osFA mina Ald~awaAb~i [ Such a one ties so many head of beasts ]. (S in art. rbT .) ― -b9- A^aEoTiniY raA^osFA mino vuwmK wa sin~FA minohu (tropical:) [ Give thou to me a head of garlic, and a clove thereof ]: and kamo fiY raA^osika mino sin~i (tropical:) [ How many cloves are there in thy head of garlic?]. (A, TA.) ― -b10- raA^osN also signifies The extremity of a thing: or, as some say, the end, or last, thereof. (MF. TA.) ― -b11- [ A head, head-land, cape, or promontory. ] ― -b12- The hilt of a sword; (A;) and so ↓ riy^aAsN ; (S, M, K; [in a copy of the A riyaAsapN ;]) or this signifies its pommel, (Sgh, K,) more correctly; (Sgh;) and is also written riyaAsN , but whether for riy^aAsN or originally with Y is doubtful. (M.) [From the first of the above-mentioned significations arise several others, which are tropical. ― -b13- Hence, Alr~aA^osu waAl*~anabu (assumed tropical:) The two nodes of a planet: see tin~iynN . ― -b14- Hence likewise,] raA^osN is also (tropical:) syn. with ray^iysN , q. v. infrà. (M, K.) You say, maA A^uriyduhu raA^osFA (tropical:) [ I do not desire him as a ry^ys , i. e. head, chief, &c.]. (A.) And it is said in a trad., raA^osu Alkufori mino qibali Alma$oriqi (tropical:) [ The head, or leader, of infidelity is from the direction of the place of sunrise ]: indicating that Ed-Dejjál or some other of the heads of error will come forth in the east. (TA.) ― -b15- raA^osu AlmaAli (tropical:) The capital, or principal, of property. (Msb, K.) [Hence the saying,] A^aqoraDatoniY Ea$arapF biraw^uwsihaA (tropical:) She lent me ten [pieces of money] as a loan whereof the principal was to be repaid without interest. (Mgh, TA. *) ― -b16- AlqaAfiyapu AlrA^osu Albayoti (assumed tropical:) [ The rhyme is the principal, or most essential, part of the verse ]: said by one of the tribe of' Okeyl, to IJ. (M.) ― -b17- raA^osu Ald~iyni Alxa$oyapu (tropical:) [ The principal part, or the beginning, of religion is fear of God]. (A, TA.) ― -b18- raA^osu Al$~ahori (assumed tropical:) The beginning of the month. (Msb.) [And in like manner, raA^osu Als~anapi (assumed tropical:) The beginning, or first day, of the year. ] ― -b19- raA^osu AlA^amori , (K, TA,) or ↓ riy^aAs , (so in the CK,) [both correct, as will be seen from what follows,] (tropical:) The beginning of the affair; the first thereof. (K, TA.) ― -b20- A^aEido EalaY~a kalaAmaka mino raA^osK , (S, M,) and mina Alr~aA^osi , but this is less common, (M,) or is a vulgar phrase, not allowable, (S,) (tropical:) [ Repeat thou to me thy speech from the beginning: ] said by a person to one talking to him. (TA.) One also says to a person talking to him, xu*ohu mino raA^osK (tropical:) [ Take thou it from the beginning ]. (A.) ― -b21- A^anota EalaYraA^osi A^amorika , and ↓ ElY riy^aAsihi (assumed tropical:) Thou art on the point of accomplishing thine affair: (M, TA:) or A^anota EalaY A^amorika ↓ riy^aAsi signifies (assumed tropical:) thou art at the beginning of thine affair; and the vulgar say, EalaY raA^osi A^amorika (S, TA.) ― -b22- A^aDoraEato EalaY raA^osi Alwaladi : see art. DrE . ― -b23- kaAna *`lika EalaY raA^osi fulaAnK (tropical:) That was in the time of such a one; in his life-time: like the phrase EalaY rijoli fulaAnK . (TA in art. rjl .) ― -b24- raA^osN also signifies (tropical:) A numerous and strong company of people. (As, S, M, K.) You say, humo raA^osN (tropical:) They are a numerous and strong company of people. (S.) And humo raA^osN EaZiymN (tropical:) They are an army by themselves, not needing any aid. (A, TA.) 'Amr Ibn-Kulthoom says, (S,) biraA^osK mino baniY ju$ami boni bikorK naduq~u bihi Als~uhuwlapa waAlHuzuwnaA [as though meaning, With a numerous and strong company of Benoo-Jusham-Ibn-Bekr, with which we beat the plains and the rugged tracts ]: (S, M:) but [J says,] I think that he means ray^iys , [i. e. head, chief, &c.,] because he says ndq~ bihi , not bihimo (S.)

definition: Hit, or hurt, in the head;
sourceDefinition: Hit, or hurt, in the head; as also ↓ marow^uwsN . (S.) Hence, $aApN ray^iysN A sheep or goat, or a ewe or she-goat, hit, or hurt, in her head: pl. raA=saY : (S, M, K:) you say ganamN raA=saY . (S, K.) ― -b2- Having his head broken, its skin being cleft. (TA.) ― -b3- Having his head affected, or overcome, by the disease called birosaAm ; as also ↓ marow^uwsN : (A:) or ↓ the latter, a man afflicted with that disease: (M, TA:*) and ↓ the same, also, a man having a complaint of his head. (TA.) -A2- (tropical:) The head, or headman, chief, commander, governor, ruler, lord, master, prince, or king, of a people; a person of authority; (S, M, A, * K;) as also ↓ ray~isN (S, K) and ↓ raA^osN [q. v.]; (M, A, K;) and [in like manner] ↓ raAy^isN , syn. of this last, waAlK : (K:) or ray^iysN signifies, [or rather signifies also,] a person high in rank or condition: (Msb:) its pl. is ruw^asaA=hu , (M, Msb,) pronounced by the vulgar ruwasaA=' : (TA:) in El-Yemen, ↓ ray~isN is applied to one who shaves the head. (TA in art. rys .) ― -b2- ray^iysu AlkilaAbi (S, M, A,) and ↓ raAy^isuhaA , (M, TA,) (tropical:) [ The chief, or leader, of the dogs; ] the dog that is' among the other dogs, as the ray^iys among a people: (S:) the chief of the dogs, that is not preceded by them in the chase. (M, TA.) ― -b3- AlA^aEoDaA='u Alr~ay^iysapu (tropical:) [ The capital parts of an animal ] are, with physicians, four; (Mgh, TA;) namely, the heart, the brain, the liver, and the testicles: (Mgh, K, TA:) the first three, because without every one of them the person cannot exist; and the last, because privation thereof is a privation of nawoE [properly species]: the assertion that they are the nose, and the tongue, and the penis, is erroneous. (Mgh, TA.)

definition: One of the [ Arabian ] months;
sourceDefinition: One of the [ Arabian ] months; (Msb;) [namely, the seventh thereof; ] so called because of the honour in which it was held in the Time of Ignorance, (S, A, * K, *) inasmuch as war, or fighting, during it was held unlawful: (S:) in a trad., (TA,) it is called rajabu muDara [ Rejeb of Mudar ], because Mudar most honoured it: (S, TA:) and it is further distinguished as being between jamaAdaY and $aEobaAn , to show that what is meant by it is not what the [pagan] Arabs called rjb according to the computation founded upon postponement; for they used to postpone it from month to month: (TA:) [it is also called rajabN Alfarodu Rejeb the separate; because it is the only sacred month that is not preceded nor followed by another sacred month; the other sacred months being AlmuHar~amu and *uw AlqaEodapi and *uw AlHaj~api :] the pl. is A^irojaAbN (S, Msb, K) and A^arojibapN and A^arojubN [all pls. of pauc.] (Msb) and rujuwbN and rijaAbN and rajabaAtN (Msb, K) and rajuwbN [or rather this last is a quasi-pl. n.] (TA) and [pl. pl.] A^araAjibu [pl. of A^arojubN ] and A^araAjiybu [pl. of A^arojaAbN ]. (Msb.) The dual, rajabaAni , (S, Msb,) or Alr~ajabaAni , (A,) [ The two Rejebs ] is applied to [ the two months ] rajabN and $aEobaAnu , (S, A, Msb,) by the attribution of predominance to the former. (Msb.) -A2- See also A^arojaAbN .

sourceDefinition: A thing by means of which a tree is propped up, because of the abundance of its fruit, lest its branches should break: sometimes it is a wall built for it to rest upon, because of its weakness: (S:) a wall, or the like, built round a palm-tree, for it to rest upon, because of its heaviness or its weakness: (Mgh in art. Erw and ErY :) a kind of wide bench of stone or brick ( duk~aAnN ) built at the foot of a palm-tree, for it to rest upon, (K, TA,) because of its leaning, and being valuable to its owner, and being weak: (TA:) accord. to As, a structure of rock with which a palm-tree is supported by means of forked pieces of wood: (TA:) it is also called rujomapN : (K * and TA in art. rjm :) pl. rujabN . (S.) [See 2.] ― -b2- Also A structure by means of which (S, K) the wolf &c., (S,) or objects of the chase, (K,) are caught: (S, K:) a piece of flesh-meat is put in it, and tied with a small cord; and when the beast pulls it, the rjbp falls upon him. (S.) -A2- See also riAjibapN .

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. ruzo'N and maroziy^apN , He got, or obtained, from him good (S, K) of any kind. (S.) And razaA^a fulaAnN fulaAnFA i. q. br~h ; [a mistake, through an oversight, for qabila bir~ahu ; i. e. Such a one accepted the bounty of such a one; ] as also razaAhu , without ' : the former said by AM to be the original. (TA.) And razaA^a Al$~aYo'a He took from the thing, diminished it, lessened it, or impaired it; (K;) and ↓ trAzA^hu signifies the same; or he took from it, diminished it, &c., by little and little. (JM.) You say, razaA^ahu maAlahu , and raziy^ahu maAlahu , aor. , inf. n. ruzo'N , He got, or obtained, somewhat of his property; as also maAlahu ↓ ArtzA^hu . (K.) And maA razaA^otuhu maAlahu , (S,) and maA raziy^otuhu maAlahu , (S, K, *) I did not take from him of his property; or did not diminish to him his property. (S, K. *) And maA raziy^otuhu $ayoy^FA I did not take from him, or it, aught. (Mgh.) And maA razaA^a fulaAnFA $ayoy^FA He did not get, or obtain, from such a one aught of his property; and did not take from him aught thereof. (TA.) And maA razaA^otuhu zibaAlFA I did not take from him, or it, as much as an ant would carry with its mouth: (Har p. 197:) or thus originally, but meaning, anything. (S in art. zbl .) And maA razaA^onaA mino maAy^ika $ayoy^FA We took not of, or from, thy water, anything: occurring in a trad. (TA.) In another trad., as some relate it, raziynaA occurs for raziy^onaA , which is the original. (IAth.) Accord. to AZ, [however,] one says, ruziy^otuhu , meaning [ I had it taken, or received, from me; or, virtually, ] it was taken, or received, from me; but not ruziytuhu . (TA.) [Hence, when relating to a moral attribute, or the like, it virtually means (assumed tropical:) It was experienced from me: see a verse cited voce mutoladN , in art. tld .] You say also, huwa yurozaA^u , [virtually] meaning He is a bountiful person; one whose gratuitous gifts people obtain. (Ham p. 722.) And A_in~ahu laqalyilu Alr~uzo'i mina AlT~aEaAmi Verily he is one who gets little of the food. (TA.) ― -b2- razaA^otuhu also signifies I afflicted him with an affliction, a misfortune, or a calamity. (Msb.) And razaA^atohu raziyoy^apN An affliction, a misfortune, or a calamity, befell him. (S, Msb.) It is said in a trad., respecting a woman who came asking for her son, A_ino A^urozaA^i A@boniY falamo A^urozaA^o A^aHobaAbiY , meaning If I be afflicted by the loss of my son, I have not been afflicted by the loss of my friends. (TA.)

(TA.)

sourceDefinition: A styptic; or a thing that is put upon blood for the purpose of stanching it, or stopping its flowing: (S, K:) a subst. from raqaA^a . (Msb.) Hence the saying, (Msb,) accord. to J, in a trad., but this is a mistake, for it is a saying of Aktham, (K,) or, accord. to the Expositions of the Fs, it was said by Keys Ibn-'Ásim El-Minkaree, (TA,) laA tasub~uwA AlA_ibila faA_in~a fiyhaA raquwo'a Ald~ami [ Revile not ye camels, or it may perhaps mean hock not ye camels, but the former, I am told, is here meant, for in them is a preventive of the flowing of blood ]; alluding to their being given in compensation for homicide, and thus preventing the shedding of blood. (S, Msb, K, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] rajulN raquwo'N bayona Alqawomi (assumed tropical:) A man who is a reconciler of the people; or a peacemaker between them: and [so] raquwo'N limaA bayonahumo , a phrase used by a poet. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, M, Msb,) inf. n. raqoSN , (S, M, Msb, CK,) or raqaSN , of the measure faEalN , like TaradN and HalabN , inf. ns. of Tarada and Halaba , (IDrd, IB, TA,) [ He danced; this is what is meant by the explanation] he played, or sported; syn. laEiba : (A, K:) said of a raq~aAS [or dancer], (A, K,) or of a laE~aAb [or player or sporter], (M,) and of a muxan~av [or effeminate man, or one who affects the manners &c. of women], and of a SuwfiY~ [or mystic, in a choral celebration of the praises of God, which is termed a *ikor , performed by certain orders of darweeshes, all of whom, more or less, pretend to be mystics]. (TA.) ― -b2- Also raqaSa , (Lth, A,) aor. , (Lth,) inf. n. raqoSN (Lth, M, A, K) and raqaSN , (Lth, M, K,) or the latter only, (IDrd, Ibn-Málik, TA,) and raqaSaAnN , (Lth, M, A, K,) (tropical:) He (a camel, A, TA) went the pace, or in the manner, termed xababN ; [i. e. ambled; ] (Lth, M, A, K, TA;) or went in a manner which was a kind of xabab : or went quickly. (TA.) One does not say yaroquSu [in speaking of any animate being] except of a player or sporter and of a camel (Lth, K, * TA) and the like: (Lth, TA:) in relation to others, one uses the terms qaqozN and naqozN : (Lth, K, TA:) or sometimes, (Lth, TA,) ― -b3- it is also said of an ass, meaning (tropical:) He played with his she-ass. (A.) ― -b5- raqaSa also signifies (tropical:) It (wine, S, K, and the beverage called nabiy* , A) estuated: (A, K:) or began to do so. (S, A.) ― -b6- And (tropical:) It (the mirage) was, or became, in a state of commotion; [ it danced; ] (S, M, A, K;) and so it signifies when said of bubbles ( HabaAb ). (M.) You say, A^anayotuhu Hiyna raqaSa Als~araAbu (A) or AlA=lu (TA) (tropical:) [ I came to him when the mirage danced; in the heat of the day]. ― -b7- And (tropical:) He hasted, or was quick, fiY kalaAmihi in his speech. (A, TA.) ― -b8- [And (tropical:) He spoke evil against another.] You say, samiEotu raqoSa Aln~aAsi EalayonaA (tropical:) I heard the evil speaking of the people against us. (A, TA.)

definition: He, or it, stayed, or arrested, what remained in him of life.
sourceDefinition: He, or it, stayed, or arrested, what remained in him of life. (TA.) [Hence,] humo yuram~iquwnahu bi$aYo'K They give him something sufficient to stay, or arrest, what remains in him of life. (O, TA.) ― -b2- [The inf. n.] taromiyqN also signifies The scanting of fodder and drink. (JK.) ― -b3- [And The drinking little by little. ] One says, ram~adati AlmiEozaY faram~iqo ram~iqo , meaning [ The she-goats have secreted milk in their udders: therefore ] drink thou their milk little by little; drink thou &c.: (IF, K, TA:) because they secrete milk some days before their bringing forth: (IF, TA:) or because they will bring forth after a while. (K, TA. [See also arts. rmd and rbq and rnq : and see 5 in the present art.]) ― -b4- Also The doing a work not well, yet so as to satisfy oneself, or to attain one's desire, thereby. (K, TA. [See also 3.]) You say, huwayuram~iqu fiY Al$~aYo'i He does not exert himself, or take pains, or exceed the usual bounds, in doing the thing. (TA.) And ram~iqo EalaY mazaAdatayoka Repair thou thy pair of leathern water-bags sufficiently to satisfy thyself. (O, TA.) ― -b5- And The interlarding, or embellishing, of speech, or discourse, with falsehood; taromiyqu AlkalaAmi signifying taloqiyquhu ; (Ibn-'Abbád, K;) as also tarobiyquhu . (Ibn-'Abbád and K in art. rbq .) You say, rm~q AlkalaAma He interlarded, or embellished, the speech, or discourse, with falsehood, ( laf~aqahu , Z, or laf~aqa bayonahu , JK,) [ adding ] thing after thing, or thing by thing. (Z, TA.) -A2- See also 1, in two places.

definition: [ rAmq seems to signify He strove, or contended, to retain what remained in him of life.
sourceDefinition: [ rAmq seems to signify He strove, or contended, to retain what remained in him of life. And hence, as implying this meaning, He was at the last gasp: see muraAmiq , below. Whence, app.,] the inf. n. muraAmaqapN signifies (assumed tropical:) The having little friendship [ remaining in the heart ]. (KL. [See, again, muraAmiqN .]) One says, h`*ihi Aln~axolapu turaAmiqu biEiroqK laA taHoyaA walaA tamuwtu ; or laA yaHoyaA walaA yamuwtu ; [as though meaning, accord. to the former reading, This palm-tree strives to retain life with a root, being neither alive nor dead; or, accord. to the latter reading, with a root that is neither alive nor dead; ] (S; [in one of my copies of which I find only the former reading; and in the other, both readings;]) or h`*ihi Aln~axolapu turaAmiqu biEiroqK means this palm-tree is neither alive nor dead. (K.) And fulaAnN yuraAmiqu Eayo$ahu i. e. yudaAriyhi [app. meaning Such a one strives by artful means to preserve his life ]. sourceDefinition: , (T, S, M, Msb,) aor. yaruwmu , (T, S, Msb,) inf. n. rawomN (T, S, M, Msb, K) and maraAmN , (Msb, K, TA,) He sought, sought for or after, or desired, syn. Talaba , (T, * M, Msb, K, *) a thing. (S, M, Msb.) ― -b2- [And hence, He attempted another person in fight &c., and a thing.] ― -b3- And [hence also] Alr~awomu , (K,) or rawomu AlHarakapi , mentioned by Sb, (S,) [as though signifying The desiring to pronounce the vowel-sound without fully accomplishing that desire, ] means [ the pronouncing ] a vowel-sound ( Harakap ) slurred ( muxotalasap ) and rendered obscure, (S, K,) for, or by, [accord. to different copies of the S,] a sort of alleviation [ of the utterance ]; (S;) it is more [ in effect ] than what is termed AlA_i$omaAm , because it is heard; (S, K;) and it is of the same measure [ in prosody ] as the vowel-sound [ fully pronounced ]; as [ in the case of what is termed ] hamozapN bayona bayona , such as in the saying of the poet, A^aAano zum~a A^ajomaAlN wafaAraqa jiyrapN wa SaAHa guraAbu Albayoni A^anota Haziynu [ Is it because that camels have had the nose-reins attached to them, and neighbours have separated, one from another, and the raven of disunion has uttered its cry, thou art mourning? ]; A^aAano zumo being scanned as faEuwluno ; and it not being allowable to make the E [ in fEwln ] quiescent: it is such also as in the phrase in the Kur [ii. 181] $ahoru ramaDaAna with him who makes [ the dammeh ] obscure; it being only with a slurred vowel-sound ( Harakap muxotalasap ); and it not being allowable for the former r [i. e. the r of $hr ] to be quiescent, because the h before it is quiescent, for this would lead to the combination of two quiescent letters in a case of continuity, [i. e. when there is no pause after them, ] without there being before them a soft letter [i. e. A or w or Y , as in dawaAb~ &c.], which is not found in any of the dialects of the Arabs: and it is such also as in the instances in the Kur [xv. 9 and x. 36 and xxxvi. 49] A_in~aA naHonu naz~alonaA A@l*~ikora and A^am~ano laA yahid~iY and yaxiS~imuwna [ for yahotadiY and yaxotaSimuwna ], and the like thereof: no regard should be paid to the saying of Fr, that in this [last] and the like instances a letter [which in this instance and in the next preceding it is t ] is incorporated into another [following it]; for they [i. e. the Arabs] do not realize this mode [of incorporation]; and he who combines two quiescent letters in an instance in which the slurring of the vowel-sound ( AixotilaAsu AlHarakapi ) is not proper errs; as in the reading of Hamzeh, in the Kur [xviii. 96], famaA A@sT~aAEuwA ; for the s of AlAisotifoEaAlu may not be made movent in any manner [and therefore it may not be incorporated into the following letter]. (S, TA.) Alr~awomu is [also] in a case of pausing after a word ending with any letter except the fem. p , [in like manner] meaning The indicating the vowel with an obscure sound: (I' Ak p. 351:) rawomu AlHarakapi in pausing after a word that is marofuwE or majoruwr is from raAma Al$~aYo'a signifying Talabahu : Sb says that those of whom one says raAmuwA AlHarakapa [ They slurred the vowel-sound ] are induced to do what this signifies [instead of suppressing the vowel-sound entirely] by eagerness to exclude it from the case of that which is necessarily made quiescent in every instance, and to show that its case is, in their opinion, not like the case of that which is made quiescent in every instance. (M.) [See also 4 in art. $wr .]

(S, M, Msb.) ― -b2- [And hence, He attempted another person in fight &c., and a thing.] ― -b3- And [hence also] Alr~awomu , (K,) or rawomu AlHarakapi , mentioned by Sb, (S,) [as though signifying The desiring to pronounce the vowel-sound without fully accomplishing that desire, ] means [ the pronouncing ] a vowel-sound ( Harakap ) slurred ( muxotalasap ) and rendered obscure, (S, K,) for, or by, [accord. to different copies of the S,] a sort of alleviation [ of the utterance ]; (S;) it is more [ in effect ] than what is termed AlA_i$omaAm , because it is heard; (S, K;) and it is of the same measure [ in prosody ] as the vowel-sound [ fully pronounced ]; as [ in the case of what is termed ] hamozapN bayona bayona , such as in the saying of the poet, A^aAano zum~a A^ajomaAlN wafaAraqa jiyrapN wa SaAHa guraAbu Albayoni A^anota Haziynu [ Is it because that camels have had the nose-reins attached to them, and neighbours have separated, one from another, and the raven of disunion has uttered its cry, thou art mourning? ]; A^aAano zumo being scanned as faEuwluno ; and it not being allowable to make the E [ in fEwln ] quiescent: it is such also as in the phrase in the Kur [ii. 181] $ahoru ramaDaAna with him who makes [ the dammeh ] obscure; it being only with a slurred vowel-sound ( Harakap muxotalasap ); and it not being allowable for the former r [i. e. the r of $hr ] to be quiescent, because the h before it is quiescent, for this would lead to the combination of two quiescent letters in a case of continuity, [i. e. when there is no pause after them, ] without there being before them a soft letter [i. e. A or w or Y , as in dawaAb~ &c.], which is not found in any of the dialects of the Arabs: and it is such also as in the instances in the Kur [xv. 9 and x. 36 and xxxvi. 49] A_in~aA naHonu naz~alonaA A@l*~ikora and A^am~ano laA yahid~iY and yaxiS~imuwna [ for yahotadiY and yaxotaSimuwna ], and the like thereof: no regard should be paid to the saying of Fr, that in this [last] and the like instances a letter [which in this instance and in the next preceding it is t ] is incorporated into another [following it]; for they [i. e. the Arabs] do not realize this mode [of incorporation]; and he who combines two quiescent letters in an instance in which the slurring of the vowel-sound ( AixotilaAsu AlHarakapi ) is not proper errs; as in the reading of Hamzeh, in the Kur [xviii. 96], famaA A@sT~aAEuwA ; for the s of AlAisotifoEaAlu may not be made movent in any manner [and therefore it may not be incorporated into the following letter]. (S, TA.) Alr~awomu is [also] in a case of pausing after a word ending with any letter except the fem. p , [in like manner] meaning The indicating the vowel with an obscure sound: (I' Ak p. 351:) rawomu AlHarakapi in pausing after a word that is marofuwE or majoruwr is from raAma Al$~aYo'a signifying Talabahu : Sb says that those of whom one says raAmuwA AlHarakapa [ They slurred the vowel-sound ] are induced to do what this signifies [instead of suppressing the vowel-sound entirely] by eagerness to exclude it from the case of that which is necessarily made quiescent in every instance, and to show that its case is, in their opinion, not like the case of that which is made quiescent in every instance. (M.) [See also 4 in art. $wr .]

definition: A species of rat which is large and deaf: or which has red hair: (K:) or which has red and beautiful hair: (TA:) or which is without hair: (K:) or a species of field-rat, of large size: one thereof...
sourceDefinition: A species of rat which is large and deaf: or which has red hair: (K:) or which has red and beautiful hair: (TA:) or which is without hair: (K:) or a species of field-rat, of large size: one thereof is called zabaAbapN : (TA:) or this signifies a deaf rat: (S:) or a deaf rat of the desert: (A:) and its pl. is zabaAbN , [or rather this is a coll. gen. n. of which it is the n. un.,] (S, TA,) and [its pl. is] zabaAbaAtN . (TA.) The Arabs make it the subject of a prov.: (S:) they say, A^asoraqu mino zabAbapi [ More thievish than a zebábeh ]. (S, A, TA. [Another reading is mentioned in the TA in art. znb ; namely, ranaAbap ; which is there said, on the authority of Ibn-'Abd-Rabbih in the Eiqod , to signify a rat, or mouse. ]) And they also liken to it an ignorant person. (S, TA.) It is said in a trad. of 'Alee, A^anaA waA@ll~`hi A_i*FA mivolu Al~atiY A^uHiyTa bihaA faqiyla zabAabo zabaAbo Hat~aY daxalato juHorahaA vum~a A@Hotufira EanohaA faA@jotur~a birijolihaA fa*ubiHato , i. e. [ I, by Allah, in that case, were ] like that animal, namely, the she-hyena, which has been surrounded, and to which it has been said Zebáb! Zebáb! [ until it has entered its hole, and then the earth has been dug away from it, and it has been dragged by its hind leg, and slaughtered: ] meaning, I will not be like the she-hyena that is decoyed to its death: for that animal probably eats the zbAb , as it does the field-rat. (TA.) -A2- Also i. q. saAEK [ A messenger, or a messenger on a beast of the post: and a collector of the poor-rates: &c.]. (CK: but omitted in the TA, and in my MS. copy of the K.)

sourceDefinition: Dried grapes; or raisins: and also dried figs: (K:) said by AHn to have been used in this latter sense by an Arab of the desert: (TA:) a coll. gen. n.; masc. and fem.: (Msb:) n. un. with p . (TA.) You say, gaDiba favaAra lahu zabiybataAni (tropical:) He was angry, and there appeared two collections of froth, or foam, in the two sides of his mouth. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: Downy: (K:) and, applied to a man, having much hair: (A, K:) or having much and long hair: (S, TA: [but accord. to the former, it seems to be applied in this sense to a camel:]) or, applied to a man, having much hair in the ears and eyebrows: and having much hair on the fore arms and the eyebrows and eyes: (TA:) or, thus applied, having much hair on the chest: (Msb:) and, applied to a camel, having much fur: or having much fur on the face: (A:) or having much hair on the face and under the lower jaw: (K:) or, in the ears and on the eyes: (TA:) or having much hair on the face and body: and ↓ zubayobN is a shortened dim. thereof: (Ham p. 140:) fem. zab~aA='u , applied to a woman as meaning having much hair in the eyebrows and on the fore arms and the hands: (A:) and to an ear as meaning having much hair: (TA:) pl. zub~N . (A.) It is said in a prov., kul~u A^azab~a nafuwrN [ Every one, of camels, that has much hair on the face &c. is wont to take fright, and run away at random ]: for the camel thinks what he sees upon his eyes to be a person seeking him, and consequently takes fright, and runs away at random: (A:) the camel to which this epithet applies is seldom, or never, other than nfwr ; because there grow upon his eyebrow small hairs, and when the wind strikes them he takes fright, and runs away at random. (S, TA.) ― -b2- AlA^azab~u is a name of One of the devils: (K, TA:) mention is made in a trad. of a certain devil named A^azab~u AlEaqabapi : (K, TA:) but in the L, and in the Seeret El-Halabee, it is written A_izobu AlEaqabapi : and it is said to be a serpent. (TA in art. Azb .) ― -b3- Alz~ab~aA='u The Aisot [i. e. podex, or anus ], (K, TA,) with its hair. (TA.) ― -b4- EaAmN A^azab~u (tropical:) A year abundant in herbage. (S, A, Msb, K.) ― -b5- yawomN A^azab~u : see A^aHaS~u , in two places. ― -b6- jayo$N A^azab~u (assumed tropical:) An army having many spears. definition: (O, K, TA) and saA*ijN (TA) arabicized from [the Pers.
sourceDefinition: (O, K, TA) and saA*ijN (TA) arabicized from [the Pers.] saAdaho : (O, K: [in some copies of the K saA*aho :]) this is the only explanation in some of the copies of the K: (TA:) Plain; i. e. without variegation, decoration, embellishment, or engraved or sculptured work: (O, TA:) or without any hair upon it: or of one unmixed colour: this last is [said to be] the correct meaning [in many instances]; but the sheykh Welee-ed-Deen El-'Irákee says, in the Expos. of the “ Sunan ” of Aboo-Dáwood, respecting a pair of boots of the Prophet, described as xuf~aAni A^asowadaAni saA*ajaAni or saA*ijaAni , that this phrase seems to mean A pair of black boots of one unmixed colour; the last word being used in this sense in the common conventional language; though he had not found it with this meaning in the lexicons, nor in the books of authors on the strange words occurring in traditions. (TA.) ― -b2- Also Free from self-constraint: and one who knows not badness, wickedness, deceit, or guile; in whom is no latent rancour, malevolence, malice, or spite, nor cunning: (O:) or free in intellect; and easy [or simple or artless ] in nature or disposition. (TA in art. sdj .) ― -b3- Huj~apN saA*ajapN , also written saA*ijapN , is used by authors on the scholastic theology of the Muslims as meaning An argument, a plea, an allegation, an evidence, or a testimony, that is undecisive: and sometimes the same epithet is used [in like manner] in other cases. (CK.)

definition: , (S, M, Msb, K,) and say^imahu , (M, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, Msb, K,) and say^imahu , (M, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. saA^amN (S, M, K) and saA^omN (K) and saA^amapN (S, M) and saA=mN and saA=mapN , (S, Msb, K,) He turned away with disgust from it; was averse from it; was disgusted at it or with it; loathed, or nauseated, it; (S, M, Msb, K;) namely, a thing; (S, M, K;) syn. mal~a , (S, M, Msb, K,) and Dajira : (Msb:) saA=mapN exceeds malaAlN . (IAth, TA in this art. and in art. swm .)

definition: A desert, syn. qaforN , (S, K,) or a plain, syn. qaAEN , (M,) in which is no herbage: (M, K:) or weak land: (TA:) and A^aroDN suboruwtN and ↓ siboriytN (As, Lh, M) and ↓ siboraAtN (M) Land in which...
sourceDefinition: A desert, syn. qaforN , (S, K,) or a plain, syn. qaAEN , (M,) in which is no herbage: (M, K:) or weak land: (TA:) and A^aroDN suboruwtN and ↓ siboriytN (As, Lh, M) and ↓ siboraAtN (M) Land in which is no herbage; (M;) or land in which is nothing: (As, Lh, M:) pl. sabaAriytu and sabaArK , the latter anomalous, mentioned by Lh: (M:) accord. to A'Obeyd, the pl. sabaAriytu signifies deserts, or waterless deserts, ( falawaAtN ,) in which is nothing: and accord. to As, land [or lands ] in which nothing grows: (TA:) and one says also A^aroDN sabaAriytu , (M, K,) a phrase of the same class as vawobN A^axolaAqN , (K,) as though the sing. suboruwtN or siboriytN were applied to every portion thereof. (M.) ― -b2- Hence, (TA,) applied to a man, (AZ, S, TA,) Needy, in want, indigent, (AZ, As, S, M, K, TA,) poor, (AZ, As, K, TA,) possessing little, (M, TA,) or, as some say, possessing nothing; (S, * M, TA;) and ↓ siboriytN signifies the same, (AZ, S, M, K,) as also ↓ siboraAtN , and ↓ suborutN : (M, K:) also bankrupt, or insolvent; syn. mufolisN : (TA in explanation of the first [but equally applying to all]:) the epithet applied to a woman is suboruwtapN and ↓ siboriytapN ; (AZ, S;) the latter of which is applied to a man [app. in intensive sense, agreeably with analogy,] as well as to a woman: (M:) and the pl. is sabaAriytu , applied to men and to women. (AZ, S.) ― -b3- [Hence, also,] applied to a youth, or young man, Beardless; or having no hair upon the sides of his face. (M, K, TA. [In the K, this signification is immediately followed by the mention of the pls. sabaAriytu and sabaArK .]) ― -b4- And Little, or small, in quantity or number; (S, M, K;) paltry, or inconsiderable: (K:) applied to a thing, (S, K,) and (S) to property, or cattle. (S, M.) ― -b5- Also Tall, or long. (M, TA.) ― -b6- And A skilful, or an expert, guide, well acquainted with the lands. (TA.) It is mentioned by Sb, who says that it is of measure fuEoluwlN , like zunobuwrN and EuSofuwrN ; and most hold him to be right: but some of the authors on inflection assert that it is of the measure fuEoluwtN , from sabarotu Al$~aYo'a meaning “ I tried, proved, or tested, the thing, or proved it by experiment or experience; ” and that the t is added to give intensiveness to the signification; which several deny: (MF, TA:) suboruwrN , however, is mentioned in the K, in art. sbr , as meaning “ poor, ” and land “ in which is no herbage. ” (TA.)

definition: A thing that one has let loose, let down, let fall, or made to hang down, and to drag [ on the ground ];
sourceDefinition: A thing that one has let loose, let down, let fall, or made to hang down, and to drag [ on the ground ]; like as na$arN signifies “ a thing that one has spread ” &c.: whence the trad., mano jar~a sabalahu mina AlxuyalaA='i laA yanoZuru A@ll~`hu yawoma Alqiy`mapi [ He who drags what he has made to hang down of his garment from pride, or self-conceit, God will not look towards him on the day of resurrection ]: (O:) or sabalN means garments made to hang down [ so as to drag ]; and is pl. of ↓ sabalapN ; [or rather a coll. gen. n. of which sabalapN is the n. un.;] whence jar~a sabalatahu , (TA,) which means [ He dragged his garment; though said to mean,] his garments. (K, TA.) ― -b2- Also (tropical:) Rain: (S, M, K:) or rain issuing from the clouds and not as yet having reached the earth: (AZ, S, TA:) or flowing rain: and likewise flowing blood. (Ham p. 359.) ― -b3- [Hence, app., as indicating swiftness,] sabalu is the name of (assumed tropical:) A certain mare, (S, K,) an excellent mare, said by As to have been the mother of A^aEowaju , and to have belonged to [ the tribe of ] Ghanee. (S, TA.) ― -b4- And sabalN [or sabalu as a fem. proper name] is a name for (assumed tropical:) A ewe, or she-goat: and such is called to be milked by saying sabalo sabalo . (Ibn-'Abbád, TA.) -A2- Also i. q. ↓ sunobulN , (S, M, Msb, K,) which signifies The ears of corn: (MA: [and in like manner both are expl. in the KL, but as singulars, app. because used as gen. ns.:]) n. un. of the former with ↓ p , and so of ↓ the latter: and the pl. of ↓ sunobulN , which is of the measure funoEulN , is sanaAbilu : (Msb:) or this is pl. of sunobulapN , (S,) as also sunobulaAtN : (Kur xii. 43 and 46:) or sunobulapN [in the CK (erroneously) subolap ] signifies an ear of corn [so I render zaroEapN (in the CK zuroEap )] that is bending, or inclining, as also ↓ sabuwlapN [mentioned in one of my two copies of the S as syn. with sunobulapN but not in the other copy] and ↓ subuwlapN (M, K) and ↓ sabalapN ; (K;) or, accord. to Lth, ↓ sabuwlapN signifies an ear ( sunobulap ) of millet ( *urap ), and of rice, and the like, when bending, or inclining: (O, TA:) and some say that sabalN signifies spreading, or expanding, awn of the sunobul [or ears of corn ]; (M, TA;) or the extremities thereof; (TA;) and the pl. is subuwlN ; (M;) or sbwl is syn. with sunobulN , in the dial. of bnw hmyAn [?]. (TA.) ↓ Als~unobulapu is also the name of A certain sign of the Zodiac [i. e. Virgo ]: (S in the present art., and K in art. snbl :) [or Spica Virginis; ] a star in Virgo; thus called by astrologers; also called Als~imaAku AlA^aEozalu . (Kzw. [See art. smk .]) AlT~iybi ↓ sunobulu is A well-known plant, [ spikenard, which is called in the present day Als~unobulu AlhinodiY~u ,] brought from India. (O. [See also art. snbl .]) ― -b2- Also sing. of A^asobaAlN , which signifies (assumed tropical:) The uppermost parts of a bucket, (O,) or the lips thereof: (S:) or ↓ sabalapN is the sing. of A^asobaAlN in these senses; and signifies (tropical:) the head of a vessel [like as it signifies the “ ear, ” which is the “ head, ” of a culm of wheat &c.]. (TA.) You say, malaA^ahaA A_ilaY A^asobaAlihaA (tropical:) He filled it (i. e. the winecup, AlkaA^osa , M, TA, or the bucket, Ald~alowa , O) to its edges, (M, K, TA,) and to its lips. (K.) And a poet says, (S,) namely Bá'ith Ibn- Sureym El-Yeshkuree, (TA,) A_i*o A^arosaluwniY maAtiHFA bidilaAy^ihimo famalaA^otuhuA EalaqFA A_ilaY A^asobaAlihaA [ When they sent me drawing with their buckets, and I filled them with blood to their brims ]: he says, they sent me seeking to execute their blood-revenges, and I slew many: AlEalaq meaning “ blood. ” (S, TA. [See also Ham p. 268, where some different readings are mentioned; and it is said that the AsbAl may mean the knots that are connected with the cross-pieces of wood of the bucket.]) ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) A number of spears, few or many. (K. [Perhaps because their heads are likened to the heads of corn.]) -A3- Also The nose: (K:) pl. sibaAlN : so in the Moheet. (TA.) One says, A^arogama A@ll~`hu sabalahu [ May God make his nose to cleave to the earth, or dust: or (assumed tropical:) abase, or humble, him ]. (TA.) -A4- And Garments made of the hards, or hurds, of flax of the coarsest of qualities: and so ↓ sabalapN [if one of these words be not a mistranscription for the other]. (TA.) -A5- And A certain disease in the eye, [thus riyHu Als~abali is expl. in the M,] resembling a film, as though it were the web of a spider, with red veins: (S:) or a film of the eye, from the swelling, or inflation, of its external veins upon the surface of the mulotaHimap , (K,) which is one of the layers of the eye, (TA,) [namely, the tunica albuginea, or white of the eye, so called in the present day,] and the appearance of a web, or thing woven, between the two, [i. e. between those veins and the white tunic, ] like smoke: (K:) or a film covering the eye; as though from A_isobaAlo meaning the “ letting down ” of a veil, or curtain. (Mgh.) -A6- Also A reviling, or vilifying. (K.) One says, bayoniY wa bayonahu sabalN Between me and him is a reviling, or vilifying: so in the Moheet. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: : see sabalN , in five places. ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) The $aArib [or mustache ]: (S:) or the daAy^irap [or small protuberance termed Hivorimap , q. v.,] in the middle of the upper lip: or the hair that is upon [app. meaning of ] the $aArib ; (M, K;) whence the saying, TaAlato sabalatuka faquS~ahaA [ thy hair of the mustache has become long, therefore clip it ]; and it is tropical: (TA:) or the extremity of that hair: (M, K:) or the two mustaches together: (M, K: *) or what is upon the chin, to the extremity of the beard: or the fore part of the beard: (M, K:) or what hangs down, of, or from, the fore part of the beard: (Zj, in his “ Khalk el-Insán: ”) or, accord. to Az, it signifies, with the Arabs, the fore part of the beard, and what hangs down thereof, or therefrom, upon the breast: or, accord. to IDrd, some of them apply it to the extremity of the beard; and some, to the hair of the mustache that hangs down on the beard: in a trad., in which it is said that he [Mohammad] was full in the sabalap , Az says that it means the hairs beneath the lower jaw: accord. to AZ, it is what appears, of the fore part of the beard, after [or exclusive of ] the hair of the side of each cheek and the Euvonuwn [here app. meaning the portion of the beard next the front of the throat ], and what is concealed [ thereof ]: (TA:) or, accord. to Th, the beard altogether: (M:) the pl. is sibaAlN , (S, K,) [to which p is sometimes added, agreeably with a common license, as appears from an ex. in what follows,] and sabalaAtN , occurring in the saying, A_in~ahu la*uw sabalaAtK , mentioned by Lh, in which the term sabalap is made to apply to every separate portion [so that the meaning is, Verily he has a sabalap ]. (M.) One says, of enemies, humo Suhobu Als~ibaAli (assumed tropical:) [ They are red, or reddish, in respect of the mustaches, &c.: see art. Shb ]. (TA.) And of a man who has come threatening, one says, jaA='a fulaAnN wa qado na$ara sabalatahu (tropical:) [ Such a one came having spread out his mustache, &c.]. (K, * TA.) And in a trad. respecting Dhu-th-Thudeiyeh, [see art. vdY ,] it is said, Ealayohi $uEayoraAtN mivolu sibaAlapi Als~in~awori [app. meaning (assumed tropical:) Having upon him small hairs like the whiskers of the cat ]. TA.) ― -b3- sabalapu AlbaEiyri means (assumed tropical:) The part of the camel, in which he is stabbed, or stuck, in the uppermost part of the breast; (T, M;) called also the tariybap : (T:) or the fur that flows down upon that part of the camel. (M, K. [In the CK, manoxarih is erroneously put for manoHarihi .]) You say lataba fiY sabalapi Aln~aAqapi , meaning (assumed tropical:) He stabbed, or stuck, the she-camel in the part above mentioned: (M in art. ltb : [in the K, in the present art., kataba is erroneously put, in this phrase, in the place of lataba :]) Az heard an Arab of the desert say latama fiY sabalapi baEiyrihi , [which means the same as lataba ,] and he supposes the sabalap to be hairs in the part above mentioned. (TA.) You say also, baEiyrN Hasanu Als~abalapi , meaning (assumed tropical:) [ A camel goodly in respect of ] the thinness of his skin ( jilodihi ): so in the O and K: but accord. to the T, of his cheek ( xad~ihi ); and this is probably the right explanation. (TA.)

definition: A way, road, or path;
sourceDefinition: A way, road, or path; (S, M, Msb, K;) and what is open, or conspicuous, thereof; (M, K;) and Er-Rághib adds, wherein is easiness: (TA:) and ↓ sabiylapN signifies the same: (Ibn- 'Abbád, K:) the former is masc. and fem.; (S, M, Mgh, Msb, K;) like zuqaAqN ; (Msb;) made fem. by the people of El-Hijáz, and masc. by Temeem; (Akh, S voce zuqaAqN ;) but mostly fem.; (IAth, TA;) in the Kur it is made masc. in vii. 143, and fem. in xii. 108: (S, M, TA:) pl. subulN , (M, K,) or, accord. to ISk, it has this pl. when masc., and subuwlN , like EunuwqN when fem., (Msb, [but this distinction and the latter pl. are both strange,]) and it has also as a pl. [of pauc.] A^asobilapN . (TA.) In the saying, wa EalaY A@ll~`hi qaSodu Als~abiyli [ And upon God it rests to show the right way (see art. qSd )], (M, K,) in the Kur [xvi. 9], (M,) it is used as a gen. n., because it is added, wa minohaA jaAy^irN . (M, K.) ― -b2- Aibonu Als~abiyli means (assumed tropical:) The son of the road; (M, K;) he whom the road has brought, or [ as it were ] brought forth; (IB;) the wayfarer, or traveller: (Mgh, Msb:) or he who travels much or often: (TA:) or the traveller who is far from his place of abode: (Er-Rághib:) as used in the verse of the Kur, (M, Mgh, Msb,) ix, 60, (M,) it means the person to whom the way has become cut short [ so that he is unable to continue his journey ]; (M, K;) to which has been added, who desires to return to his country, or town, and finds not what will suffice him: (TA:) or the traveller who is cut off from his property: (Mgh, Msb:) or the person who desires to go to a country, or town, other than his own, for a necessary affair: or, accord. to Ibn-'Arafeh, the guest who has become disabled from proceeding in his journey, his means having failed him: to such should be given as much as will suffice him to his home. (TA.) ― -b3- taqoTaEuwna Als~abiyla , in the Kur [xxix. 28], means (assumed tropical:) [ And ye cut off ] the way of offspring [by your unnatural practices]: or and ye oppose yourselves to men in the roads [or road ] for the purpose of that which is excessively, or enormously, foul or abominable. (TA.) ― -b4- [ sabiylu A@ll~`hi means (assumed tropical:) The way, or cause, of God, or of religion; or the way whereby one seeks approach to God, or advancement in his favour. ] It is said in the Kur [ii. 191], wa A^anofiquwA fiY sabiyli A@ll~`hi , meaning (assumed tropical:) And expend ye in warring against unbelievers and the like, and in every good work commanded by God; (M, K;) such being of the ways [that lead] to God: (M:) mostly used in relation to warring against unbelievers and the like. (M, K.) And in the same, iii. 163, A@l~a*iyna qutiluwA fiY sabiyli A@ll~`hi , meaning [ Who have been slain in the cause of God, or of his religion, i. e.,] for the sake of the religion of God. (Jel.) And you say, jaEala DayoEatahu fiY sabiyli A@ll~`hi (assumed tropical:) [ He made his estate to have its profit, or revenue, or usufruct, employed in the cause of God, or of religion ]. (S.) ― -b5- sabiylN also signifies (assumed tropical:) A means of access; a connexion, or a tie: so in the saying, in the Kur [xxv. 29], yaA layotaniY A@t~axa*otu maEa A@lr~asuwli sabiylFA (assumed tropical:) [ O would that I had obtained, with the Apostle, a means of access to Paradise]: (S, Msb, TA:) thus it has been explained: (TA:) or the meaning is, [ O would that I had taken, with the Apostle, ] a way to safety: or one way, the way of truth. (Bd.) ― -b6- [Also, in the present day, applied to A public drinking-fountain. ]

definition: Travelling upon a road: pl.
sourceDefinition: Travelling upon a road: pl. sawaAbilu and [coll. gen. n.] ↓ saAbilapN ; (TA:) this last signifies travellers, (S, M, *) or a company of people, (Mgh, K,) following, or succeeding, one another, or going repeatedly to and fro, (S, M, Mgh, K,) upon the roads, (S, Mgh,) or upon the road, (M, K,) for the accomplishment of their wants: it is made fem. as denoting a jamaAEap . (Mgh.) ― -b2- Also, ↓ saAbilapN , (TA in art. $gr ,) or sabiylN saAbilapN , (M, K, * TA,) A travelled road; (M, K, TA;) a beaten road. (TA in art. $gr .) -A2- gayovN saAbilN (assumed tropical:) Rain falling continuously, or in successive showers, and in large drops, and copiously. (TA.)

definition: A certain kind of trees, (S, K,) the heads of which, when it grows tall, bend and hang down;
sourceDefinition: A certain kind of trees, (S, K,) the heads of which, when it grows tall, bend and hang down; [a coll. gen. n.;] n. un. with p : (TA:) it resembles the A_i*oxir ; (K;) or it is like the vumaAm [or panic grass ], and has a [ root such as is termed ] jurovuwmap ; its branches, or twigs, are, in abundance, like the krAv [app. karaAv , a certain large tree, growing on the mountains]; and its fruits resemble brooms of reeds, or are more slender: (AHn:) serpents make their abodes at its roots. (TA.) It is related in a trad. of Ibn-Ez-Zubeyr, that he said to Mo'áwiyeh, laA tuToriqo A_iToraAqa AlA^ufoEuwaAni fiY A^uSuwli Als~axobari [ Do not thou look down upon the ground like as does the male viper at the roots of the sakhbar ]; meaning (assumed tropical:) do not thou affect heedlessness of the state in which we are, or of the affair in which we are engaged. (TA.) One says also, rakiba fulaAnN Als~axobara , meaning, (assumed tropical:) Such a one acted perfidiously, treacherously, or unfaithfully. (S.) And a poet says, waAlgadoru yanobutu fiY A^uSuwli Als~axobari (assumed tropical:) [ And perfidy grows at the roots of the sakhbar ]: (S:) [because the viper lives there: or] the poet means, that the people of whom he speaks dwelt in places where the sakhbar grew; and they are thought to have been of the tribe of Hudheyl: IB says that he likens the perfidious to this tree because, when it is full-grown, its head hangs down, not remaining erect; and that he means, ye do not remain faithful, like as this tree does not remain in one state. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, Mgh, * Msb, K,) inf. n. suTuwEN (S, K) and saToEN (TA) and saTiyEN , which last is rare, (K,) It rose: (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA:) or it spread, or diffused itself: (Mgh, TA:) said of duct, and of the dawn, (S, Msb, K,) [meaning as above, and it radiated, gleamed, or shone, (see saATiEN ,)] and of light, (TA,) and of lightning, and of the rays of the sun, (K,) and (tropical:) of odour, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) in relation to which last it is tropical, and signifies it diffused itself, and rose: or it was originally said only of light; and was then used absolutely, as meaning it appeared, or became apparent. (TA.) You say also saTaEa Als~ahomu The arrow, being shot, rose into the sky, glistening. (TA.) And yasoTaEu , the aor. of saTaEa , is used by Dhu-r-Rummeh, in describing an ostrich, as meaning He raises his head, and stretches his neck. (TA.) And you say, saTaEa liY A^amoruka (assumed tropical:) Thine affair became, or has become, apparent, or manifest, to me. (Lh.) ― -b2- saTaEatoniY raAy^iHapu Almisoki (tropical:) The odour of the musk rose to my nose. (K, TA.) -A2- saTaEotu Al$~aYo'a I laid hold of the thing with the palm of the hand, or with the hand, striking [ the thing ]. (Msb.) And saTaEa biyadayohi , inf. n. saToEN , He clapped with his hands: whence the subst. saTaEN [q. v.]. (IDrd, K.) -A3- saTiEa , aor. , (K,) inf. n. saTaEN , (TK,) He was long-necked; he had a long neck. (K.) [See A^asoTaEu .]

And you say of a woman, safarato , (S, M, A, Mgh, K,) aor. , (M,) inf. n. sufuwrN , (M, Mgh,) meaning She removed her veil (M, A, Mgh) Eano wajohihaA from her face: (A, M:) and [elliptically] (M) she uncovered her face: (S, M, K:) [for] safarotu Al$~aYo'a , [being for sfrt Eani Al$~aYo'i ,] aor. , inf. n. saforN [or sufuwrN ?], signifies I uncovered the thing; made it apparent, or manifest: (Mgh:) [but accord. to Mtr,] the phrase tasofiru wajohahaA [meaning she uncovers her face ] is of weak authority. sourceDefinition: The tree had its leaves blown off [ and swept away ] by the wind; (K, * TA;) they having become changed in colour, and white. (TA.) ― -b2- And Asfr , (inf. n. (Mgh.) ― -b6- Asfrt AlHarobu (tropical:) The war became vehement. (A, K.) -A2- See also 1, last sentence but one.

definition: A book, or writing: (S, M:) or a great, or large, book: or a section of the Book of the Law revealed to Moses: (M, K:) or a book that discovers, or reveals, truths: (TA:) or a book is thus called...

A^asofaArN . (M, TA.)

definition: Journey, or travel;
sourceDefinition: Journey, or travel; the act of journeying or travelling; (S, A, K;) contr. of HaDarN : (M, K:) thus called because of the going and coming in it, like the going and coming of the wind sweeping away fallen leaves: (M:) or the act of going forth to journey; an inf. n. used as a simple subst.: (Msb:) [therefore] the pl. is A^sofaArN : (S, M, A, Msb, K:) [and therefore it is often used as a n. un.; but, properly speaking, the n. un. is ↓ saforapN :] you say, kaAnato saforatuhu qariybapF [ His journey was near ]: and the pl. of saforapN , accord. to rule, is safaraAtN . (Msb.) In law, [as relating to the obligation of fasting &c.,] The going forth with the intention of performing a journey of three days and nights, or more. (KT.) -A2- Also The whiteness of dawn or daybreak: (A:) or the whiteness of the day: (S, M:) and i. q. SabaAHN [ dawn, or morning, or forenoon; but app. here used in the first of these senses]: (M:) and ↓ safiyrN , the whiteness [ of the sky ] before night: (A, TA:) or the former, the remains of the whiteness of day after sunset. (K.) You say safarFA i. e. SabaAHFA [app. as meaning In the dawn ]. (A.) And the prose-rhymer says, A_i*aA TalaEati Al$~iEoraY safarFA lamo tarafiyhaA maTarFA (S, * TA) i. e. definition: The food of the traveller;
sourceDefinition: The food of the traveller; (M, K;) the food that is prepared for the traveller, (S, Msb,) or for a journey: (TA:) pl. asufarN . (Msb.) This is the primary signification. (TA.) You say, A^akaluwA Als~uforapa They ate the food for the journey. (A.) ― -b2- Hence, (tropical:) The receptacle thereof; (TA;) the piece of skin in which it is put. (S, * M, * Msb, K, * TA.) [This is commonly of a round form, with a running string; so that it is converted into a bag to contain the food, at one time, and at another time is spread flat upon the ground, when persons want to eat upon it.] ― -b3- And hence, (tropical:) The thing [ whatever it be ] upon which one eats: (TA:) [in the desert, it is generally a round piece of skin, such as I have described above: in the towns, in the houses of the middle classes, a round tray of tinned copper, which is usually placed on a low stool; and in the dwellings of some of the highest classes, and the lowest, respectively, of silver and wood:] accord. to the T, suforapN has the last of the significations given before this, and the thing which it denotes is thus called because it is spread when one eats upon it. (TA.)
