And garayotu Als~ahoma signifies the same as garawotuhu [i. e. I glued the feathers upon the arrow: see the two pass. part. ns.]. (TA.) [And accord. to present usage, ↓ gar~aAhu , inf. n. tagoriyapN , signifies He glued it. ] ― -b2- garaA Als~imanu qalobahu , (K, TA,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (TA,) Fatness adhered to his heart, and covered it: (K, TA:) mentioned by ISd. (TA.) -A2- gariYa bihi It adhered to it [ as glue or the like ]. (Ksh and Bd in v. 17. [And used in this sense in the S and K as an explanation of lazija bihi .]) ― -b2- And [hence], aor. yagoraY , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. garFA (Abu-l-Khattáb, Msb, K, TA) and giraA='N , (K, TA,) like kisaA='N , but in the M like saHaAb [i. e. garaA='N ], which J [in the S] pronounces to be a subst., (TA,) He became attached to it, or fond of it; was eagerly desirous of it; he adhered, clung, or clave, to it; or loved it; syn. A^uwliEa bihi ; (Msb, K, TA;) and lazimahu ; (TA;) without his being incited thereto by another; (Msb, TA;) and bihi ↓ A^ugoriYa signifies the same, (Msb, * K, TA,) as also bihi ↓ gur~iYa , (K, TA,) each with damm, (K,) and the latter with teshdeed, as is stated in the M. (TA.) ― -b3- See also 3. ― -b4- And gariYa fulaAnN Such a one persisted, or persevered, in his anger. (S, TA.) ― -b5- gariYa said of what is termed Eid~N , [i. e. of the water thus termed,] (M, and so in some copies of the K,) or of a gadiyr , [or pool of water left by a torrent,] (so in other copies of the K [but the former is said in the TA to be the right],) It became cold, or cool, (M, TA,) or its water became cold, or cool. (K.) -A3- garawotu , (inf. n. garowN , S, * Msb,) also signifies I wondered. (S, Msb, TA.) [See garowN , below.]

You say, A^agorayotu Alkaloba biAlS~ayodi (S) I incited, urged, or instigated, the dog, to, or against, the object, or objects, of the chase. (Kull.) ― -b3- And AgrAhu bihimo He set him upon them, or over them; or made him to have mastery, dominion, or authority, over them. (Jel in xxxiii. 60.) ― -b4- AgrY bayonahumu AlEadaAwapa (tropical:) He occasioned enmity between them: (Jel in v. 17:) he cast enmity between them, as though he made it to cleave to them: (K, TA:) a tropical phrase. (Msb.) -A2- AgrY Al$~aYo'a , said of God, He made, or rendered, the thing goodly, or beautiful. (IKtt, TA.)

It is said in a prov., A^adorikoniY walawo biA^aHadi Almugoruw~ayoni , meaning [ Reach thou me, though ] with one of the two [ feathered ] arrows: or, as Th says, with an arrow or with a spear: (S:) El-Mufaddal says, there were two brothers, of the people of Hejer, a people to whom the Arabs ascribe stupidity, and one of those two rode an intractable she-camel, and the one that did not ride had with him a how, and his name was Huneyn; so the one that was riding called to him, and said, yaA hunayonu wayolaka A@noziloniY walawo biA^aHadi Almagoruw~ayoni , [in which AnzlnY seems to be a mistranscription for AdrknY ,] meaning, with his arrow; whereupon his brother shot at him and laid him prostrate; and his saying became a prov., applied on an occasion of necessity, or difficulty, and of the after failing of stratagem. (Meyd.) One says also qawosN magoruw~apN [ A glued bow ] (S, Msb, K) and ↓ magoriy~apN . (S, K.)

definition: A hard portion of flesh [app.
sourceDefinition: A hard portion of flesh [app. a gland ] around [or app. on either side of ] the Huloquwm [which seems to mean here, as it often does, the Haloq , i. e. fauces, or upper part of the throat ]; (O, K;) thus expl. by Lth; as also ↓ Algunodubu ; (O;) or ↓ Algunoduwbu : (K:) pl. ganaAdibu : and it is said that the gunodubataAni are [ two things ] like two ganglions ( $ibohu gud~atayoni ) in the nakofataAni ; (O, K;) in each nakofap [q. v.] is a gunodubap , and between the gndbtAn is the place of swallowing: (O:) the ganaAdib and the flesh that is upon them, or above them, around the lahaAp [app. here meaning the arches, or pillars, of the soft palate, or the furthest part of the mouth ], compose the lagaAniyn [pl. of lugonuwnN , q. v.], which are also called the nagaAnig , pl. of nugonugapN [or nugonugN , q. v.]: (TA:) or the gndbtAn are two glands ( EuqodataAni ) in, or at, ( fiY ,) the root of the tongue: (K, TA:) and they are said to be the two amygdalæ of the fauces; i. e. the tonsils: ( All~awozataAni : TA:) or two portions of flesh which are situate on either side of the lahaAp [app. meaning as expl. above, i. e. the arches, or pillars, of the soft palate, or the furthest part of the mouth ], (K, TA,) and between which is a space: (TA:) and gunodubataA AlEuro$ayoni is expl. as meaning the two things that conjoin ( All~ataAni taDum~aAni ) the lagaAniyn [above mentioned (I read AllgAnyn instead of AlEyn , an evident mistranscription in my original, for I can only suppose the description to mean the tonsils, as lodged between, and thus conjoining, the anterior and posterior pillars of the soft palate, )] on the right and left. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [ A kind of animal, ] well known, (M, K,) [the genus mus; the rat; the mouse; and the like ]; with ' , (Lth, S, Msb,) and without ' ; (Msb;) [a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. with p : (Lth, T:) [in the S and O and Msb, faA^orN is said to be pl. of faA^orapN , but in the last is added, like tamorapN and tamorN , showing that by pl. is meant coll. gen. n.:] the pl. of fA^r , (Lth, T, M, K,) or of fA^rp , (O, Msb,) is fiy^oraAnN (Lth, T, M, O, K, Msb) and fiy^irapN : (M, K:) accord. to IAar, (T, TA,) ↓ fuw^arN , like SuradN , (O, K, TA,) is applied to the male: (T, O, K, TA:) but this last word occurs in the phrase AlfaA^or Alfuw^ar , [in which AlfA^r is evidently used in a sense mentioned below, namely, “ the muscles, ” as is indicated in the T and O,] and, accord. to some, [ Alfuw^ar is a corroborative epithet, for they say that] this phrase is like layolN laAy^ilN and yawomN A^ayowamu : (O:) faA^orapN is applied [accord. to some] to the female; (M;) or [more correctly] to the male and the female, (M, K,) like as HamaAmapN is applied to the male and the female of the [genus] HamaAm . (M, TA.) ― -b2- Also Musk: (M, K:) this is sometimes called faA^orN because it is from the [animal, or from a kind of animal, called] faA^or , as some say. (M.) ― -b3- And faA^orapu Almisoki signifies The bag, follicle, or vesicle, ( naAfijap , S, M, O, K, or naAfiqap , T,) of musk: (T, S, M, O, K:) and is also without ' ; (M, Msb;) or it should correctly be mentioned in art. fwr , [as being called faArapN ] because of the spreading ( fawaraAn ) of its odour: or it may be with ' because it has the appearance, or form, of the [animal called] faA^orap . (O, K.) sourceDefinition: A certain plant, the grain of which is made into bread, (S, M, O, K,) and eaten, (S, M, O,) in the time of drought, or dearth: (S, M, O, K:) in some of the copies of the K, yuxotabaA^u is put for yuxotabazu : (M, F:) the bread made of it is coarse, or thick, resembling the bread that is baked in hot ashes [which is generally made in the form of thick round cakes]: (S, O:) a grain resembling [ the species of millet called ] jaAwaros , which is made into bread, and eaten: (IAar, T:) it is a wild grain, which the Arabs of the desert take, in the times of hunger, and pound, or bruise, and make into bread; and it is a bad kind of food, but sometimes, or often, they are content with it for days: (T:) or, as some say, it is [ a plant ] of the species called najiyl , growing in salt lands, of the [ plants termed ] HumuwD [pl. of HamoD ], of which bread is made: [a coll. gen. n.:] n. un. fav~apN : (Th, M:) Aboo-Ziyád El-Kilábee says, the fav~ , like the duEaAE , is a herb ( baqolap ) in which comes forth grain, and each of them spreads [ upon the ground ], not growing up high; and when they become dry, the people collect what is dry thereof, then pound, or bruise, it, and winnow it, and take forth from it a sort of black grain, with which they fill sacks, and lade the camels: it is a black sort of grain like the $ahoniyz [q. v.], and they make bread of it, and make EaSiydap ( yaEotaSiduwna ): (O:) in the Bári' it is said to be a species of tree or plant ( $ajarN ) growing in the plain, or soft, lands, and on the [ eminences called ] A=kaAm , having a sort of grain like the Him~aS [or chick-peas ], of which are made bread and sawiyq . (Msb.) ― -b2- And accord. to IF, Alfav~u signifies The habiyd , (O, Msb,) meaning the pulp of the colocynth, $aHomu AlHanoZali , (O,) or the colocynth-plant, $ajaru AlHanoZali . (Msb: and this is one of the meanings assigned to Alfav~u in the K. [In the TK, $aHomu AlHanoZali is said to be the correct explanation: but from what will be seen voce habiydN , I think it most probable that the right meaning is The seeds of the colocynth. ]) ― -b3- IF also says that it signifies The fasiyl [i. e. shoot, or shoots, of the palm-tree, ] which is, or are, plucked forth [ entire, ] from the base thereof. (O.) -A2- tamorN fav~N Dates that are scattered; (Lth, Kr, M, K;) not in a provision-bag or other receptacle; like bav~N : (Kr, M:) or dates that are separate, each one from others; not sticking together; (T, O;) and so fa*~N and ba*~N and faD~N . (T.)

definition: , a word occurring in the Kur ii.
sourceDefinition: , a word occurring in the Kur ii. 58, (T, S, M, &c.,) is expl. as signifying the same as vuwmN [which generally means Garlic; but is said to have also the meaning here next following]; (T, S, M, Msb, K;) said to be a dial. var. of the latter word, but app. [if meaning “ garlic ”] formed, as IJ says, by the substitution of f for v ; (M;) and 'Abd-Allah [Ibn-Mes'ood] read [in the Kur ubi suprà] wavuwmihaA [instead of wafuwmihaA ]: (Fr, T, S:) it is also expl. as signifying wheat; (T, S, M, Msb, K;) which is said by Lh to be a meaning of vuwm and fuwm ; and if Ibn-Mes'ood read the word as vwm , the meaning is fwm , i. e. “ wheat; ” (T;) accord. to Fr, it is an old word, signifying thus, (T, S, *) and also bread; (T, S, K;) Zj says that there is no difference of state- ment among the lexicologists as to its having the former of these two meanings, that it is said to have the latter also, and that it also signifies the other grains, beside wheat, whereof bread is made [which last meaning is also mentioned in the K]; (T;) and IJ holds that it is rightly expl. as having the first of these three meanings (i. e. “ wheat ”) and the last of them: (M:) another meaning assigned to it is Him~aSN [i. e. cicer arietinum; or chick-peas ]; (S, K;) which is of the dial. of Syria: (S:) and it signifies also any Euqodap [app. meaning head of a plant, such as that] of an onion, or of a garlic: or a great gobbet of food: (K: [for A^awo luqomapK EaZiymapK in the CK, I read Aw luqomapN EaZiymapN as in other copies of the K:]) in the dial. of Azd-es-Saráh, it is applied to ears of corn; and ↓ fuwmapN is its n. un.; (M;) this latter signifying an ear of corn, (S, K, TA,) as expl. by IDrd: (TA:) fuwmN has fuwmaAnN [of the measure fuEolanaAnN ] for a pl., this being [virtually] a pl. pl.; mentioned by IJ, who says that the dammeh in fuwmN is different from the dammeh in fuwmaAnN . (M, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yafiylu , (S, M, O, K,) inf. n. fuyuwlapN , (S,) thus in some copies of the K and in the A, (TA,) or fayoluwlapN , (M, O,) thus in other copies of the K, (TA,) and fayaAlapN , thus in the O, but in the copies of the K fayolap , (TA,) His judgment, or opinion, was weak, (S, M, O, K,) and erroneous; (M, K;) as also ↓ tfy~l ; (M, Z, K, TA;) and [in like manner] fiY raA^oyihi ↓ fay~ala [not fuy~ila ] he was incorrect in his judgment, or opinion; and ↓ fay~aluwA occurs in a trad. as meaning fAl raA^oyuhumo : (TA:) [and faAla alone, said of a man, signifies the same as fAl raA^oyuhu , as is shown by a verse of El-Kumeyt cited in the T and M and O and TA: but it seems from what here follows (taken from a passage unconnected with the foregoing) that the first and third of what are mentioned above as inf. ns. are regarded by some as simple substs.:] and one says, ↓ fiY raA^oyihi fayaAlapN , (T, M, K, TA,) the last word like saHaAbapN , (TA, [in the CK, erroneously, fY riwaAyapK fiyaAlapN ,]) and ↓ fuyuwlapN , (M, K, TA,) meaning [ In his judgment, or opinion, is ] a weakness. sourceDefinition: [The elephant; Pers. Pyl ;] a certain animal, (TA,) well known: pl. [of pauc.] A^afoyaAlN and [of mult.] fuyuwlN and fiyalapN ; (S, M, O, Msb, K;) not A^afoyilapN : (ISk, S, O, Msb:) accord. to Sb. fiylN may be originally of the measure fuEolN , (S, M, O,) pronounced with kesr because of the Y , like as they said A^aboyaDu and byDN ; but Akh says, this is not the case in the sing, but only in the pl.: (S, O:) fem. with p . (M, K) ― -b2- Hence, layolapN mivolu lawoni Alfiyli [lit. A night like the colour of the elephant; ] meaning a night that is black. (M, TA,) and dust-coloured; (M;) in which one knows not the right course to pursue: the colours of the fyl being of this kind. (M, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence, also, daA='u Alfiyli The disease called by us the tumid Barbadoes leg; because the leg of the patient resembles that of the elephant by reason of its enormously-swollen state: not (as some have supposed it to be) elephantiasis; this latter being termed ju*aAm (q. v.) [― -b4- And hence, likewise, used as an epithet,] fiylN signifies also (tropical:) Heavy [or dull ]; and low, ignoble, or mean. (K, TA.) ― -b5- And one says rajulN fiylu Alr~aA^oYi , meaning A man weak in respect of judgment, or opinion; (T, S, M, O, K;) and so ↓ fiyoluhu ; (M, K;) and ↓ faAy^iluhu : (T, M, O, K;) and ↓ fay~iluhu , (ISk, T, S, M, O, K,) of the measure fayoEil ; (O:) and ↓ faAluhu , (T, M, O, K,) and faAlN alone. (TA.)

definition: -A2- AlfaAy^ilu [as a subst.
sourceDefinition: : see fiylN , latter half, in two places. -A2- AlfaAy^ilu [as a subst.] signifies The flesh that is upon the xurobap , (S, O,) or xurob , (K, [in the M, accord. to the TT, Hrf , app. a mistranscription,]) of the warik ; (S, M, O, K;) [which, I think, will be plainly seen from what follows to mean the flesh that is upon the sacro-ischiatic foramen; though xurobapu Alwariki and xurobu Alwariki are said in the TA, in art. xrb , to mean “ the hole where the head of the thigh-bone is inserted; ”] so says A 'Obeyd: (S, O:) or, (S, M, O, K,) as some say, so adds A 'Obeyd, (S, O,) a certain vein (T, S, M, O, K) in the xurobap of the warik , descending into the leg, (T,) or in the thigh: (S, O:) As says, in “ the Book of the Horse, ” in the warik is the xurobap , which is a nuqorap wherein is flesh, no bone being in it; and in that nuqorap is the faAy^il , and there is no bone between the said nqrp and the belly, but only skin and flesh; (T, * S, O;) and he cites the saying of El-Aashà, qado naxoDibu AlEayora fiY makonuwni faAy^ilihi waqado ya$iyTu EalaY A^aromaAHinaA AlbaTalu [ Oft we stain the ridge of the spear-head in what is concealed in the interior of his fAy^l , and oft the man of valour dies by means of our spears ]; makonuwnu AlfaAy^ili means his blood: he says [by implication], we are skilful in respect of the place of piercing: (S, O:) but As said mino in the place of fiY ; and AA, qado naToEunu ; which has been pronounced to be wrong: (O:) or the faAy^ilaAni , (T, M,) or the ↓ faAy^ilataAni , (so in the K, [app. a mistranscription,]) are two veins entering into the interior parts of the thighs (T, M, K,) in the hinder parts thereof; (M, K;) and they adduce as an evidence thereof the verse of El-Aashà cited above, saying that the epithet mknwn would not have been used if the fAy^l were not a vein; but others say that [the poet meant that] he made the spear-head to become concealed in the furthest part of the flesh; [or n. un.] is ↓ qaDobapN : (K:) or it signifies, (S, O, Msb,) or signifies also, (K,) [ a species of trefoil, or clover; i. e.] i. q. raTobapN , (S, O, Msb,) which is the same as fiSofiSap , (Msb,) or qat~N , [which is also the same,] (K,) the name by which the people of Mekkeh call qat~ , (Fr, TA,) and (K) called in Pers. (S, O) A_isofisot , (S, Mgh, K,) or A_isobisot ; (O;) as also ↓ qaDobapN ; (S;) or this is the sing. [or rather n. un.] of qaDobN , which signifies faSaAfiSu [pl. of fiSofiSapN ]; (M;) called qaDobN because it is cut. (Mgh.) ― -b2- And Any tree of which the branches grow long and lank: (K, * TA:) basaTato in the K is a mistranscription for sabiTato . (TA.) ― -b3- And Certain trees from which bows are made; (En-Nadr, O, K;) said to be of the kind called naboEN . (O.) AHn says that qDb [accord. to the L and TA app. qaDobN , but accord. to a copy of the M ↓ qaDabN , which I think a mistranscription,] is the name of Certain trees of the plains, or soft tracts, growing among collections of [ other ] trees; having leaves like those of the pear-tree, except that they are thinner, and more soft; and as trees [ in general ] resembling pear-trees: the camels feed upon its leaves and the extremities of its branches; but when the camel has become satiated therewith, he forsakes it for a time, for it sets his teeth on edge, and irritates his chest, and occasions him cough. (M, L, TA.) sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, A, Msb, K,) inf. n. kuborN (A, Msb, K) and kibarN and kabaArapN , (A, K,) He, (TA,) or it, (Msb,) was, or became, great, [ big, or large in body, or corporeal substance: and in years, or age; (when said of a human being, often particularly signifying he attained to puberty; ) and in estimation or rank or dignity; ] contr. of Dagura ; (A, K;) syn. EaZuma , (S, Msb, K,) and jasuma . (K.) [In the K the pret. is twice mentioned: where it is explained as signifying the contr. of Sagura , the above inf. ns. are mentioned, as in the A: where it is explained by EaZuma and jasuma in the K, no inf. n. is mentioned; but in the TA it is there said that in the sense of EaZuma it relates to an affair or case, and that the inf. n. is kibarN and kabaArapN ; and that in the sense of jasuma it relates to anything.] ― -b2- kabura AlA^amoru [ The affair, or case, was, or became, of great moment; it was, or became, momentous: or it signifies as in the phrase next following]. (A.) ― -b3- kabura Ealayohi AlA^amoru The affair, or case, was, or became, difficult, hard, severe, grievous, distressing, afflictive, troublesome, or burdensome, to him or in its effect upon him; syn. $aq~a . (A, * TA.) In this sense the verb is used in the Kur, x, 72, (TA,) and xlii, 11. (Bd, ii. 42.) And so in the Kur again, xvii, 53, A^awo xaloqFA mim~aA yakoburu fiY Sduwrikumo , (TA,) meaning, A^awoxaloqFA mim~aA yakoburu Einodakumo Eano qubuwli AlHayaApi [ Or a created thing of those which are too difficult in your minds to receive life ], as being the thing most remote from capability to receive life. (Bd.) [This signification is from the primary application of the verb.] -A2- kabira , aor. , inf. n. kibarN and makobirN , He (a man, S, a human being, and a beast, TA, and a child, Msb,) became full-grown, or old, or advanced in age. (S, K.) Hence the prov., kabira Eamoruw Eani AlT~awoqi : see art. Twq .] ― -b2- [In modern Arabic, and, I believe, sometimes, in classic authors, it also signifies He became big; (said of a boy, or child, in the TA in art. rE , &c.;) i. e. attained to full growth: and to adolescence: and to puberty: see kabiyrN .] This form of the verb and that first mentioned are sometimes erroneously used, each for the other, by persons of distinction as well as by the vulgar. (TA.) ― -b3- See kaborapN , below. -A3- kaAbarotuhu fakabarotuhu , aor. of the latter, : see 3. ― -b2- kabarahu bisanapK , aor. , He exceeded me in age by a year. (K.) And maA kabaraniY A_il~aA bisanapK He did not exceed me in age save by a year. (IAar.)

definition: and ↓ Astkbr (S, K) and ↓ tkAbr (K) He magnified himself;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ Astkbr (S, K) and ↓ tkAbr (K) He magnified himself; behaved proudly, haughtily, or insolently; (K;) syn. taEaZ~ama : (S:) or tkb~r signifies, as used in the Kur, vii. 143, he considered himself as of the most excellent of the creation, and as having rights which others have not: (Zj:) or this verb has two significations: one of them, he did really good and great actions, exceeding the good actions of others; and hence Almutakab~iru [applied to God] in the Kur, lix. 23: the other, he affected to do such actions, and boasted of great qualities which he did not possess; as do the generality of men; and hence, mutakab~ir in the Kur, xl. 37; and the verb itself in the Kur, vii. 143: and ↓ Astkbr is nearly syn. with tkb~r , and likewise has two significations: one of them, he endeavoured, and sought, to become great; and to do so, when the manner and place and time are such as are requisite, is praiseworthy: the other, he boasted of qualities which he did possess, and feigned such qualities; and to do so is blameable; and in this sense the verb is used in the Kur, ii. 32: (El-Basáïr:) and ↓ tkAbr signifies he feigned himself great in estimation or rank or dignity, or in age. (A, TA.) ― -b2- tkb~r EalaY A@ll~`hi He magnified himself against God, by refusing to accept the truth. (El-Basáïr.) ― -b3- [ tkb~r Eano ka*aA He was disdainful of such a thing; he disdained it; turned from it with disdain; he held himself above it; like taEaZ~ama and taEaAZama and tajaAl~a and taraf~aEa .]

definition: Greatness [ in corporeal substance, and in estimation or rank or dignity ].
sourceDefinition: Greatness [ in corporeal substance, and in estimation or rank or dignity ]. (IKoot, Msb.) ― -b2- Nobility; eminence; highness; (K, * TA;) as also ↓ kuborN : (K:) eminence, or highness, in, or with respect to, nobility; (K;) as also ↓ kuburN , with two dammehs. (TA.) ― -b3- I. q. EaZamapN [which, as an attribute of God, signifies greatness, or majesty, or the like: (see munakab~irN :) and as an attribute of a man, pride ]: (S, Msb, K:) a subst. from Alt~akab~uru : (Msb:) as also ↓ kiboriyaA='u ; (S, Msb, K;) a word, says Kr, of which there is not the like [in measure], except siymiyaA='u and jirobiyaA='u ; for, he adds, as to kiymiyaA='u , I think it a foreign word: (TA:) the latter [↓ kiboriyaA'u ] occurs as an attribute of God, in the sense of EaZamapN , (A, Mgh, Jel,) in the Kur, xlv. 36: (Jel:) and as an attribute of men, in the Kur, x. 79, where it is said to signify proud behaviour towards others, (Bd,) or dominion: (IAmb, Bd, Jel:) and both signify pride, haughtiness, or insolence: (K:) or the former, self-admiration, or self-conceit; and the holding one's self greater than others: and the ↓ latter, disdain of submission; an attribute to which none but God has a right. (El-Basáïr.) ― -b4- Unbelief: the association of any other being with God. So in a trad., in which it is said, that he who has in his heart the weight of a grain of mustard-seed of kibor shall not enter paradise. (TA.) ― -b5- See also kabiyrapN . -A2- The main, or greater, or greatest, part of a thing; (Fr. ISk, Az, S, Mgh, K;) as also ↓ kuborN , (Fr, Mgh, Sgh, K,) like EuZomN ; (Fr;) thought by Ibn-ElYezeedee to be a dial. form; but Az says, that the Arabs used the other form [ kiborN ]. (TA.) So in the Kur, xxiv. 11, waA@l~a*iY tawal~aY kiborahu (Fr, S) And he who took upon himself, or undertook, the main part thereof; namely, of the very wicked lie against 'Áïsheh: (Jel:) thus accord. to the “ Seven Readers ”: and ↓ kuborahu , which is an extr. reading, (Msb,) the reading of Homeyd Ibn-El-Aaraj, (Fr, Sgh,) and of Yaakoob. (Sgh, Bd.) kuboru siyaAsapi Aln~aAsi fiY AlmaAli , [app. signifies The main part of men's management is with respect to property, or camels, &c.]. (S.)

sourceDefinition: : see kabiyrapN . -A2- huwa kiboratuhumo , (K,) and ↓ kubur~atuhumo , (Az, K,) so in the handwriting of AHeyth., (TA,) and ↓ A_ikobir~atuhumo , and ↓ A^akobir~atuhumo , and ↓ kuboruhumo , and ↓ kubur~uhumo , (K,) He is the greatest of them (K, TA) in age, or in headship: (TA:) or he is the nearest of them in kin to his chief, or oldest, ancestor; (K, TA;) his intermediate ancestors being fewer in number: (TA:) but some of these epithets are differently explained, as follows:] h`*aA kiborapu A^abiyhi this is the greatest, or oldest, ( A^akobaru ,) of the children of his father; (S, TA;) in which sense, qawomihi ↓ kaAna kubora is said of El-'Abbás, in a trad., because there remained not, in his lifetime, any one of the descendants of Háshim more nearly related to him than he: (L:) and in another trad. it is said, AlawlA='u llkubori (S, Mgh, Msb) the right to the inheritance of the property left by an emancipated slave belongs to the nearest in kin [ to the emancipater ] (Mgh, Msb) of the sons of the emancipater; (Mgh;) i. e., when a man [who has emancipated a slave] dies, leaving a son and a grandson, the right to the inheritance of the property left by the emancipated slave belongs to the son, not the grandson. (S.)

definition: Great [ in body, or corporeal substance, and in estimation or rank or dignity;
sourceDefinition: Great [ in body, or corporeal substance, and in estimation or rank or dignity; contr. of SagiyrN , but see EaZiymN ]; (S, K;) as also kibiyrN , as asserted by En-Nawawee and others, (TA,) and ↓ kubaArN (S, K) [in an intensive sense, like EuTaAmN ,] and ↓ kaAbirN and ↓ kub~aArN : (K:) or the last signifies excessively great: (S, TA:) and kaAbirN is an epithat applied to a man, and signifying great in dignity and nobility; (S, TA;) or great and noble; (Msb;) or one overcoming in greatness; (A;) or a lord, or chief; and the greatest, or oldest, ancestor: (AA:) the fem. [of kabiyrN ] is with p : (K:) and the pl. is kibaArN (S, K) and kubaraA='u , applied to men, (TA,) and makobuwraA='u , (S, * K,) [or rather the last is a quasi-pl. n.,] like ma$oyuwxaA='u ; [see $ayoxN ;] (TA;) and [of kub~aArN ] kub~aAruwna . (K.) [See also A^akobaru , and mutakab~irN .] You say tawaAravuwA ↓ A@lomajoda kaAbirFA Eano kaAbirK They inherited by degrees dignity, or nobility, one great in dignity and nobility from another great in dignity and nobility: (S:) or one great and noble from another great and noble: (Msb:) or Eano is here used in the sense of baEoda [ after ]: (TA voce TabaqN :) or one overcoming in greatness from another overcoming in greatness. (A.) definition: A foul, or an abominable, sin, or crime, or offence, forbidden by the law, of great magnitude;
sourceDefinition: A foul, or an abominable, sin, or crime, or offence, forbidden by the law, of great magnitude; such as murder and adultery or forni- cation, and fleeing from an army proceeding against an enemy [ of the Muslims ], &c.; [contr. of SagiyrapN ;] an epithet in which the quality of a subst. predominates: (TA:) and ↓ kiborN and ↓ kiborapN [in like manner] signify a great sin, or crime, or offence, for which one deserves punishment: (M, K:) the p is to give intensiveness to the signification: (TA:) or ↓ kiborN signifies [simply] a sin, a crime, or an offence, for which one deserves punishment, [as kabiyrapN is said, not well, to signify, in the Msb,] and is from kabiyrapN , like xiTo from xaTiyoy^apN : (TA:) pl. of the first, kabaAy^iru , (Msb, TA,) and kabiyraAtN also occurs. (Msb.) ― -b2- And see kabiyrN .

definition: [ Greater, and greatest, in body, or corporeal substance, and in estimation or rank or dignity: and] more, or most, advanced in age;
sourceDefinition: [ Greater, and greatest, in body, or corporeal substance, and in estimation or rank or dignity: and] more, or most, advanced in age; older, and oldest: (Msb:) fem. kuboraY : (S, Msb:) pl. masc. A^akaAbiru (S, Msb) and A^akobaruwna ; but not kuborN , because this is of a form specially appropriated to an epithet such as A^asowadu and A^aHomaru , and you do not use Akbr in the manner of such an epithet, for you do not say h`*aA rajulN A^akobaru , unless you conjoin it with a following word by mino , or prefix to it the article Al : (S:) [but see the phrase daEaA bikuborihi , below:] the pl. fem. is kubarN (S, Msb, K) and kuborayaAtN . (Msb.) ― -b2- A^akobaru is also used in the sense of kabiyrN : (Msb:) accord. to some, Aall~`hu A^akobar means God is great; (Az, Mgh, Msb;) like as huwa A^ahowanu Ealayohi [in the Kur, xxx. 26,] means huwa hay~inN Ealayohi ; (Az, TA;) but this explanation is of weak authority: (Mgh:) accord. to others, the phrase is elliptical, and means God is the greatest great [ being ]: (Az, TA:) or God is greater than every [ other ] great [ being ]: (Msb:) or greater than every [ other ] thing: (Mgh, TA:) or greater than such as that one knows the measure of His majesty: (TA:) [or it may be rendered God is most great, meaning, greater than any other being:] it is considered as elliptical because it is necessary that Akbr should have the article Al , or be followed by a noun in the gen. case [or by the prep. mino ]. (TA.) In the phrase Aall~`hu A^akobaru kabiyrAF , the word kbyrA is put in the accus. case [as a corroborative] in the place of the inf. n. takobiyrAF , as though one said A^ukab~iru takobiyrFA [ I magnify Him greatly, after saying All~`h Akbr ]. (TA.) ― -b3- yawomu AlHaj~i AlA^akobari [ The day of the greater pilgrimage, ] means the day of the sacrifice: or, as some say, the day of 'Arafeh: and others say otherwise. (TA.) ― -b4- In the following words, in a trad. of Mázin, buEiva nabiY~N mino muDara bidiyni A@ll~`hi Alkubari , there is an ellipsis, and the meaning is, bi$aray^iEi diyni A@ll~`hi Alkubari [ A prophet of Mudar hath been sent with the greatest, or greater, or great, ordinances of God ]. (TA.) ― -b5- In a trad. respecting burial, wayujoEalu A@loA^akobaru mim~aA yaliY A@loqibolapa means, And the most excellent shall be placed towards the Kibleh: or, if they be equal [in dignity], the oldest. (TA.) [Agreeably with the former rendering,] A^akobaru , in the Kur, xxix. 44, is explained as signifying Better. (TA, art. *kr .) [And agreeably with the second rendering of the above trad.,] you say h`*aA A^akobaru mino zayodK , meaning, This is older than Zeyd. (Msb.) ― -b6- In a trad. of Ibn-Ez-Zubeyr, the phrase daEaA bikuborihi means He summoned his sheykhs, and elders, or great men: kubor being here [notwithstanding what has been said above,] pl. of A^akobaru , like as HumorN is pl. of A^aHomaru . (TA.) ― -b7- h`*ihi AljaAriyapu mino kuboraY banaAti fulaAnK means, [ This girl is of those advanced in age of the daughters of such a one, ] mino kibaAri banaAtihi . (Ibn-Buzurj.) ― -b8- huwa A^akobaru qawomihi : see kiborapN .

sourceDefinition: , aor. yakiysu , (S, Msb, TA,) inf. n. kayosN (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and kiyaAsapN (S, A, K) and kuwsaY , with w put in the place of Y , [originally kuyosaY ,] (Seer [mentioned by him as syn. with kayosN ]) He (a boy, S [but often said of a man also,]) was, or became, acute, or sharp, or quick, in intellect; shrewd; clever; ingenious; skilful; knowing; intelligent: kayosN being the contr. of HumoqN ; (S, A, K;) and i. q. ZarofN , (Mgh, Msb,) and xiq~apN , and tawaq~udN , (TA,) and fiTonapN , (Msb, TA,) and fiqohN , (TA,) and EaqolN . (IAar, A, Msb, K.) ― -b2- kaAsa fiY AlA^amori , aor. yakiysu , (A, TA,) inf. n. kayosN ; (Mgh, TA;) and ↓ tky~s ; and ↓ tkAys ; (A, TA;) He acted gently, (TA,) or with good gentleness or moderation or calmness, (Mgh,) in the affair. (Mgh, TA.) -A2- kaAsahu , aor. yakiysuhu , (S, * K,) inf. n. kayosN , (A, TA,) He overcame him, or surpassed him, (S, A, K,) in kiyaAsap (A, K) or kayos (A, Nh) [i. e. acuteness or sharpness or quickness of intellect; &c.: see above]. (TA.) ― -b2- kayisa , [aor. yakoyasu ,] inf. n. kayasN , is also mentioned by IKtt as a dial. form of kaAsa in the sense of He overcame or surpassed [ in acuteness &c.] (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [ A purse; ] a well known receptacle; (TA;) a thing made of pieces of rag sewed together; (Msb;) for money, (S, K, TA,) and for pearls and sapphires: (TA:) [so called] because it comprises them: (K, TA:) [a remark that seems to indicate a signification of kaAsa or some other word from the same root which I do not find elsewhere pointed out: but the more probable derivation is from the Persian kiysaho :] that which is tied up, of leather, and of pieces of rag, is not called thus, but is called xariyTapN : (Msb:) pl. (K, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also, (assumed tropical:) The scrotum. ]

definition: (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ kayosN , (TA,) [like hiy~inN and hayonN , &c.
sourceDefinition: (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ kayosN , (TA,) [like hiy~inN and hayonN , &c.,] Acute, or sharp, or quick, in intellect; clever; ingenious; skilful; knowing; intelligent: (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K, TA:) fem. kay~isapN : (S, A:) and ↓ kiysaY , applied to a woman, is syn with kay~isapN , and is, as also kuwsaY , [each originally kuyosaY ,] fem. of A^akoyasu : (S:) [whence it appears that this last word is accord. to J syn. with kay~isN ; i. e., a simple epithet, like its contr. A^aHomaqu : but it has another signification, for which see below:] or, accord. to Kr, kiysaY and kuwsaY are pls. of kay~isapN ; and there are no similar instances except DiyqaY and DuwqaY , pls. of Day~iqapN , and TuwbaY , pl. of Tay~ibapN : but ISd holds them to be fems. of the measure A^afoEalu : (TA: [see DuwqaY in art. Dyq :]) the pl. of kay~isN is A^akoyaAsN (A, Mgh, Msb, TA) and kayosaYi , (A, K, TA [in the CK, erroneously, kiysY ,]) like HamoqaY , (A,) having this latter form in order that it may resemble its contr., HamoqaY : (TA:) and kiyaAsN is pl. of kay~isapN , (A, TA,) [and A^akaAyiysu is app. pl. of kiyaAsN : see an ex. voce Ti$~apN .] You also say, ↓ rajulN kay~isN mukay~asN , meaning, A man acute or sharp or quick in intellect, &c.: (S:) or [ acute &c., and] described as being so; or having the attribute of kayos ascribed to him: (A:) or ↓ rajulN mukay~asN signifies, as also kay~isN , a man known as possessing kayos [or acuteness &c.]. (TA.) And A_imoraA^apN kay~isapN A woman well educated, or well bred. (TA.) And rajulN kay~isu AlfiEol A man good in action or conduct. (TA.) And banaY daArFA kay~isapF (A) (tropical:) He built an elegant house; syn. ZariyfapF . (TA.) [The dim. kuway~isN , more properly kuyay~isN or kiyay~isN , is much used in the present day as signifying (tropical:) Elegant, pretty, or beautiful. ]

sourceDefinition: , aor. yamuwtu , (inf. n. mawotN ; Msb,) and maAta , (originally mawita , like xaAfa , originally xawifa , MF) [sec. per. mit~a ,] aor. yamaAtu , (S, K,) which latter is of the dial. of Teiyi; (TA;) and maAta , (in which the medial radical letter is originally Y , like baAEa , MF) aor. yamiytu , (K,) a form which some have disapproved; (MF;) and maAta , (originally mawita , Kr,) sec. pers. mit~a , aor. yamuwtu , like daAma , (originally dawima , Kr,) aor. yaduwmu , (Kr, Msb, &c.,) and like the sound verbs naEima , aor. yanoEumu , and faDila , aor. yafoDulu , (TA,) of the class of words in which two dial. forms are intermixed; (Msb;) He died; contr. of HayiY . (K,) ― -b2- [ maAta Eano baniyna wabanaAtK He died having passed away from, i. e. leaving behind him, sons and daughters. And maAta Eano vamaAniyna sanFp He died having passed beyond eighty years; i. e. being eighty years old. ] ― -b3- All~abanu laA yamuwtu [ The milk will not die ], in a saying of 'Omar, in a trad., means, that if a child sucks the milk of a dead woman, it becomes unlawful for him afterwards to marry any of her relations who would be unlawful to him if he sucked her milk while she was living: or it means, that, if milk taken from the breast of a woman is given to a child to drink, and he drinks it, the consequence is the same; that the effect of the milk in producing this consequence is not annulled by its separation from the breast; for whatever is separated from a living being is termed myt , or dead, except the milk and hair and wool on account of the necessity of making use of these. (TA.) ― -b4- maAtati AlA^aroDu , inf. n. mawataAnN and mawaAtN , (tropical:) The land became destitute of cultivation and of inhabitants. (Msb.) ― -b5- maAta (tropical:) It (soil) became deprived of vegetable life. Hence an expression in the Kur, xxx. 18. (Az, Er-Rághib.) ― -b6- maAta (tropical:) He became deprived of sensation; [ dead as to the senses ]. So in the Kur, xix. 23: [but this appears to me doubtful]. (Az, Er-Rághib.) ― -b7- maAta (tropical:) He became deprived of the intellectual faculty; [ intellectually dead; ] or ignorant. Hence an expression in the Kur, vi. 122; and another in the Kur, xxvii. 82; and xxx. 51. (Az, Er-Rághib.) ― -b8- maAta (tropical:) [ He became as though dead with grief, or sorrow, and fear; ] he experienced grief, or sorrow, and fear, that disturbed his life. Hence what is said in the Kur, xiv. 20. (Az, Er-Rághib.) ― -b9- maAta (tropical:) He or it, was or became, still, quiet, or motionless. (K.) ― -b10- mAtati Alr~iyH (tropical:) The wind became still, or calm. (TA.) ― -b11- maAta (tropical:) He slept. (AA, K.) ― -b12- maAtati Aln~aAru , inf. n. mawotN , (tropical:) [ The fire died away; ] the ashes of the fire became cold, or cool, and none of its live coals remained. (TA.) ― -b13- maAta (tropical:) It (heat or cold) became assuaged. (TA.) ― -b14- maAta (tropical:) It (water) became dried up by the earth. (TA.) ― -b15- maAta (and ↓ AstmAt , TA.) (tropical:) It (a garment, TA,) wore out; became worn out. (A, K.) ― -b16- mAt (tropical:) It (a road) ceased to be passed along. (TA.) ― -b17- baladN tamuwtu fiyhi Alr~iyHu [ A town, or country, &c., in which the wind becomes broken, or loses its force ]. (TA.) ― -b18- maAta fuwqu Alr~ajuli (tropical:) The man slept heavily; became heavy in his sleep. (TA.) ― -b19- yamuwtu mina AlHasadi (tropical:) [ He dies, or will die, of envy ]. (TA.) ― -b20- maAta (tropical:) He became poor; was reduced to poverty: he became a beggar. (TA.) ― -b21- (tropical:) He became base, abject, vile, despicable, or ignominious. (TA.) ― -b22- (tropical:) He became extremely aged, old and weak, or decrepit. (TA.) ― -b23- (tropical:) He became disobedient, or rebellious. Iblees is said, in a trad., to be A^aw~alu mano maAta because he was the first who became disobedient, or rebellious. (TA.) ― -b24- maAta (assumed tropical:) He (a man) became lowly, humble, or submissive, to the truth. (TA.)

definition: (tropical:) A fainting, or swoon;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) A fainting, or swoon; (K;) and languor in the intellect: (TA:) or [ an affection ] like a fainting, or swoon: (Lh:) madness, or insanity, or diabolical possession; syn. junuwnN ; (AO, K;) because it occasions a stillness like death: (TA:) or a kind of madness or diabolical possession ( junuwnN ), and epilepsy, that befalls a man; on the recovery from which, his perfect reason returns to him, as to one who has been sleeping, and to one who has been drunk. (S.) [See humozN .]

definition: and ↓ mayotN signify the same, [ Dead, or dying ]: (Zj, S, K:) the former is originally mayowitN , of the measure fayoEilN : (S:) the latter is contracted from the former;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ mayotN signify the same, [ Dead, or dying ]: (Zj, S, K:) the former is originally mayowitN , of the measure fayoEilN : (S:) the latter is contracted from the former; and is both masc. and fem.; (Zj, S;) as is also the former. (Zj.) 'Adee Ibn-Er-Raalà says, ↓ layosa mano maAta faA@sotaraAHa bimayotK A_in~amaA Almayotu may~itu AlA^aHoyaA='i [ He who has died and become at rest is not dead: the dead is only the dead of the living ]. (S, TA.) Or ↓ mayotN signifies One who has died (actually, TA,); and may~itN , as also ↓ maAy^itN , one who has not yet died, (K,) but who is near to dying: or, accord. to a verse cited by AA, to Kh, mayotN is applied to him who is borne to the grave; [i. e., who is dead, or lifeless ]; and may~itN , to him who [ is dying, but ] has life in him. (TA.) Fr says, you say of him who has not died, A_in~ahu maAy^itN , Eano qaliylK ↓ and may~itN ; but you do not say of him who has died ↓ h*A maAy^itN : (S:) but some say, that this is an error, and that may~itN is applicable to that which will soon die. Those who assert that my~t is applicable only to the living adduce the following words of the Kur, [xxxix. 31,] A_in~aka may~itN waA_in~ahumo may~ituwna : (TA:) i. e. Verily thou wilt die, and verily they will die. (Msb.) MF observes, that mayotN is asserted to be contracted from may~itN ; and if so, that there can be no difference in their meanings: that the making a difference between them is contrary to analogy; agreeably with which, they should be like hayonN and hay~inN , and layonN and lay~inN : and also contrary to what has been heard from the Arabs; for they made no difference in their use of these two words. (TA.) [See also what is said of mayotapN , below.] The pls. are A^amowaAtN and mawotaY and may~ituwna and mayotuwna . (S, K.) The first of these is pl. of may~itN , and consequently of mayotN , because this latter is contracted from the former: as may~itN is of the measure fayoEilN , and this measure resembles faAEilN , it has received a form of pl. which is sometimes applicable to the measure fAEl : (Sb:) or AmwAt is [only] pl. of mayotN . (Msb.) [The second form (which is applied to rational beings, Msb,) is also pl. of my~t and myt .] The third and fourth are [only] applied to rational beings. (Msb.) The fem. epithet is may~itapN and mayotapN and may~itN (K, TA) and mayotN . (TA; and so in some copies of the K, in the place of may~itN .) may~itapN is an epithet applied to a female rational being; [and its pl. is may~itaAtN :] mayotapN , to a female brute, for the sake of distinction; and its pl. is mayotaAtN : the latter is contracted because it is more in use than the former epithet applied to a female rational being: (Msb:) the pl. of my~t and myt as fem. epithets is as above [ A^amowaAtN and mawotaY ]. (TA.) ― -b2- ↓ mayotapN signifies That which has not been slaughtered (AA, S, K) [ in the manner prescribed by the law, i. e., carrion ]: or that of which the life has departed without slaughter: so in the classical language and in the language of practical law: all such is unlawful to be eaten, except fish and locusts, which are lawful by universal consent of the Muslims: (En-Nawawee:) or, in the common acceptation of the language of law, what has died a natural death, or been killed in a state or manner different from that prescribed by the law, either the agent or the animal killed not being such as is so prescribed; as that which is sacrificed to an idol, or slaughtered [by a person] in the state of A_iHoraAm , or not by having the throat cut, and that which it is unlawful to eat, such as a dog: (Msb:) [and any separated part of an animal of which the flesh is not lawful food: see EaAjN .] ― -b3- baladN may~itN A tract of land without herbage, or pasture, (Msb, in art. bld .) ― -b4- may~itN (assumed tropical:) An unbeliever; like as HaY~N means a Muslim. (TA, in art. HY .)

(TA.) [See also what is said of mayotapN , below.] The pls. are A^amowaAtN and mawotaY and may~ituwna and mayotuwna . (S, K.) The first of these is pl. of may~itN , and consequently of mayotN , because this latter is contracted from the former: as may~itN is of the measure fayoEilN , and this measure resembles faAEilN , it has received a form of pl. which is sometimes applicable to the measure fAEl : (Sb:) or AmwAt is [only] pl. of mayotN . (Msb.) [The second form (which is applied to rational beings, Msb,) is also pl. of my~t and myt .] The third and fourth are [only] applied to rational beings. (Msb.) The fem. epithet is may~itapN and mayotapN and may~itN (K, TA) and mayotN . (TA; and so in some copies of the K, in the place of may~itN .) may~itapN is an epithet applied to a female rational being; [and its pl. is may~itaAtN :] mayotapN , to a female brute, for the sake of distinction; and its pl. is mayotaAtN : the latter is contracted because it is more in use than the former epithet applied to a female rational being: (Msb:) the pl. of my~t and myt as fem. epithets is as above [ A^amowaAtN and mawotaY ]. (TA.) ― -b2- ↓ mayotapN signifies That which has not been slaughtered (AA, S, K) [ in the manner prescribed by the law, i. e., carrion ]: or that of which the life has departed without slaughter: so in the classical language and in the language of practical law: all such is unlawful to be eaten, except fish and locusts, which are lawful by universal consent of the Muslims: (En-Nawawee:) or, in the common acceptation of the language of law, what has died a natural death, or been killed in a state or manner different from that prescribed by the law, either the agent or the animal killed not being such as is so prescribed; as that which is sacrificed to an idol, or slaughtered [by a person] in the state of A_iHoraAm , or not by having the throat cut, and that which it is unlawful to eat, such as a dog: (Msb:) [and any separated part of an animal of which the flesh is not lawful food: see EaAjN .] ― -b3- baladN may~itN A tract of land without herbage, or pasture, (Msb, in art. bld .) ― -b4- may~itN (assumed tropical:) An unbeliever; like as HaY~N means a Muslim. (TA, in art. HY .)

A^anojudN , (S, L, K,) a pl. of pauc., (TA,) and A^anojaAdN , (L, K,) [also a pl. of pauc.,] and nijaAdN and nujuwdN (S. L, K) and nujudN ; (IAar, L, K;) and pl. of nujuwdN , A^anojidapN ; [another pl. of pauc.;] (S, K;) or this is a mistake, and it is pl. of nijaAdN , like as A^aHomirapN is pl. of HimaArN ; or it is a pl. deviating from common rule. (IB, L.) You say A^uEolu haAtiyka Aln~ijaAda Ascend thou these high lands; and haA*aAka Aln~ijaAda this high land, making it singular. (L.) ― -b2- najodN , (S, L, K, &c.,) and najudN , (K,) the latter of the dial. of Hudheyl, (Akh,) of the masc. gender, [ The high land, or country; ] a division of the country of the Arabs; opposed to Algaworu , [or the low country,] i. e., Tihámeh; all the high land from Tihámeh to the land of El-'Irák; (S, L;) above it are Tihámeh and El-Yemen, and below it El-'Irák and Esh-Shám; (K;) it begins, towards El-Hijáz, at Dhát-'Irk, (Msb, K,) and ends at Sawád of El-'Irák, and hence it is said to form no part of El-Hijáz: (Msb:) or it comprises all that is beyond the moat, or fosse, which Kisrà made to the Sawád of El-'Irák until one inclines to the Harrah ( AlHar~ap ), when he is in El-Hijáz; (El-Báhilee, T, L, Msb;) and it extends to the east of El-Ghowr, or El-Ghór; which is all the tract of which the torrents flow westwards: Tihámeh extends from Dhát-'Irk to the distance of two days' journey beyond Mekkeh: the tract beyond this, westward, is Ghowr, or Ghór; and beyond this, southwards, is Es-Saráh, as far as the frontiers of El-Yemen: (El-Báhilee, L:) or, as the Arabs of the desert have been heard to say, the country which one enters when, journeying upwards, he leaves behind him 'Ijliz, which is above El-Karyateyn, and which he quits when he descends from the mountain-roads of Dhát- 'Irk, where he enters Tihámeh, and when he meets with the stony tracts termed HiraAr in Nejd, where El-Hijáz commences: (As, L:) or the high country from Batn-er-Rummeh to the mountain-roads of Dhát-'Irk: (ISk, L:) or the country from El-'Odheyb to Dhát-'Irk, and to El-Yemámeh, and to El-Yemen, and to the two mountains of Teiyi, and from El-Mirbed to Wejreh: Dhât-'Irk is the beginning of Tihámeh, extending to the sea and Juddeh: El-Medeeneh is not of Tihámeh nor of Nejd, but of El-Hijáz, higher than El-Ghowr, or El-Ghór, and lower than Nejd. (IAar, L.) ― -b3- najodN An elevated road: (S:) or an elevated and conspicuous road. (L, K.) A road in a mountain. (L.) [Hence Tal~aAEu AlA^anojudi , expl. below, and in art. TlE .] ― -b4- hadayonaAhu Aln~ajodayoni [Kur, xc. 10] We have shown him the two ways; the way of good and that of evil: (Beyd, Jel, L:) or the two conspicuous ways: (L:) ― -b5- or We have given him the two breasts; (Beyd, L;) for najodN also signifies a woman's breast; (L, K;) the belly beneath it being like the [country called] gawor . (TA.) ― -b6- A^amaA wanajodayohaA maA faEalota *`lika Now, by her two breasts, didst thou not that? A form of oath of the Arabs. (MF.) ― -b7- najodN and ↓ naAjidN A thing, or an affair, apparent, manifest, plain, or evident. (L.) ― -b8- huwa Tal~aAEu A^anojudK , and Tl~AE A^anojidapK , (S, L, K,) and Tl~AE nijaAdK , (L, K,) and AlA^anojudi , (K, art. TlE ,) and AlnijaAdi , (L, K,) (tropical:) He is one who surmounts difficult affairs: (A:) or he is one who manages affairs thoroughly, (L, K,) and masters them: (L:) or he is a man expert in affairs, who surmounts and masters them by his knowledge and experience and excellent judgment: or, who aims at lofty things: (K, art. TlE :) or he is one who rises to eminences, or to lofty things or circumstances, or to the means of attaining such things: (S:) as also Tal~aAEu Alv~anaAyaA . (S, K, art. TlE .) See najidN , and munaAjidN . -A2- najodN , sing. of nujuwdN (A 'Obeyd, S, L, K) and of nijaAdN , (L, K,) which signify The articles of household farniture and the like ( mtAE ) with which a house or tent ( byt ) is ornamented, or decorated; (A 'Obeyd, S, L;) the carpets and beds or other things that are spread, and the pillows, used for that purpose: (L, K:) the cloths or stuffs used for this purpose, with which the walls are hung, and which are spread; (L;) the curtains which are hung upon the walls: (A:) and A^anojaAdN , pl. of najodN , household furniture, consisting of such things as are spread, and pillows, and curtains. (L.) -A3- najodN A skilful, or an expert, guide of the way. (L, K.) -A4- najodN , (K,) or ↓ nujudN , (L,) A place in which are no trees. (L, K.) -A5- najodN A kind of tree resembling the $uborum (L, K) in its colour and manner of growth and its thorns. (L.)

sourceDefinition: , a coll. gen. n., [I find it said to have been written with tenween by J himself: but it appears to have been also used as a generic proper name; and as such, having the measure of a verb, it must be written tanoDubu , being imperfectly declinable:] A certain tree: the t is augmentative, because there is no word of the measure faEolulN ; whereas there are words of the measure tafoEulu , as taqotulu and taxoruju : n. un. tanoDubapN : (S:) a certain tree of El-Hijáz: (K:) it grows large, in the form, or manner, of the saroH , having white and thick branches; and folds, such as are called HaZaAy^ir , are made of it: [this is the only meaning I can assign to the words whw mHtZr , supposing bihi to be omitted after mHnZr , though yuHonaZaru would be better:] its leaves are contracted; and it always appears as though it were dry and dusty, though growing: (TA:) its thorns are like those of the Eawosaj : (K, TA:) and it has a fruit [called magodN (L, K, art. mgd )] like small grapes, which is eaten, of a reddish colour: AHn says, that its smoke is white, of the colour of dust; and that poets therefore liken dust to it: and in one place he says, that it is a large tree, without leaves [ properly so called ], which has a trunk, and from which grow thick boughs, with many branches; its leaves [ if such they may be called ] being only shoots, which are eaten by the camels and sheep and goats: Aboo-Nasr says, that it is a tree having short thorns: not of the trees that grow on lofty mountains; frequented by chameleons: [see HirobaA'N , in art. Hrb : and see an ex. in a verse cited voce saAqN :] ISd thinks that it is thus called because of its little sap: AM says, that it is a large tree, from which are cut tentpoles: (TA:) and Ibn-Selemeh says, that it is a tree from which arrows are made. (S.) ― -b2- nuwqN kaqidaAHi Alt~anoDubi [ She-camels like arrows made of the wood of the tendub ]. (TA).

definition: He took extraordinary pains, or exceeded the usual bounds, in cleansing or purifying himself, or in removing himself far from unclean things or impurities: (As, S:) or he shunned, or removed himself...
sourceDefinition: He took extraordinary pains, or exceeded the usual bounds, in cleansing or purifying himself, or in removing himself far from unclean things or impurities: (As, S:) or he shunned, or removed himself far from, unclean things: (M, A, K:) and he was dainty, nice, exquisite, refined, or scrupulously nice, and exact, syn. taA^at~aqa , (As, M, A, K,) in cleanliness; (K;) and in speech, (A, K,) so as never to speak otherwise than chastely; (TA;) and in diet and apparel, (A, K,) so as never to eat or wear anything but what was clean, (A,) or so as never to eat anything but what was clean nor wear anything but what was good; (TA;) and in all affairs. (S, M, A.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, Msb,) inf. n. nafoDN , (S, Mgh, Msb,) He shook (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) a thing, (Mgh, Msb,) or a garment, or piece of cloth, (S, A, K,) in order that what was upon it, of dust &c., might fall off (S, * A, * Mgh, K, *) or to remove from it dust and the like; (Msb:) he took a thing with his hand, and shook it, or shook it violently, to remove the dust from it: (TA:) and in like manner a tree, in order that what was upon it [ of face or of leaves ] might fall of; (S, A;) as, for instance,] a tree of the kind called EiDAh , to shake off its leaves. (TA) You say also, nafaDa Eanahu AlgubaAra and Alt~uraAba [ He shook off from it the dust (A.) And nafaDatu Alwaraqa mino Al$~ajarap . inf. n. as above, [ He shook off the leaves from the tree; ] be made the leaves to fall from the tree. (Msb,) And nafoDN also signifies The sprinkling or scattering in drops, (syn. ra$~N ,) water and blood. (A, K, in art. r$ ,) and tears, (K, ibid.) &c. (A,ibid.) ― -b2- [Hence,] nafaDatohu AlHum~aY (S, A, K) (tropical:) The fever made him to shiver, or tremble (As, TA ― -b3- And nafaDati AlmaroA^apu , (K,) or nafDatN kar$ahaA (S,) or nafaDato waladahaA mino baTonhA , (A,)‡ The woman bore many children; was prolific (S, K. TA) And nafaDat AlA_ibilu (assumed tropical:) The she-camels brought forth, (S, L, K,) all of them: (L;) and ↓ AnEDt signifies the same. (IDrd, S, K.) And bayoDahA nagaDati Ald~aHaAjaPu (tropical:) [ The hen laid her eggs. or all her eggs A. TA.) ― -b4- Hence also,] faAma yanafuDu AlkraY , He arose, shaking off drowsiness ]. (A. TA.) And nafaDa AlA^asofaAma Eanohu waA@sotaSaH~ ; [ He shook off maladies from him, and recovered from his sickness] ; i. e. his health became in a sound state (A. TA.) And nafaDa mino maraDihi (A,) inf. n. nufuwDN , (TA, K,) (tropical:) He recovered, or became free, from his disease (A, K, * TA.) ― -b5- And nafaDotu lahu maA fiY jiraAbiY † I showed him what was in my heart. (Er-Rághib, TA, in art. $kw and $kY ― -b6- And nafaDa AlT~ariyqa (tropical:) He cleared the road of robbers, and intercepters of travellers: (tropical:) he guarded the road. (A, TA. [The latter signification is shown by an explanation or the act. part. n.] It is said in the trad. of Aboo-Bekr and the cave [ in which Mohammad was hiding himself], A^anaA A^anafuDu maA Hawolaka (tropical:) I will guard what is around thee, and go round about to try if I can see a pursuer. (TA.) You say also, nafaDa AlmakaAn , (S, K,) aor. as above, (TA.) inf. n. nafaDN (S, TA.) and ↓ AstnfDhu , and ↓ tnf~Dhu ; (S, K;) (tropical:) He looked trying to see all that was in the place: (S;) or he looked at all that was in the place so as to know it. (K) And hence nafaDa signifies (tropical:) He searched to the at most. (L.) And A_i*aA takal~amut nahaArFA faA@nofuDo waA_i*aA takal~amota layolFA faA@xofiDo (S, K, * TA) (tropical:) When thou speakest by day, look aside, or about, to try if thou see any one whom thou dislikest; (S, K, TA;) and when thou speakest by night, lower thy voice. (TA.) And Alqawoma ↓ AstnfD (tropical:) He looked at the people, or company of men, endeavouring to obtain a clear knowledge of them; or considered, or examined, them repeatedly, in order to know them. (TA.) The saying of El-'Ojeyr Es-Saloolee, Alqawoma Tarofuhu ↓ A_ilaY malikK yasotanofiDu means (tropical:) [ To a king whose eye ] looks at the people, or company of men, and knows who among them has the right on his side: or looks to see in whom among them is mental perception, sagacity, intelligence, forecast, or skill in affairs, and which of them is of the contrary description: (TA:) [or] Tarofuhu Alqawoma ↓ fulaAnN yasotanofiDu means (tropical:) [ The eye of ] such a one makes the people, or company of men, to tremble, by reason of his awfulness. (A, TA.) ― -b7- You also say, AlA_ibilu tanofuDu AlA^aroDa (assumed tropical:) The camels traverse the land. (IAar.) ― -b8- And nafaDa AlquroA=na , (IAar,) or Als~uwara , (K,) aor. , inf. n. nafoDN , (IAar,) (tropical:) He read, or recited, (IAar, K,) the Kur-án, (IAar,) or the chapters thereof. (K.) ― -b9- And nafaDonaA HalaAy^ibanaA , inf. n. nafoDN ; and ↓ AisotanofaDonaAhaA ; (tropical:) We milked our milch beasts to the uttermost, not leaving any milk in their udders: (TA:) and AlfaSiylu maA fiY AlD~aroEi ↓ AntfD (tropical:) the young camel sucked out all that was in the udder. (A, TA.) -A2- [It is also used intransitively in the following exs., as well as in some instances given above. Thus nafaDa Al$~ajaru app. signifies The trees shook off, or dropped, their leaves or fruit. (See an ex. voce EatiyqN , last sentence but one.) ― -b2- And hence] one says, nafaDa maA fiY Aljul~api [app. meaning What was in the palm-leaf basket became exhausted; like nafida ; or it may be syn. with AntfD ]; (A, K;) or jamiyEu maA fiyhaA [ all that was in it; which shows that mA in the former instance is virtually in the nom. case]. (TA.) See also 4, in two places. ― -b3- And nafaDa AlS~ibogu , (ISh, Mgh, K,) inf. n. nafoDN , (ISh, TA,) or nufuwDN , (TA,) (tropical:) The dye (ISh, K, TA,) of a red or yellow garment, or piece of cloth, (ISh, TA,) lost somewhat of its colour. (ISh, K, TA.) And hence, (Mgh,) nafaDa Alv~awobu , (A, Mgh,) aor. , (A,) inf. n. nufuwDN , (A, Mgh,) (tropical:) The garment, or piece of cloth, lost its dye: (A:) or lost somewhat of its colour, of redness, or yellowness: (Mgh:) or the colour of its dye faded away so that there remained nothing but the trace. (TA.) nafoDN , accord. to the lawyers, signifies (assumed tropical:) The being scattered, strewn, strewed, or dispersed: and accord. to [the Hanafee Imám] Mohammad, the non-transition of the trace of the dye to another thing: or its exhaling a sweet odour. sourceDefinition: It (a thing, Mgh, Msb, or a garment, or piece of cloth, S, A, K, and a tree, S, A) shook, or became shaken, (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) so that what was upon it, of dust &c., fell off, (Mgh,) or so that the dust and the like became removed from it. definition: (tropical:) A company sent forth into the land to see whether there be in it an enemy, (S, K,) or not, (K,) or any [ cause of ] fear;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) A company sent forth into the land to see whether there be in it an enemy, (S, K,) or not, (K,) or any [ cause of ] fear; (S;) like TaliyEapN ; (S, TA;) as also ↓ nafaDapN ; [pl. of ↓ naAfiDN , like as TalabapN is of TaAlibN :] (S, K:) or the former signifies men going before an army as scouts, or explorers: (As, in TA, voce HaDiyrapN :) or men who explore a place thoroughly: and also, a single person: (A 'Obeyd, in TA, ibid.:) or a scout, or scouts, stationed on a mountain or other elevated place: (TA:) or one who guards the road: (A, TA:) or a company [ of men ]: (TA:) and ↓ the latter, persons who clear the roads of robbers and of intercepters of travellers; or who guard the roads; (A, TA:) the pl. of the former is nafaAy^iDu ; (S;) which also signifies persons who throw pebbles in order to know if there be behind them anything that they dislike, or an enemy. (K.) ― -b2- Also, the pl., (assumed tropical:) Lean, or emaciated, camels; (S, K:) accord to AA, as occurring in a verse of Aboo-Dhu-eyb, in which he says, tuloqiY Aln~afaAy^iDu fiyhi Als~ariyHaA (S, TA,) In which the lean, or emaciated, camels cast the shoes; meaning that these have become dissundered; or, as Akh says, the thongs so called [ by which their shoes are fastened ], these being dissundered; fyh referring to the road; but some read, fiyhaA , referring to the roads, mentioned before: (TA:) As reads nfAy^D , as well as AA: (S, TA:) but others read the word with q , as pl. of niqoDN , and signifying “ jaded ” camels: (so in a copy of the S:) or nfAy^D signifies camels which traverse the land. (IAar, K.) ― -b3- The sing. is also said to signify Waters where there is not any one. (IAar, Sh; both in the TA. voce HaDiyrapN , q. v., and the former also in this art.)

definition: [ A wailing woman ]: (Msb:) pl.
sourceDefinition: [ A wailing woman ]: (Msb:) pl. nawaAy^iHu and naAy^iHaAtN : and you also say ↓ nisaA='N nawoHN , and A^anowaAHN , and ↓ nuw~aHN : (S, K:) nawaAy^iHu is an epithet applied to women who assemble in a manaAHap : and ↓ manaAHapN (also) and ↓ nawoHN signify women who assemble together for the purpose of mourning. definition: and waraA='u and waraA='i , indecl.
sourceDefinition: and waraA='u and waraA='i , indecl., (K,) an adverbial noun of place or time: (Bd, &c.:) J mentions it in art. wrY , regarding the as substituted for Y ; and this is the opinion of the Koofees, and of all writers on inflexion, though disapproved by F, who, however, mentions it again in art. wrY as though belonging to that art.: (TA:) Behind: and, contr., before. (K.) In like manner, AlwaraA='u [ The location that is behind, or beyond; and the time past: and, contr. that is before, or preceding ]. (K.) Or it does not bear contr. meanings; but one meaning; namely, what is concealed from one. (K, art. wrY .) Or it is a homonym; [but not a word of contr. meanings; as it signifies what is behind, or beyond, in respect of place, and what is before in respect of time ]. Fr. says, It is not allowable to say, of a man behind thee, that he is bayona yadayoka ; nor of a man before thee, that he is waraA='ak ; these expressions being only allowable [as synonymous] in cases relating to particular times of events or actions: thus one may say, waraA='aka barodN $adiydN and bayona yadayoka brd $dyd [meaning Before thee is intense cold ]: each of these expressions is allowable because the intense cold is a thing that is coming; so, as it will overtake thee, it is, as it were, behind thee; and as thou wilt attain to the period thereof, it is, as it were, before thee. It is said in the Kur, [xviii. 78,] kaAna waraA='ahumo malikN There was before them a king: [because it has reference to a certain period, which might be said to be before them as they would attain to it, and behind them as it would overtake them: this passage Jelál-ed-Deen explains by saying, “ there was behind them when they returned, and before them now, a king. ”] Of the same kind also is the phrase min waraAy^ihi jahan~amu [Kur, xiv. 19,] Before him is hell: [for the same reason]. (TA.) ― -b2- wayakofuruwna bimA waraA='ahu , [Kur, ii. 85,] signifies And they disbelieve in what [ hath been revealed ] beside that: syn. siwaAhu : (IAar:) or it may mean after that. (Jel.) ― -b3- wrA' is masc. and fem. (TA.) Its dim. is wuray~iy^apN , (K,) accord. to those who hold the to be a radical letter, not substituted for Y ; namely, the Basrees: accord. to others, wuray~apN and wuraY~N . (TA.) ― -b4- [See also art. wrY .] ― -b5- rajulN maAniEN maA waraA='a Zhorihi : see zab~uwnapN . ― -b6- waraA='N A son's son, or son's offspring. (K.) ― -b7- waraA='N Bulky, and thick in the A^alowaAH , or shoulder-blades. (AAF.)

definition: It (lightning) flashed, gleamed, or shone, slightly, (S, A, Msb, K,) not extending sideways in the adjacent tracts of cloud;
sourceDefinition: It (lightning) flashed, gleamed, or shone, slightly, (S, A, Msb, K,) not extending sideways in the adjacent tracts of cloud; (S, K;) for when it does thus, it is termed xafowN ; and when it extends high in the sky, without extending sideways to the right and left, it is termed EaqiyqapN : (S:) it is also said of other things, beside lightning: (M:) and ↓ wamaDa , (S, M, A, Msb, K,) aor. yamiDu , (S, Msb, K,) inf. n. wamiyDN and wamoDN (S, M, A, K) and wamaDaAnN (S, A, K) and tawomaADN , (M,) signifies the same; (S, M, A, Msb, K;) or it (lightning) flashed faintly or weakly, and then disappeared, and then flashed again; (IAar;) and is also, sometimes, said of fire, (M, TA,) and of anything of a clear [or bright] colour: (El-' Eyn:) or both verbs signify it (lightning) gleamed, or shone. (Ham, p. 785.) ― -b2- Hence, A^awomaDati AlmaroA^apu (tropical:) The woman smiled, so as to display her teeth: the glistening of her front teeth being likened to the flashing of lightning. (A, TA.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) The woman stole a glance, or glances; (S, M, K;) as also AwmDt biEayonihaA : (A:) or this last,(assumed tropical:) the woman looked, or gazed with widely opened eyes. (L.) ― -b4- And AwmD lahu biEayonihi (assumed tropical:) He made a sign to him with his eye: (M:) or AwmD fulaAnN (tropical:) such a one made a private, or secret, sign, (K, TA,) A_ilay~a to me. (TA.) -A2- Also, He saw the slight flashing, or gleaming, or shining, of lightning, or of fire. (M, TA.)

definition: Shields, of the kind called tirosapN , (K,) pl.
sourceDefinition: Shields, of the kind called tirosapN , (K,) pl. of turosN ; or of the kind called daraqN , as is said in the R and M; which two kinds differ in this, that the drq , like the Hajaf , are of skin, or leather, without any wood or sinews (or nerves), whereas trs is a more general appellation: (TA:) or coats of defence, syn. duruwEN , (K,) of the fabric of El-Yemen: (TA:) made [app. whether shields or coats of defence] of skins; (K;) i. e., of the hides of camels: (TA:) or coats of defence ( drwE ) of the fabric of ElYemen, made of skins sewed together: a coll. gen. n., of which the n. un. is yalabapN : 'Amr Ibn Kulthoom says: EalayonaA AlbayoDu waAlyalabu AlyamaAniY waA^asoyaAfN yaqumona wayanoHaniynaA [ Upon us ( were ) helmets, and leathern coats of defence of the fabric of El-Yemen, and swords that are straight (so accord. to the above reading, of yaqumona , which I find in an excellent copy of the S: but some read yuqamona , which, I think, affords not so good a sense:) and that curve ]: (S:) or helmets made of camel's hides: [see also A^alabN and A^alabapN :] or [ head-coverings made of ] plaited thongs of leather ( nusuwEN ) woven together, which are put on the head in lieu of the helmet: (TA:) or skins which are sewed together, and worn on the head, specially: (K:) or skins which are worn beneath the [ kind of coat called ] diroE , or [ beneath that of ] diybaAj ; one of which is called yalabapN : or skins which are worn like the coats of defence called drwE : or skins of which such coats are made: (TA:) or any defensive coverings, or armour, of skins; not of iron; and hence, shields ( daraqN ) [ of skins ] are thus called: a poet says, Ealayohimo kul~u saAbigapiK dilaASK wafiY A^ayodihimi Alyalabu AlmudaAru [ Upon them ( are, or were, ) all ( kinds of ) ample coats of mail, smooth and glistening; and in their hands, round shields of skins ]: and yalabN , originally is a name of that skin [ of which such coverings are made ]: Aboo-Dahbal El-Jumahee says, diroEiY dilaASN $ak~uhaA $ak~N Eajabo wajawobuhaA AlqaAtiru mino sayori Aloyalabo [ My coat of mail is smooth and glistening: its cleaving (or sticking close ) is an admirable cleaving: and its shield, of good dimensions, is of strips of skin: so accord. to explanations in the S, in arts. $k and qtr : but I incline to think that jwbhA here is the same as jayobuhaA ; and that a word is understood, which makes the meaning to be its opening at the neck and bosom, of good dimensions, is bordered with an edge of thongs ]: (S:) or simply skin, or hide. (K.) ― -b2- Also defensive coverings, or armour, of pieces of felt ( lubuwd ), with a stuffing of honey ( Easal ) and sand. (K.) ― -b3- Also, Steel; (K;) pure iron: (ISh, T, K:) n. un. yalabapN . (TA.) Of this signification, the following hemistich is cited as an ex., wamiHowarN A^axolaSu man m~aA'i Alyalaba [ And a pulley-axis clearer ( in its brightness ) than the lustre of pure iron, or steel ]: but ISk says that it is by an Arab of the desert, who, hearing the verse of 'Amr Ibn-Kulthoom quoted above, erroneously supposed ylb to signify the most excellent kind of iron; and IDrd also asserts that the meaning assigned to it in this hemistich is founded upon a mistake. (TA.) See also A^alabapN . ― -b4- Also, Anything great, big, or large in size. (K.)

(K;) i. e., of the hides of camels: (TA:) or coats of defence ( drwE ) of the fabric of ElYemen, made of skins sewed together: a coll. gen. n., of which the n. un. is yalabapN : 'Amr Ibn Kulthoom says: EalayonaA AlbayoDu waAlyalabu AlyamaAniY waA^asoyaAfN yaqumona wayanoHaniynaA [ Upon us ( were ) helmets, and leathern coats of defence of the fabric of El-Yemen, and swords that are straight (so accord. to the above reading, of yaqumona , which I find in an excellent copy of the S: but some read yuqamona , which, I think, affords not so good a sense:) and that curve ]: (S:) or helmets made of camel's hides: [see also A^alabN and A^alabapN :] or [ head-coverings made of ] plaited thongs of leather ( nusuwEN ) woven together, which are put on the head in lieu of the helmet: (TA:) or skins which are sewed together, and worn on the head, specially: (K:) or skins which are worn beneath the [ kind of coat called ] diroE , or [ beneath that of ] diybaAj ; one of which is called yalabapN : or skins which are worn like the coats of defence called drwE : or skins of which such coats are made: (TA:) or any defensive coverings, or armour, of skins; not of iron; and hence, shields ( daraqN ) [ of skins ] are thus called: a poet says, Ealayohimo kul~u saAbigapiK dilaASK wafiY A^ayodihimi Alyalabu AlmudaAru [ Upon them ( are, or were, ) all ( kinds of ) ample coats of mail, smooth and glistening; and in their hands, round shields of skins ]: and yalabN , originally is a name of that skin [ of which such coverings are made ]: Aboo-Dahbal El-Jumahee says, diroEiY dilaASN $ak~uhaA $ak~N Eajabo wajawobuhaA AlqaAtiru mino sayori Aloyalabo [ My coat of mail is smooth and glistening: its cleaving (or sticking close ) is an admirable cleaving: and its shield, of good dimensions, is of strips of skin: so accord. to explanations in the S, in arts. $k and qtr : but I incline to think that jwbhA here is the same as jayobuhaA ; and that a word is understood, which makes the meaning to be its opening at the neck and bosom, of good dimensions, is bordered with an edge of thongs ]: (S:) or simply skin, or hide. (K.) ― -b2- Also defensive coverings, or armour, of pieces of felt ( lubuwd ), with a stuffing of honey ( Easal ) and sand. (K.) ― -b3- Also, Steel; (K;) pure iron: (ISh, T, K:) n. un. yalabapN . (TA.) Of this signification, the following hemistich is cited as an ex., wamiHowarN A^axolaSu man m~aA'i Alyalaba [ And a pulley-axis clearer ( in its brightness ) than the lustre of pure iron, or steel ]: but ISk says that it is by an Arab of the desert, who, hearing the verse of 'Amr Ibn-Kulthoom quoted above, erroneously supposed ylb to signify the most excellent kind of iron; and IDrd also asserts that the meaning assigned to it in this hemistich is founded upon a mistake. (TA.) See also A^alabapN . ― -b4- Also, Anything great, big, or large in size. (K.)

definition: A herd, troop, or drove;
sourceDefinition: A herd, troop, or drove; a distinct collection or number; of beasts, &c.; a flock, or bevy, of sheep, birds, &c.; a party, or group, or collection, of men, &c.; a pack of dogs. The term “ herd ” is applied to “ a collective number ” of camels by several good writers. We say a “ flock ” of sheep, and of geese; and “ herd ” or rather “ herd ” of goats; and a “ herd ” of oxen or kine, of camels, and of swine, and of antelopes; and a “ swarm ” of bees, &c. ― -b2- qaTiyEN A whip cut from the skin of a camel. ― -b3- qaTiyEapN A portion of land held in fee. definition: as used by the Arabs, [ A mile: ] The distance to which the eye reaches along land: accord.
sourceDefinition: as used by the Arabs, [ A mile: ] The distance to which the eye reaches along land: accord. to the ancient astronomers, three thousand cubits: accord to the moderns, four thousand cubits: but the difference is merely verbal; for they agree that its extent is ninety-six thousand digits; [about 5166 English feet;] each digit being the measure of six barley-corns, each placed with its belly next to another; but the ancients say that the cubit is thirty-two digits; which makes the mile three thousand cubits. (Msb, which see for more.) See also muTolibN ― -b2- myilN i. q. mulomuwlN , [ A style ]. (K.)
